families.name: Compute
families.plain: Renting the machines, or renting the moments of machine time, that run your code.

families.name: Containers & Kubernetes
families.plain: Packing an app into a shipping box and having someone run fleets of boxes for you.

families.name: Storage
families.plain: Places to keep bytes: files, disks, buckets and tape-priced archives.

families.name: Databases
families.plain: Managed places to keep structured data, each shaped for a different kind of question.

families.name: Data & analytics
families.plain: Moving, cleaning, storing and questioning large amounts of data.

families.name: AI, ML & agents
families.plain: Training, hosting and calling models, and now running the agents built on them.

families.name: Networking & delivery
families.plain: Private networks, the doors into them, and getting bytes to users fast.

families.name: Security & identity
families.plain: Who may do what, keys and secrets, and spotting trouble.

families.name: Developer tools & DevOps
families.plain: Writing, building, testing and shipping code.

families.name: Management & operations
families.plain: Watching, controlling and paying for what you run.

families.name: Application integration
families.plain: Letting separate programs talk: queues, events, APIs and workflows.

families.name: Migration & hybrid
families.plain: Getting from the old data centre into the cloud, and running across both.

families.name: End user, web & mobile
families.plain: Desktops, apps, messages and the front doors people actually touch.

families.name: Industry & specialised
families.plain: IoT, media, games, quantum, satellites and other corners.

rows.plain: Renting a computer by the hour that lives in someone else's data centre, like leasing a flat instead of building a house.

aws.name: Amazon EC2
aws.note: The original rentable server, with hundreds of instance types across Intel, AMD, Graviton Arm and accelerator families. You pick a shape, an image and a purchase option: on-demand, Savings Plan, Reserved or Spot.
pros: Widest choice of instance types, regions and purchase options anywhere
Graviton Arm instances cost up to a fifth less than x86 for the same performance
Deepest ecosystem of images, agents and third-party tooling
cons: Discounts require one or three year commitments you must forecast
Sixty-second minimum per instance start hurts very short-lived jobs
Instance family sprawl makes right-sizing a permanent chore

gcp.name: Compute Engine
gcp.note: Google's VM service, notable for custom machine shapes that dial in vCPU and memory separately. Live migration moves running VMs off hosts needing maintenance without a reboot, and sustained-use discounts apply automatically on N1, N2, C2 and M series, not E2, C3 or Tau.
pros: Automatic sustained-use discounts with no commitment paperwork
Custom machine types stop you paying for memory you do not need
Live migration keeps VMs up through host maintenance
cons: Smaller instance catalogue and fewer regions than AWS
Resource-based commitments are tied to a region and machine family
Default quotas are low and quota increases take time

azure.name: Azure Virtual Machines
azure.note: Azure's VM service with sizes grouped into series letters (B, D, E, F, N and so on). Its edge is Windows and SQL Server licensing: Azure Hybrid Benefit lets you bring on-premises licences and cut the bill sharply.
pros: Azure Hybrid Benefit reuses existing Windows and SQL Server licences
Reserved instances can be cancelled within a yearly refund cap; exchanges end 1 February 2027
Tight integration with Entra ID and Microsoft management tooling
cons: Capacity for popular sizes is regularly constrained in busy regions
Size naming and the quota model are harder to learn than rivals
Linux-first teams find fewer idiomatic tools and images

rows.pick: Interchangeable for a plain Linux server. Choose Azure when Windows Server or SQL Server licences are already paid for, GCP when workloads are bursty and you refuse to forecast commitments, AWS when you need an unusual instance type or region.
rows.gotcha: GCP bills per second and discounts automatically the longer a machine runs. GCP and Azure both live-migrate most VMs through host maintenance; only AWS still expects you to design for reboots, and AWS and Azure want one- or three-year commitments for the deepest discounts.

rows.job: VM fleets that grow and shrink
rows.plain: A group of identical servers that automatically adds machines when busy and removes them when quiet, like a supermarket opening more tills at lunchtime.

aws.name: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling
aws.note: Auto Scaling groups keep a fleet of EC2 instances at a target size and replace unhealthy ones. Launch templates define the instance; policies react to CloudWatch metrics, schedules or predictive forecasts, and mixed-instance policies blend Spot with on-demand.
pros: Predictive scaling and warm pools cut cold-start lag
Mixed instance policies blend Spot and on-demand in one group
Free: you pay only for the instances
cons: Attaching to load balancers and target groups is extra wiring
Instance refresh for new images is slow and fiddly
Regional only; multi-region fleets need separate groups

gcp.name: Managed instance groups
gcp.note: A Compute Engine feature rather than a separate product: a MIG stamps VMs from an instance template and autoscales on CPU, load-balancer serving capacity or custom metrics. Regional MIGs spread across zones and attach natively as backends of Cloud Load Balancing.
pros: Regional MIGs spread across zones with one setting
Native backend for the global load balancer
Rolling updates and canaries built into the group
cons: Autoscaler signals are fewer than CloudWatch offers
Stateful MIGs exist but are clumsy for databases
Template changes require a new template version each time

azure.name: Virtual Machine Scale Sets
azure.note: Scale sets create and autoscale groups of identical VMs; Flexible orchestration mode mixes sizes and lets you attach existing VMs. Autoscale rules live in Azure Monitor, and Azure Compute Fleet (2025) adds allocation strategies across sizes, zones and pricing models.
pros: Flexible orchestration mixes VM sizes in one set
Automatic OS image upgrades and instance repairs
Azure Compute Fleet handles very large mixed-pricing fleets
cons: Autoscale rules are configured in Azure Monitor, a separate surface
Uniform mode caps at one thousand instances per set
Scale-in can be slow and is throttled by default

rows.pick: Interchangeable: all three keep N copies of a VM alive and scale on metrics. Differences show at the edges, GCP for one-setting regional spread behind a global load balancer, AWS for predictive scaling and Spot blending.
rows.gotcha: GCP MIGs plug into the global load balancer natively. On AWS and Azure the load balancer, health check and scaling group are separate resources you wire together, and a health check mismatch is the usual reason a fleet flaps.

rows.plain: Hand over a piece of code and the cloud runs it only when something happens, charging by the millisecond, like a light that burns only when someone enters.

aws.name: AWS Lambda
aws.note: The service that defined serverless: upload code or a container image, wire it to an event source and pay per request and per millisecond of memory-time. Durable Functions and Managed Instances (2025) added long-running workflows and dedicated capacity.
pros: Richest set of native event sources across AWS
Per-millisecond billing with a generous free tier
Durable Functions now cover multi-step workflows without Step Functions
cons: Fifteen minute ceiling per invocation on standard Lambda; Managed Instances functions reach 90 minutes asynchronously
Cold starts hurt Java and .NET without provisioned concurrency
Deep coupling to AWS triggers makes code hard to move

gcp.name: Cloud Run functions
gcp.note: Since 2024 Cloud Functions is a deployment shape of Cloud Run: your function is built into a container and runs on the same platform as Cloud Run services. You get Cloud Run's concurrency, GPU and traffic-splitting features with a function-style programming model.
pros: Same platform as Cloud Run, so functions can grow into services
Concurrent requests per instance cut cost and cold starts
Sixty minute timeout for HTTP functions
cons: Fewer native triggers than Lambda; most arrive via Eventarc
Naming churn confuses documentation and tooling
Request-based or instance-based billing choice changes the cost maths

azure.name: Azure Functions
azure.note: Azure's event-driven functions with a bindings model that declares inputs and outputs in configuration rather than code. Hosting plans range from Consumption and Flex Consumption to Premium, or running inside App Service or Container Apps.
pros: Bindings model removes boilerplate for queues, blobs and Cosmos DB
Durable Functions offer mature stateful orchestration
Runs on Consumption, Premium, App Service or Container Apps plans
cons: Plan choice is confusing and affects limits and cold starts
Consumption plan drags in a storage account dependency
Runtime version upgrades have broken apps in the past

rows.pick: Interchangeable for glue code and event handlers. Lambda when the rest of the estate is AWS and triggers are native; Azure Functions for .NET shops and Durable Functions; Cloud Run functions when the function might become a full service.
rows.gotcha: Azure Functions matches Lambda closely; Google folded Cloud Functions into Cloud Run. The trap is concurrency: Lambda runs one request per instance, Cloud Run functions and Azure Functions handle many, so shared state and connection pools behave differently.

rows.plain: Give the cloud a packaged application and it runs and scales it with no servers to patch, like a kitchen cooking any dish you bring boxed.

aws.name: AWS Fargate
aws.note: Fargate is a capacity engine rather than a product: ECS or EKS schedules tasks and Fargate runs them without nodes. AWS App Runner, the push-a-container-get-a-URL option, closed to new customers in April 2026, so Fargate on ECS is the default path.
pros: No nodes to patch; pay per vCPU-second and GB-second of task
Works under both ECS and EKS
Spot pricing for Fargate tasks on ECS
cons: Needs an ECS or EKS definition, a load balancer and IAM before hello world
Costs more than EC2 for steady workloads
App Runner retiring leaves no simple source-to-URL option

gcp.name: Cloud Run
gcp.note: The simplest of the three: deploy a container image or source, get an HTTPS URL, scale to zero and pay per request or per instance. Services, jobs, worker pools (2026) and functions all share the platform, with GPUs available since 2025.
pros: Fastest path from container to URL of any cloud
Scale to zero and per-request billing suit spiky traffic
GPUs, jobs and worker pools cover batch and AI serving too
cons: Request timeout and one-process-per-container model limit some servers
Reaching private Google networking needs a VPC connector or direct egress
Portable only in principle; Knative serving on GKE is not the same product

azure.name: Azure Container Apps
azure.note: Container Apps runs microservices, jobs and AI apps on a managed Kubernetes-based environment you never see, with KEDA scaling and optional Dapr sidecars. Azure Container Instances is the lower-level option for a single container group on demand.
pros: KEDA scalers scale on queues, Kafka or HTTP, not just CPU
Dapr sidecars for service invocation, state and pub/sub
Revisions and traffic splitting for blue-green releases
cons: Environment and networking setup is heavier than Cloud Run
Consumption plan fixes vCPU and memory ratios you cannot escape
Container Instances lacks autoscaling and load balancing

rows.pick: Cloud Run is the obvious choice for a stateless web service on GCP. On AWS, Fargate on ECS is the mainstream path now that App Runner is retiring; on Azure, Container Apps for microservices and Container Instances for one-off containers.
rows.gotcha: Cloud Run is the simplest to adopt; Container Apps covers the longer-running cases that need Fargate on AWS. Cloud Run scales to zero by default and Fargate does not by default, though a service auto scaling policy with a minimum of zero can get an idle service there, so an idle Fargate service still bills for a running task.

rows.plain: Upload your website code and the platform handles servers, runtimes and scaling, like renting a furnished, serviced office rather than an empty shell.

aws.name: AWS Elastic Beanstalk
aws.note: Beanstalk wraps EC2, Auto Scaling and a load balancer around your application in a supported runtime. It is stable and free to use, but AWS invests little in it and most new work goes to ECS on Fargate or Lambda.
pros: No extra charge beyond the EC2 resources it creates
Full access to the underlying instances when you need it
Supports Docker, Java, .NET, Node, Python, Ruby, Go and PHP
cons: Feature development has largely stopped
Platform version upgrades can break deployments
Hides then leaks infrastructure, so debugging means learning EC2 anyway

gcp.name: App Engine
gcp.note: Google's original platform, older than Compute Engine, with Standard (sandboxed, scale to zero) and Flexible (container on VMs) environments. First-generation runtimes were deprecated in 2026 and Google steers new projects to Cloud Run.
pros: Standard environment scales to zero and starts in milliseconds
Traffic splitting and versions built in
Legacy apps with a decade of uptime still run
cons: Legacy-leaning: new features land in Cloud Run instead
Standard runtime sandbox constrains libraries and networking
First-generation runtimes deprecated in 2026, forcing migrations

azure.name: Azure App Service
azure.note: Still central on Azure: hosts web apps, APIs and containers on Windows or Linux plans with deployment slots, custom domains and managed certificates. It carries the Windows and .NET licence story and integrates deeply with Entra ID and Azure DevOps.
pros: Best home for .NET and Windows web apps anywhere
Deployment slots give zero-downtime swaps
Actively developed, with Container Apps as the sibling for microservices
cons: Plan-based billing charges for the plan even when idle
Networking integration and private endpoints add cost and complexity
Windows plans cost more than Linux for the same size

rows.pick: App Service is the obvious pick for a .NET or Windows web app and the only one of the three still growing. On AWS and GCP, new work usually skips the classic PaaS and lands on Fargate or Cloud Run.
rows.gotcha: App Service is the strongest; Beanstalk and App Engine are legacy-leaning. App Engine Standard scales to zero, while Beanstalk and App Service dedicated plans (Free and Shared tiers aside) keep at least one instance billing, which reverses the cost picture for low-traffic sites.

rows.plain: A queue that takes thousands of independent jobs, finds machines to run them and retries failures, like a print shop working through a stack of orders overnight.

aws.name: AWS Batch
aws.note: Queues jobs onto compute environments made of EC2, Spot, Fargate or EKS capacity, with job definitions, dependencies and array jobs. Slurm-style HPC clusters live in AWS Parallel Computing Service, covered in the HPC clusters row.
pros: No charge for the scheduler, only for the compute
Runs on EC2, Spot, Fargate or EKS from one queue
Array jobs and dependencies handle large parameter sweeps
cons: Compute environment tuning is opaque when jobs sit RUNNABLE
Container-only: every job needs an image
No MPI-friendly scheduler; that needs Parallel Computing Service

gcp.name: Batch
gcp.note: Google's newest batch scheduler (2022): submit jobs as scripts or containers and it provisions Compute Engine VMs, including Spot and GPUs, then tears them down. Cluster Director and Cluster Toolkit cover Slurm-style HPC.
pros: Script jobs need no container image
Provisions and deletes VMs per job, so nothing idles
Native Spot and GPU support with simple job specs
cons: Youngest of the three, with fewer scheduling features
Regional quotas often gate large runs
Little integration with third-party HPC schedulers

azure.name: Azure Batch
azure.note: Runs large parallel and HPC-style jobs on managed VM pools, with task dependencies, MPI support and application packages. Azure CycleCloud provides Slurm and other schedulers on top of Azure, see the HPC clusters row.
pros: Runs plain executables on Windows or Linux pools, containers optional
Built-in MPI multi-instance tasks
Spot pools cut costs, though they need a user subscription Batch account
cons: Pool sizing and autoscale formulas are arcane
Slower to provision than rivals for short bursts
Windows pool licences add cost

rows.pick: Interchangeable for embarrassingly parallel work: the choice follows where the data already sits. Azure Batch if jobs are Windows executables; GCP Batch if you want to skip containers; AWS Batch if the estate already runs ECS or EKS.
rows.gotcha: All three schedule bulk compute onto cheap interruptible capacity, so the pricing model matters more than the scheduler. None of them saves job state on a Spot reclaim, so a long job on cheap capacity must write its own checkpoints or restart from zero.

rows.plain: Spare machines sold at a steep discount on the condition that the cloud can take them back at short notice, like standby airline tickets.

aws.name: EC2 Spot Instances
aws.note: A purchase option of EC2 rather than a service: unused capacity at up to ninety per cent off, priced by a slowly moving market per instance pool. You get a two-minute interruption notice, and rebalance recommendations arrive earlier.
pros: Deepest discounts and the largest pool of spare capacity
Two-minute warning plus earlier rebalance signals
Integrated with Auto Scaling, ECS, EKS and Batch
cons: Prices float with demand, so budgets are estimates
Popular GPU pools are often empty
Diversifying across instance types is mandatory for stability

gcp.name: Spot VMs
gcp.note: Compute Engine's interruptible successor to preemptible VMs, with published discounts of up to 91 per cent that can change at most once a day. Pre-emption gives a best-effort shutdown of up to thirty seconds (a 120-second notice is in preview) with no 24-hour maximum runtime.
pros: Predictable, published discounts rather than a live market
No 24-hour cap, unlike the old preemptible VMs
Works with MIGs, GKE and Batch
cons: Only thirty seconds of warning
Smaller spare pools in less popular regions
No rebalance-style early signal

azure.name: Azure Spot Virtual Machines
azure.note: Discounted spare capacity for VMs and scale sets, evicted when Azure needs the capacity or the price exceeds a maximum you set. You choose between deallocate and delete eviction policies and receive a thirty-second notice via Scheduled Events.
pros: Set a maximum price to cap what you pay
Deallocate policy keeps disks for quick restarts
Spot priority mix in scale sets blends with regular VMs
cons: Thirty-second eviction notice
Eviction rates in constrained regions can be brutal
Not available for B-series and some promotional sizes

rows.pick: Interchangeable for fault-tolerant, stateless or checkpointed work. GCP if you want a discount you can put in a budget spreadsheet; AWS if you need the deepest pools and the longest warning; Azure if you want a hard price cap.
rows.gotcha: GCP Spot prices change at most once a day while AWS Spot prices float with demand. Warning windows differ: AWS gives two minutes, Azure thirty seconds and GCP a best-effort thirty (a 120-second notice is in preview), so write save-and-exit code for the shortest warning.

rows.plain: Renting a whole physical server for yourself instead of a slice shared with strangers, usually because a software licence or regulator insists on it.

aws.name: Amazon EC2 Dedicated Hosts
aws.note: Dedicated Hosts are physical servers reserved for your EC2 instances, with socket and core visibility for licensing; Dedicated Instances are a lighter tenancy flag. Bare metal instance types (the .metal sizes) give the whole box with no hypervisor.
pros: Socket and core visibility satisfies Windows and Oracle licence audits
Bare metal sizes exist in most modern instance families
Host affinity and auto-placement reduce manual juggling
cons: You pay for the host whether instances are running or not
Capacity for a specific host type may not exist in your zone
Dedicated tenancy raises the bill without any performance benefit

gcp.name: Sole-tenant nodes
gcp.note: Sole-tenant nodes are Compute Engine hosts reserved for your project, with node affinity labels and optional CPU overcommit. Bare Metal Solution, its non-virtualised hardware option, is now allowlist-only for existing customers; new Oracle estates are steered to Oracle Database@Google Cloud.
pros: Per-node pricing includes sustained-use style discounts
Live migration still works within your node group
CPU overcommit can recover cost on bursty VMs
cons: Bare Metal Solution is allowlist-only for existing customers; new estates cannot get it
Limited node types compared with EC2 host types
Bring-your-own-licence rules for Windows are stricter

azure.name: Azure Dedicated Host
azure.note: Physical servers dedicated to one subscription that host your normal Azure VMs, chosen by SKU family and priced per host. Azure Hybrid Benefit applies, and maintenance control lets you schedule platform updates within a window.
pros: Hybrid Benefit makes it the cheapest legal home for Windows Server Datacenter
Maintenance control gives a 35-day window for updates
Fault domain placement across hosts is explicit
cons: Host SKU choice limits which VM sizes you can place
Billing is per host, idle or not
No true bare-metal instance option for general workloads

rows.pick: Pick by licence term, not technology. AWS for bare metal (.metal sizes) and hypervisor work; Azure for Windows Server licensing; GCP sole-tenant nodes for Compute Engine estates, Oracle Database@Google Cloud for stubborn Oracle now Bare Metal Solution is allowlist-only.
rows.gotcha: Physical isolation usually answers a licence clause, not a technical need. The trap is capacity: a dedicated host is a specific SKU in a specific zone, and when it sells out you cannot fall back to shared tenancy without breaking the licence argument.

rows.plain: Running your existing VMware virtual machines on hardware inside a public cloud, so you can move without rewriting anything, like towing your caravan to a new campsite.

aws.name: VMware Cloud on AWS
aws.note: vSphere, vSAN and NSX on dedicated AWS bare-metal hosts, with AWS services next door. Since 2024 the offer is sold and supported by Broadcom rather than AWS, which changed pricing, licensing and the buying relationship.
pros: Mature since 2017 with proven large-scale migrations
Direct access to AWS services from the same VPC
Elastic DRS adds and removes hosts automatically
cons: Sold through Broadcom since 2024, so pricing and roadmap sit outside AWS
Multi-host minimums make small footprints expensive
Costly per host compared with native EC2

gcp.name: Google Cloud VMware Engine
gcp.note: A Google-operated vSphere stack on dedicated nodes with NSX-T and vSAN, sold and billed by Google. Private clouds start at three nodes, with a single-node option that has no time limit but no SLA, and Google bundles the VMware licences into the node price.
pros: Google sells and supports it, so one bill and one support desk
VMware licences bundled into the node price
Fast provisioning, often under an hour
cons: Fewer regions than Azure VMware Solution
Node types are limited
Thinner migration partner ecosystem than Azure or AWS

azure.name: Azure VMware Solution
azure.note: Native vSphere clusters on Azure bare metal, operated by Microsoft with NSX and vSAN, and eligible for Azure Hybrid Benefit and reserved pricing. It has the largest regional footprint of the three and the deepest partner ecosystem for lift-and-shift programmes.
pros: Widest regional footprint and reserved-instance pricing
Extended Security Updates for old Windows Server run free here
Microsoft owns the whole relationship including VMware licences
cons: Three-node minimum and per-node cost is high
Capacity in some regions requires advance requests
NSX networking adds a learning curve for Azure-native teams

rows.pick: Azure VMware Solution is the obvious choice for a Windows-heavy estate on a deadline: most regions, Hybrid Benefit and Microsoft holding the contract. Google if you want Google to own it; VMware Cloud on AWS if you buy from Broadcom.
rows.gotcha: Broadcom's VMware changes reshaped all three offers in 2024 and 2025. Only on AWS does the contract sit with Broadcom rather than the cloud; on Google and Azure the cloud bundles the VMware licence, which changes who you negotiate with when prices move.

rows.plain: Running small pieces of logic in the cloud's many local points of presence so requests are handled close to the user, like a receptionist in every branch.

aws.name: Lambda@Edge / CloudFront Functions
aws.note: Two tiers of code at CloudFront's edge. CloudFront Functions run sub-millisecond JavaScript for header and URL rewrites at every edge location, while Lambda@Edge runs full Node or Python functions at regional edge caches for heavier logic such as auth or A/B routing.
pros: Two tiers let you match cost to the job
CloudFront Functions bill per million invocations at very low cost
Lambda@Edge can call other AWS services
cons: Lambda@Edge deploys only from us-east-1 and propagates slowly
Tight size and duration limits, no environment variables on Lambda@Edge
Debugging across hundreds of locations is painful

gcp.name: Service Extensions
gcp.note: Google has no edge function runtime; Service Extensions insert WebAssembly plugins or callouts into Cloud Load Balancing and Media CDN data paths for header manipulation and routing. Anything heavier runs in Cloud Run behind Cloud CDN, in a region rather than at the edge.
pros: WebAssembly plugins run in the load balancer path with low latency
Callouts can reach your own gRPC service for complex logic
Cloud Run plus Cloud CDN covers most edge needs from a region
cons: Not a general-purpose edge function runtime
Plugins are limited to Rust, C++ and other Wasm-compiling languages
Fewer edge points of presence than CloudFront

azure.name: Azure Front Door
azure.note: Front Door's rules engine performs header, URL and redirect manipulation at the edge from configuration, but runs no customer code there. Compute lives in Azure Functions or Container Apps in a region; the classic Azure CDN retires in 2027.
pros: Rules engine covers redirects, rewrites and header logic without code
WAF and CDN in the same product
Private Link origins keep back ends off the internet
cons: No customer code at the edge at all
Premium tier needed for Private Link and managed rules
Rule complexity has hard limits per profile

rows.pick: AWS is the obvious choice when you genuinely need code at the edge: it alone has a programmable edge runtime. On GCP and Azure, do the rewrite in the load balancer and run logic in a region.
rows.gotcha: The word edge means different places: CloudFront Functions run in hundreds of locations, Lambda@Edge in about a dozen regional caches, and Google and Azure run your code in a region behind the CDN. Latency budgets built on one cloud's edge do not transfer.

rows.plain: Tightly coupled clusters with a job scheduler such as Slurm for simulations and model training that need many machines working in lockstep, like a rowing eight.

aws.name: AWS Parallel Computing Service
aws.note: Managed Slurm clusters (2024) where AWS runs the scheduler and you define node groups on EC2, EFA networking and shared storage such as FSx for Lustre. It succeeds the self-managed AWS ParallelCluster tooling for teams who want a supported control plane.
pros: Managed Slurm controller with AWS support
EFA networking and FSx for Lustre integrate directly
Node groups can mix instance types and Spot
cons: Per-cluster management fee on top of compute
Newer and less flexible than ParallelCluster
Limited to Slurm; no other scheduler options

gcp.name: Cluster Director
gcp.note: Cluster Director deploys and manages densely colocated accelerator clusters with Slurm or GKE as the scheduler, focused on AI training. Cluster Toolkit, the open-source successor to Cloud HPC Toolkit, builds classic HPC clusters from blueprints.
pros: Colocated capacity blocks for very large GPU and TPU jobs
Slurm or GKE as the scheduler on the same hardware
Cluster Toolkit blueprints are open source and reusable
cons: Two products with overlapping roles confuse newcomers
Cluster Director skews to AI; classic CPU HPC leans on the Toolkit
Renamed from Hypercompute Cluster in 2025

azure.name: Azure CycleCloud
azure.note: CycleCloud orchestrates HPC clusters on Azure with Slurm, PBS Pro, LSF or Grid Engine, autoscaling nodes as the queue fills. CycleCloud Workspace for Slurm simplifies deployment, and it pairs with InfiniBand-connected HPC VM sizes.
pros: Choice of Slurm, PBS Pro, LSF and Grid Engine
InfiniBand-connected HB and HC series are excellent for MPI
Free software; pay for the VMs
cons: You run the CycleCloud server VM yourself
Cluster templates use an unusual configuration format
Capacity for InfiniBand sizes needs advance requests

rows.pick: Azure CycleCloud is the obvious choice for classic MPI simulation with InfiniBand and a non-Slurm scheduler. Cluster Director for very large GPU training. Parallel Computing Service when the estate and data already sit in AWS.
rows.gotcha: The scheduler is the same Slurm everywhere, but the fast interconnect is not: EFA on AWS, InfiniBand on Azure and Google's own fabric behave differently for MPI collectives, so benchmark before assuming a tuned job moves across clouds.

rows.plain: A pipeline that bakes a fresh, patched server template on a schedule so new machines start clean, like a bakery producing tomorrow's bread every night.

aws.name: EC2 Image Builder
aws.note: Pipelines that build, test and distribute AMIs and container images from components you write or AWS provides, on a schedule or when a base image changes. Output can be shared across accounts and regions and integrates with Systems Manager and Inspector.
pros: Free: you pay only for the build instances and storage
Builds container images as well as AMIs
Cross-account and cross-region distribution built in
cons: Component YAML is verbose and AWS-specific
Slower than Packer for iterative work
Testing steps are limited to what runs on the build instance

gcp.note: No dedicated product. Compute Engine supports custom images and image families, and the community cloud-builders repository offers an unsupported Packer builder for Cloud Build, so the usual pattern is Packer in Cloud Build feeding an image family that MIGs consume.
pros: Image families give MIGs a rolling latest pointer
Packer in Cloud Build is portable and well documented
cons: You own the pipeline, testing and cleanup
No native image lifecycle automation beyond image families
gcp.none: Google offers no image pipeline service; teams use Packer with Compute Engine custom images, usually run from Cloud Build.

azure.name: Azure VM Image Builder
azure.note: Builds and customises VM images from marketplace or custom sources using Packer under the hood, with shell and PowerShell customisers, then publishes to Azure Compute Gallery. Runs in your subscription with a managed identity and integrates with Azure DevOps.
pros: Publishes straight into Azure Compute Gallery with versioning and replication
Packer-based, so existing HCL skills transfer
Windows customisers and Sysprep handled for you
cons: Build VM networking and the staging resource group are fiddly
Slow builds, often over half an hour for Windows
Errors surface as opaque Packer logs

rows.pick: Use the native builder where it exists: EC2 Image Builder on AWS, VM Image Builder on Azure, both free apart from build resources. On GCP, Packer in Cloud Build is the de facto standard and works fine.
rows.gotcha: Golden images are a cross-cloud trap because image formats, agent sets and boot conventions differ: an AMI is not a Compute Engine image is not an Azure managed image. Keep the build recipe cloud-neutral, Packer for instance, and the output cloud-specific.

rows.plain: Containers are sealed boxes holding one program and everything it needs. Kubernetes runs fleets of them: a control room (the control plane) tells worker machines (nodes) which boxes (pods) to run, and the cloud runs that control room for you.

aws.name: Amazon EKS
aws.note: Managed Kubernetes control plane with node groups, Fargate profiles and, since late 2024, Auto Mode, which provisions and patches nodes for you. Hybrid Nodes join on-premises machines to a cloud control plane, and EKS Anywhere runs clusters entirely on your hardware.
pros: Auto Mode removes node management, catching up with GKE Autopilot
Deep IAM integration with Pod Identity
Largest ecosystem of add-ons and vendor support
cons: Control plane fee per cluster-hour plus an Auto Mode uplift
Historically the most assembly required of the three
Upgrades and add-on version matrices demand attention

gcp.name: Google Kubernetes Engine
gcp.note: The most mature managed Kubernetes, from the company that wrote it. Autopilot mode manages nodes entirely and bills per pod; since 2025 GKE is a single tier with fleet management, Config Sync and Policy Controller included rather than a separate Enterprise SKU.
pros: Autopilot: no nodes, per-pod billing, hardened defaults
Fastest upstream version adoption and the best release channels
Fleets, Config Sync and Policy Controller now included
cons: Autopilot restricts privileged workloads and some DaemonSets
Control plane fee applies beyond one free zonal cluster
Google-specific extras such as Autopilot do not travel to other clouds

azure.name: Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)
azure.note: Managed Kubernetes with a free control plane tier and, since 2025, AKS Automatic, a preconfigured mode with node auto-provisioning and opinionated defaults. Kubernetes Fleet Manager coordinates upgrades and placement across many clusters.
pros: Free control plane tier for non-production clusters
AKS Automatic gives Autopilot-style defaults with Entra ID integration
Kubernetes Fleet Manager for multi-cluster estates
cons: Free tier has no uptime SLA
Add-on sprawl and node image update cadence need governance
Windows node pools remain second-class

rows.pick: Interchangeable in the sense that a Kubernetes manifest runs anywhere. GKE Autopilot is the obvious choice if you never want to see a node; otherwise choose the cloud where your identity, network and data already live.
rows.gotcha: GKE Autopilot manages nodes entirely; EKS Auto Mode and AKS Automatic followed in 2024 and 2025. Pricing shapes differ: Autopilot bills per pod request, Auto Mode adds a percentage to instance cost, AKS bills nodes plus an optional control plane fee.

rows.plain: A cloud's own, non-Kubernetes system for placing and running containers on a pool of machines, simpler than Kubernetes but only found in that cloud.

aws.name: Amazon ECS
aws.note: AWS's own orchestrator, older than EKS, with task definitions, services and clusters on EC2, Fargate or on-premises via ECS Anywhere. It is simpler than Kubernetes, free to use and deeply woven into IAM, ALB and CloudWatch.
pros: No control plane charge
Far fewer concepts than Kubernetes for a web service
First-class Fargate and IAM task role integration
cons: Complete AWS lock-in; task definitions run nowhere else
Smaller open-source ecosystem than Kubernetes
Service discovery and mesh options lag Kubernetes

gcp.note: No proprietary orchestrator. Cloud Run takes the simple stateless case and GKE the rest; Knative serving on GKE bridges the two for teams wanting Cloud Run semantics on their own cluster.
pros: Cloud Run is simpler than ECS for a stateless service
GKE Autopilot removes most node work an ECS user would fear
cons: Stateful or long-running ECS tasks land on GKE, a bigger learning curve
No single console that mirrors ECS clusters and services
gcp.none: Google never built one; Cloud Run covers simple services and GKE everything else, so an ECS estate maps to Cloud Run or GKE.

azure.name: Azure Service Fabric
azure.note: Microsoft's own distributed systems platform, running stateless and stateful services and containers on clusters, including managed clusters. It still underpins many Azure services, but Microsoft points new container work to Container Apps and AKS.
pros: Reliable Services and Actors give stateful patterns Kubernetes lacks
Runs on-premises and in Azure with the same model
Managed clusters remove most node operations
cons: Legacy-leaning: new investment goes to Container Apps and AKS
Steep programming model with a small community
Proprietary APIs lock in more deeply than ECS

rows.pick: ECS is the obvious choice on AWS for a team that finds Kubernetes too heavy. Service Fabric is only a pick for teams already invested in its stateful programming model; new Azure work goes to Container Apps.
rows.gotcha: Google has no proprietary orchestrator, and Azure's Service Fabric is legacy-leaning, with Microsoft steering new container work to Container Apps and AKS. Translating an ECS estate therefore means choosing Kubernetes or a serverless container service, each of which changes networking, identity and deployment tooling.

rows.plain: A private library where your built application images and software packages are stored, scanned for vulnerabilities and handed out to the machines that run them.

aws.name: Amazon ECR
aws.note: Private and public container image registries with Inspector-powered scanning, lifecycle policies, cross-region replication and pull-through caches. Language packages (npm, Maven, PyPI, NuGet) live in a separate service, AWS CodeArtifact.
pros: IAM-native auth; nodes pull with instance or pod roles
Pull-through cache for Docker Hub and other upstreams
Public gallery with generous free egress
cons: Images only; packages need CodeArtifact, a second bill and API
Repositories must exist before the first push unless a creation template enables create-on-push
Storage and cross-region egress add up for large images

gcp.name: Artifact Registry
gcp.note: One registry for container images and language packages: Docker, Maven, npm, Python, Go, apt and yum, with remote and virtual repositories. It replaced Container Registry, which shut down in March 2025, and pairs with Artifact Analysis for vulnerability scanning.
pros: Images and language packages in one product and one IAM model
Remote repositories proxy upstream sources with caching
Regional or multi-regional placement per repository
cons: Scanning is a separate charge via Artifact Analysis
Container Registry migration caught many teams out in 2025
Virtual repositories add indirection that confuses build tooling

azure.name: Azure Container Registry
azure.note: Private registry for images and OCI artifacts with geo-replication, ACR Tasks for building in the cloud and Defender for Containers scanning on any tier. Language packages live in Azure Artifacts, part of Azure DevOps.
pros: Geo-replication serves images from multiple regions under one name
ACR Tasks builds images without a CI runner
Entra ID and managed identity for pull auth
cons: Premium tier required for geo-replication and private endpoints
Packages live in Azure Artifacts, a separate product
Per-day storage pricing is easy to misread

rows.pick: Interchangeable: each cloud's registry is the right one for that cloud's runtimes because node identity, scanning and networking are wired in. Artifact Registry is the obvious pick if you want images and packages under one roof.
rows.gotcha: Artifact Registry also handles language packages, while AWS splits that into CodeArtifact and Azure into Azure Artifacts. Cross-cloud pulls cost egress and need credentials outside the native identity model, so mirror images into each cloud's own registry.

rows.plain: A layer that sits between your services to encrypt traffic, retry failures and record who called whom, like a switchboard operator for internal calls.

aws.name: Amazon VPC Lattice
aws.note: AWS App Mesh, the Envoy-based sidecar mesh, ends support on 30 September 2026. VPC Lattice is the replacement direction: an application-layer network that connects services across VPCs and accounts with IAM auth policies, without sidecars.
pros: No sidecars to operate; a managed data plane
Cross-account and cross-VPC service connectivity with IAM policies
Works for EC2, Lambda, ECS and EKS targets alike
cons: Not a mesh in the Istio sense: no mTLS between arbitrary pods
Per-hour and per-GB pricing adds up at high traffic
Regional; no multi-region service network

gcp.name: Cloud Service Mesh
gcp.formerName: Anthos Service Mesh and Traffic Director
gcp.note: Managed Istio with a Google-hosted control plane, formed in 2024 by merging Anthos Service Mesh and Traffic Director. It runs on GKE, on-premises GKE clusters and Compute Engine VMs, with sidecar or proxyless gRPC data planes.
pros: Most opinionated managed Istio anywhere
Managed control plane; Google upgrades it
Proxyless gRPC option avoids sidecar cost
cons: Istio complexity still surfaces in debugging
Pricing depends on control plane choice and is easy to misjudge
Renamed twice; documentation and samples lag

azure.name: Istio-based service mesh add-on for AKS
azure.note: An AKS add-on that installs and upgrades Istio with Microsoft support, replacing the Open Service Mesh add-on, unsupported from 30 September 2027 after the upstream project was retired. The control plane runs inside your cluster, closer to self-managed Istio with a supported install path.
pros: Supported Istio with managed upgrades and no extra licence
Standard Istio APIs, portable to any cluster
Integrates with AKS ingress and Entra Workload ID
cons: Control plane consumes your cluster's nodes
Lags upstream Istio releases
Single cluster focus; multi-cluster mesh is manual

rows.pick: Cloud Service Mesh is the obvious choice for a large GKE estate wanting managed Istio. On AWS, VPC Lattice suits cross-account connectivity rather than pod-level mTLS. Most teams on all three clouds do not need a mesh at all.
rows.gotcha: AWS App Mesh reaches end of support in 2026 and VPC Lattice is the replacement direction. Lattice is not Istio: it has no pod-to-pod mTLS or traffic mirroring, so an Istio design does not port to AWS without rethinking identity and observability.

rows.plain: Running the same cloud-managed Kubernetes experience on your own servers, at the edge or in another cloud, with one control console for all of it.

aws.name: Amazon EKS Anywhere
aws.note: EKS Anywhere creates and runs Kubernetes clusters on your own vSphere, bare metal, Nutanix or Snow hardware with AWS-supported tooling. EKS Hybrid Nodes (2024) takes the opposite shape: the control plane stays in AWS and your machines join as worker nodes.
pros: Two shapes: fully local clusters, or cloud control plane with local nodes
Consistent EKS Distro builds and tooling
Hybrid Nodes need only a VPN or Direct Connect route to the VPC
cons: EKS Anywhere is free but enterprise support is a paid subscription
You operate the on-premises control plane yourself
No managed presence in other public clouds

gcp.name: Google Distributed Cloud software only
gcp.formerName: Google Distributed Cloud Virtual (earlier Anthos clusters on bare metal and on VMware)
gcp.note: GKE on your own bare metal or VMware, formerly Anthos clusters, then Google Distributed Cloud Virtual under the GKE Enterprise umbrella, now Google Distributed Cloud's software-only tier. Fleets moved into plain GKE in 2025; GKE on AWS and Azure retire March 2027, leaving attached clusters.
pros: Same GKE tooling, Config Sync and Policy Controller on your hardware
Fleets now included in GKE, no Enterprise SKU
Air-gapped and connected hardware editions for sovereign sites
cons: Three renames in five years; documentation and skills lag
GKE on AWS and Azure retiring, so multi-cloud shrinks to attached clusters
Per-vCPU subscription pricing for on-premises clusters

azure.name: Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes
azure.note: Arc projects any CNCF-conformant cluster, on-premises or in another cloud, into Azure for policy, GitOps, monitoring and Defender. For new clusters on your hardware, AKS runs on Azure Local, and AKS Edge Essentials targets small edge devices.
pros: Manages clusters you already have, including EKS and GKE
Arc-enabled services such as SQL Managed Instance run on those clusters
AKS on Azure Local gives the same AKS experience on-premises
cons: Arc manages but does not create clusters; lifecycle stays with you
Arc is free; Policy, Defender and Monitor add-ons bill per vCPU, Azure Local per physical core
Feature parity between Arc, Azure Local and cloud AKS is uneven

rows.pick: Azure Arc is the obvious choice for one console over clusters you already run anywhere. Google Distributed Cloud when you want GKE itself on-premises, including air-gapped sites. EKS Hybrid Nodes when your data centre is just extra AWS capacity.
rows.gotcha: Arc is the odd one out: it manages clusters you already have rather than giving you new ones. Google's story has been renamed from Anthos to GKE Enterprise to Google Distributed Cloud, and its clusters on AWS and Azure retire in 2027.

rows.plain: OpenShift is Red Hat's opinionated, batteries-included version of Kubernetes; two clouds run it for you jointly with Red Hat, on one bill.

aws.name: Red Hat OpenShift Service on AWS
aws.note: ROSA: OpenShift clusters jointly operated by Red Hat and AWS site reliability engineers, billed through AWS. Hosted control planes (ROSA HCP) put the control plane in a Red Hat-managed account, cutting cost and provisioning time.
pros: One AWS bill including the OpenShift subscription
Hosted control planes lower cost and speed up cluster creation
Red Hat and AWS jointly on the hook for support
cons: OpenShift subscription roughly doubles the per-node price of EKS
Fewer regions than EKS
Opinionated platform constrains custom Kubernetes configuration

gcp.note: No Google-operated OpenShift. Red Hat sells and operates OpenShift Dedicated on Google Cloud infrastructure, or you self-manage OpenShift on Compute Engine; GKE is the Google-native path.
pros: GKE Autopilot delivers much of OpenShift's opinionated experience
Red Hat-operated OpenShift Dedicated still runs on Google infrastructure
cons: Two vendors and two bills if you go through Red Hat
No Google support desk for the OpenShift layer
gcp.none: Google does not sell a managed OpenShift; Red Hat's own OpenShift Dedicated runs on Google Cloud, and most teams use GKE.

azure.name: Azure Red Hat OpenShift
azure.note: ARO: OpenShift clusters jointly engineered, operated and supported by Microsoft and Red Hat, provisioned from the Azure portal and billed by Azure. It is the oldest of the joint offers (2019) and integrates with Entra ID and Azure Monitor.
pros: Single Azure bill and unified Microsoft and Red Hat support
Longest track record of the joint offers
Entra ID login and Azure Monitor integration out of the box
cons: Premium price over AKS for the OpenShift subscription
Slower to adopt new OpenShift versions than self-managed
Minimum cluster size makes small deployments expensive

rows.pick: Only a pick if your organisation has standardised on OpenShift and wants to keep developer tooling, operators and security policies intact. Then AWS and Azure are interchangeable; on Google Cloud you buy from Red Hat directly or move to GKE.
rows.gotcha: OpenShift on the cloud is Kubernetes with Red Hat's opinions, so plain manifests mostly work but OpenShift Routes and SecurityContextConstraints do not exist on EKS, GKE or AKS, and OperatorHub is OpenShift's own; operators themselves are ordinary Kubernetes. A move off OpenShift is a real migration, not a re-point.

rows.plain: A bottomless filing cabinet (a bucket) for files of any size, each fetched by name over the internet, paid for by the gigabyte kept and moved.

aws.name: Amazon S3
aws.note: The original object store, with storage classes from Express One Zone to Deep Archive under one API. Buckets are regional; multi-region access is built from replication plus Multi-Region Access Points, not from a single bucket.
pros: Deepest ecosystem: nearly every AWS and third-party tool speaks S3
Objects up to 50 TB, Metadata and Annotations make objects queryable
Fine-grained classes let cold data cost a fraction of hot
cons: Every class beyond Standard carries retrieval fees or minimum durations
Cross-region replication and egress are billed separately and add up
Requests are metered, so millions of tiny objects cost more than a few big ones

gcp.name: Cloud Storage
gcp.note: One bucket can be regional, dual-region or multi-region, replicated for you with a single endpoint. Classes Standard, Nearline, Coldline and Archive share millisecond access; Autoclass moves objects between them on observed use.
pros: Native multi-region buckets remove replication plumbing from the design
Autoclass tiers automatically with no lifecycle rules to write
Strong consistency and turbo replication across regions are built in
cons: Minimum storage durations of 30, 90 or 365 days on colder classes
Retrieval charges apply on colder classes even at millisecond latency
Fewer third-party tools speak the native API than speak S3

azure.name: Azure Blob Storage
azure.note: Object storage inside a storage account that also holds Files, Queues and Tables. Hot, cool, cold and archive tiers apply per blob, and redundancy is chosen per account rather than per bucket.
pros: Redundancy options from local to geo-zone-redundant with read access are one setting
Same account can switch on hierarchical namespace for analytics
Tight integration with Entra ID, Defender and Microsoft Fabric
cons: Storage account limits and quotas shape how you partition data
Cool and cold tiers charge early-deletion penalties within 30 or 90 days
Lifecycle tiering is rule-driven, so you write the policy yourself

rows.pick: Interchangeable for ordinary blob storage. Cloud Storage is the obvious choice when one bucket must serve two continents without you running replication; S3 wins when the surrounding tooling assumes S3.
rows.gotcha: One Cloud Storage bucket can be multi-region natively and every class keeps millisecond access; S3 buckets are regional and Glacier Flexible and Deep Archive need a thaw step. Blob archive also needs rehydration. Latency and replication assumptions do not port.

rows.plain: The virtual hard drive plugged into a cloud server: raw disk space the operating system formats and treats as its own.

aws.name: Amazon EBS
aws.note: Network-attached volumes for EC2 in gp3, io2 Block Express and throughput or cold HDD types, with snapshots landing in S3. Every volume lives in exactly one Availability Zone.
pros: gp3 sets IOPS and throughput independently of size
Snapshots are incremental, cross-region copyable and feed AMIs
io2 Block Express reaches very high IOPS with Multi-Attach for clustering
cons: Single-AZ only, so zone loss means restoring from snapshot
Billed for provisioned size whether or not the VM is running
Volume type and instance type together cap achievable performance

gcp.name: Hyperdisk
gcp.note: Current-generation block storage with IOPS and throughput dialled separately from capacity, plus Storage Pools that share provisioned performance. Persistent Disk remains for older machine families; both offer regional variants synchronously replicated across two zones.
pros: Regional disks survive a zone failure with synchronous replication
Performance is tuned independently of size, so small fast disks are possible
Storage Pools let many disks share one provisioned budget
cons: Hyperdisk is only available on newer machine series
Regional replication roughly doubles the storage bill
Two product lines with different limits complicate templates

azure.name: Azure Disk Storage
azure.note: Managed disks in Standard HDD, Standard SSD, Premium SSD, Premium SSD v2 and Ultra tiers, attached to VMs and snapshotted independently. Zone-redundant disks are available for some tiers.
pros: Premium SSD v2 and Ultra tune IOPS and throughput without resizing
Zone-redundant option for Premium and Standard SSD
Shared disks support Windows and Linux clustering
cons: Premium SSD bills in fixed size tiers, so you round up
Ultra and Premium v2 exclude some features such as OS disk use
Disks are billed while the VM is deallocated

rows.pick: Largely interchangeable. Google's regional disks are the obvious choice when a single VM must survive a zone loss without a restore step; on AWS that requirement forces snapshots or an application-level replica.
rows.gotcha: Persistent Disk and Hyperdisk can be regional, synchronously replicated across two zones; EBS is single-AZ, full stop. Azure zone-redundant disks exist for a subset of tiers. Any design that relies on a disk outliving its zone must change on AWS.

rows.plain: A shared network folder many Linux servers can mount at once, with the cloud running the file server for you.

aws.name: Amazon EFS
aws.note: Serverless NFS that grows and shrinks with the data and bills per gigabyte stored. Regional file systems span several Availability Zones; One Zone is cheaper for scratch or reproducible data.
pros: No capacity to provision; pay for what is stored
Multi-AZ by default, so a zone loss does not lose the share
Lifecycle moves cold files to Infrequent Access automatically
cons: Per-gigabyte price is several times block storage
Elastic and provisioned throughput charges are easy to underestimate
NFS only, no SMB path for Windows clients

gcp.name: Filestore
gcp.note: Provisioned-capacity NFS in Zonal, Regional and Enterprise (Multishares for GKE) tiers, plus legacy Basic HDD and SSD, where performance scales with the size you buy. Common as persistent volumes for GKE and for lift-and-shift Linux workloads.
pros: Predictable, provisioned performance with no throughput surprises
Regional tier replicates synchronously across zones
Simple GKE integration through the Filestore CSI driver
cons: Minimums of 100 GiB on Regional and 1 TiB or more elsewhere, paid even if unused
Capacity, not usage, drives the bill
Basic tier is zonal with limited snapshots and no replication

azure.name: Azure Files
azure.note: File shares in one storage account, offered over SMB and, on premium SSD shares, NFS 4.1. NFS shares need a private endpoint or VNet and use POSIX permissions rather than Entra identities.
pros: Same service serves Windows SMB and Linux NFS estates
Premium shares give provisioned IOPS with burst credits
Snapshots and Azure Backup integrate without extra agents
cons: NFS only on SSD shares, minimum 32 GiB on provisioned v2 (100 GiB on v1)
No identity-based access for NFS, network isolation is mandatory
Standard tier performance limits catch teams moving from Filestore

rows.pick: Interchangeable for an ordinary Linux share. EFS is the obvious choice when demand is unknown, since it needs no capacity planning; Filestore or premium Azure Files when steady, predictable throughput matters more than pay-per-use.
rows.gotcha: EFS bills on usage; Filestore and Azure SSD shares bill on provisioned capacity, with minimums of 32 GiB (Azure v2), 100 GiB (Filestore Regional) and 1 TiB (Filestore Zonal, Basic). A small EFS share ported literally becomes an over-provisioned invoice, and Filestore tiers by performance.

rows.plain: Shared drives for Windows machines and old-school enterprise apps, with domain permissions and the same NetApp appliance features on-premises admins already know.

aws.name: Amazon FSx
aws.note: Four managed file systems under one brand: Windows File Server for SMB with Active Directory, NetApp ONTAP for multi-protocol with SnapMirror, plus Lustre and OpenZFS. Provisioned capacity and throughput, single or Multi-AZ.
pros: Native Active Directory, DFS namespaces and shadow copies for Windows estates
ONTAP brings dedupe, thin cloning and replication from on-premises arrays
Multi-AZ options give a zone-failure story for file servers
cons: Four products with separate pricing, limits and consoles
Provisioned throughput and capacity are billed whether busy or idle
ONTAP and Windows variants need AD plumbing before first use

gcp.name: Google Cloud NetApp Volumes
gcp.note: Managed NetApp ONTAP delivering SMB, NFS and multi-protocol volumes in service levels from Flex to Extreme, with SnapMirror to on-premises ONTAP. Filestore has no SMB, so this is the SMB route on Google Cloud.
pros: Full ONTAP feature set: snapshots, replication, dedupe, Active Directory SMB
Multi-protocol volumes let Windows and Linux share one dataset
Familiar to on-premises NetApp administrators
cons: Only SMB option, so no cheaper native alternative
Capacity pools with minimum sizes and per-service-level pricing
Narrower regional footprint than Filestore

azure.name: Azure Files
azure.note: SMB shares with Entra ID or Active Directory Kerberos identities, snapshots and Azure File Sync to on-premises servers. Azure NetApp Files sits above it for ONTAP features and very high throughput.
pros: Identity-based access with on-premises or cloud Kerberos
Standard tier is pay-as-you-go, cheap for cold departmental shares
Azure NetApp Files covers the demanding SAP and ONTAP cases
cons: Standard shares have low IOPS and throughput ceilings
Provisioned v2 and premium pricing needs careful sizing
Azure NetApp Files is billed by capacity pool, not by usage

rows.pick: For a Windows file server, Azure Files or FSx for Windows are the obvious homes; Google Cloud only has NetApp Volumes. For a lift-and-shift that depends on ONTAP semantics, the same NetApp appliance exists in all three and is interchangeable.
rows.gotcha: The same NetApp appliance runs in all three, but only FSx for Windows and Azure Files offer a cheaper non-NetApp SMB share. A Windows workload ported to Google Cloud lands on NetApp Volumes whether or not it needs ONTAP, so the storage budget changes.

rows.plain: Deep storage for records you must keep but rarely open, priced like a warehouse rather than a desk drawer, with a fee when you fetch something.

aws.name: Amazon S3
aws.note: Archive lives in the S3 Glacier storage classes: Instant Retrieval in milliseconds, Flexible Retrieval in minutes to hours, Deep Archive in up to twelve hours. The standalone Glacier vault API is in maintenance; the classes continue.
pros: Deep Archive is the cheapest per-gigabyte tier of the three clouds
Same bucket and lifecycle rules as hot data
Object Lock gives regulatory write-once retention
cons: Flexible and Deep Archive need a restore step measured in hours
Minimum durations of 90 or 180 days plus retrieval fees
Restore requests and expedited retrievals are priced separately

gcp.name: Cloud Storage
gcp.note: Archive is a storage class of the same bucket, not a separate product. Data stays online at millisecond latency; you pay a retrieval fee per gigabyte and commit to a 365-day minimum.
pros: No thaw step, so archive data is readable in milliseconds
One API and bucket for hot and archive objects
Autoclass can demote to Archive without lifecycle rules
cons: 365-day minimum duration, early deletion is billed in full
Retrieval fees make frequent reads expensive
Per-gigabyte price is above Deep Archive

azure.name: Azure Archive Storage
azure.note: The archive tier of Blob Storage, an offline tier that must be rehydrated to hot or cool before reading. Standard rehydration takes hours; high priority is faster for small objects.
pros: Lowest Azure tier price, set per blob rather than per account
Rehydration priority is selectable per request
Immutable storage policies apply for compliance retention
cons: Offline: no read until rehydration completes, which can take hours
180-day minimum with early-deletion charges
Not available with every redundancy option

rows.pick: Cloud Storage Archive is the obvious choice when archived data must still be readable on demand, such as evidence or compliance lookups. Deep Archive wins on pure cost for data you truly expect never to read.
rows.gotcha: Archive class on Google Cloud keeps millisecond latency; you pay retrieval fees but never wait hours. Glacier Flexible, Deep Archive and Azure Archive are offline and need a restore job first. A disaster recovery plan built on one does not survive the move.

rows.plain: One place to set rules like 'copy everything nightly, keep 30 days' and have them applied to servers, databases and files automatically.

aws.name: AWS Backup
aws.note: Policy-based backup plans and vaults spanning EC2, EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, EFS, FSx, S3 and more, with cross-account and cross-region copies. Logically air-gapped vaults add ransomware isolation.
pros: One policy covers dozens of services, replacing per-service snapshot scripts
Cross-account, cross-region copies and vault lock for immutability
Tag-based assignment picks up new resources automatically
cons: Billed per gigabyte of backup storage plus restore charges
Coverage and restore granularity vary by service
Some services still keep native snapshot features outside AWS Backup

gcp.name: Backup and DR Service
gcp.note: Centralised backup with immutable backup vaults for Compute Engine, Cloud SQL, AlloyDB and databases in VMs, inherited from Actifio. Backup for GKE is a separate service for Kubernetes workloads.
pros: Immutable, indelible vaults with enforced retention
Application-consistent database backups including SAP and Oracle in VMs
Console-driven plans for Compute Engine need no appliance
cons: Younger and less uniform than the two rivals, with appliance-based paths for some workloads
Kubernetes lives in a separate product
Fewer supported managed services than AWS Backup or Azure Backup

azure.name: Azure Backup
azure.note: Recovery Services and Backup vaults protecting Azure VMs, SQL and SAP HANA in VMs, Azure Files, blobs, disks, PostgreSQL and AKS. On-premises Windows servers join through the MARS agent.
pros: Broad coverage including AKS and on-premises Windows servers
Soft delete on by default; immutable vaults are opt-in and can be locked
Long-term retention tiers for years-long compliance
cons: Billed per protected instance plus storage, which surprises at scale
Two vault types with different capabilities to learn
Restore of large VMs can be slow from the vault tier

rows.pick: Interchangeable, and almost always better than the per-service snapshot scripts they replace. Pick whichever cloud hosts the workload; cross-cloud backup is a job for third-party tools, not these three.
rows.gotcha: Backup and DR Service keeps Kubernetes in a separate Backup for GKE product and still uses appliances for some databases, while AWS Backup and Azure Backup are single control planes. Pricing also splits: per gigabyte on AWS, per instance plus storage on Azure.

rows.plain: Posting a rugged hard-drive box to the cloud provider because shipping a lorry of disks beats months of uploading over the network.

aws.name: AWS Snow Family
aws.note: Rugged Snowball Edge devices shipped to you, loaded, and returned for import into S3. Legacy devices were shut down in 2025 and remaining models are in maintenance; AWS Data Transfer Terminal locations are the newer path.
pros: Proven at petabyte scale with edge compute on the device
Data Transfer Terminal offers walk-in high-speed uploads instead
Encryption and chain of custody are handled end to end
cons: Retiring: closed to new device models, so avoid new commitments
Per-job and per-day device fees plus shipping
Terminal locations exist only in a few cities

gcp.name: Transfer Appliance
gcp.note: Rack-mountable appliances in tens or hundreds of terabytes, shipped, filled on-site and returned for upload into Cloud Storage. Rental is per device with a fixed number of included days.
pros: Straightforward rental model with days included
Fills into any Cloud Storage bucket class
Online-first alternative via Storage Transfer Service when links allow
cons: Available only in selected countries
Late-return fees accumulate quickly
No edge compute on the device

azure.name: Azure Data Box
azure.note: Disk, Data Box and Heavy appliances from a few terabytes to about a petabyte, for import and export to Blob, Files and managed disks. A flat per-order fee plus shipping.
pros: Supports export out of Azure, not just import
Sizes scale from disks to petabyte-class Heavy
Lands data directly in Files or managed disks, not only blobs
cons: Regional availability and lead times vary
Heavy devices need data-centre logistics on your side
Per-day charges after the included period

rows.pick: Data Box or Transfer Appliance are the obvious choices for a new bulk import; the Snow Family is in maintenance, so on AWS plan around Data Transfer Terminal or DataSync over a fat link instead.
rows.gotcha: Physical shipping exists in all three, but AWS is winding the Snow Family down and points new work to Data Transfer Terminal or online transfer. A migration runbook that assumes a Snowball order will not port to 2026 AWS.

rows.plain: A managed conveyor belt that copies files from your servers or another cloud into cloud storage over the network, checking every byte arrived.

aws.name: AWS DataSync
aws.note: Agent-based transfer between NFS, SMB, HDFS, object stores and AWS storage, including Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob as sources, with scheduling and verification. AWS Transfer Family covers managed SFTP and FTPS endpoints.
pros: Verifies data end to end and preserves metadata
Cross-cloud sources make it a repatriation and multicloud tool
Bandwidth throttling and scheduling fit production windows
cons: Billed per gigabyte moved, so recurring syncs add up
Agents run on your VMs or hardware and need care
Cloud-to-cloud pulls pay the other cloud's egress too

gcp.name: Storage Transfer Service
gcp.note: Agentless transfers from S3, Azure Blob and HTTP sources into Cloud Storage, plus agent-based transfers from on-premises POSIX and HDFS. The service itself is free for cloud sources, you pay only egress and operations, and Cloud FTP adds managed SFTP.
pros: No service charge for cloud-to-cloud into Cloud Storage
Agentless for the common S3 and Azure sources
Event-driven and scheduled transfers with bandwidth caps
cons: Destinations are Cloud Storage or file systems only
Agent pools needed for on-premises, with their own operations
Source-cloud egress still dominates the cost

azure.name: Azure Storage Mover
azure.note: A managed migration service that moves NFS and SMB shares through agent VMs and pulls S3 buckets agentlessly into Azure Files and Blob, with job-based tracking. AzCopy is the command-line tool for ad hoc copies.
pros: No charge for the service beyond storage and egress
Job history and progress live in the portal
Handles both file shares and object migrations
cons: Youngest of the three with fewer source types
Agent VMs run on your hypervisor
Designed for migration, less so for continuous sync

rows.pick: Storage Transfer Service is the obvious choice for pulling data out of another cloud, since it is agentless and unpriced beyond egress. DataSync wins for on-premises file estates; Storage Mover is fine for Azure-bound migrations.
rows.gotcha: DataSync charges per gigabyte moved; Storage Transfer Service is free for agentless cloud sources but bills agent-based file transfers per GiB; Storage Mover charges only storage and egress. A 10 TB nightly file-server sync is free only on Azure, which changes where the pipeline runs.

rows.plain: A box in your office that looks like a normal file server or tape drive but quietly keeps the real data in the cloud.

aws.name: AWS Storage Gateway
aws.note: A VM or hardware appliance offering S3 File Gateway for NFS and SMB, Volume Gateway for iSCSI and Tape Gateway as a virtual tape library. FSx File Gateway is no longer available to new customers.
pros: Tape Gateway retires physical tape libraries without changing backup software
Local cache keeps hot data fast on-site
Data lands as native S3 objects other services can read
cons: Cache sizing and appliance patching are your job
Per-gigabyte write charges plus S3 request costs
FSx File Gateway is in maintenance, so the FSx path is closing

gcp.none: No managed gateway appliance. Teams mount buckets with Cloud Storage FUSE, replicate ONTAP to NetApp Volumes, or buy partner appliances.

azure.name: Azure Files
azure.note: Azure File Sync, a feature of Azure Files, turns a Windows Server into a cache of an Azure file share with cloud tiering and multi-site sync. Azure Stack Edge is the hardware appliance for edge storage and compute.
pros: Runs on existing Windows Servers, no new appliance
Multi-site sync gives branch offices one namespace
Stack Edge adds local compute and AI at the edge
cons: Windows Server only, no NFS or iSCSI gateway mode
Per-server sync fees on top of share storage
No virtual tape library equivalent

rows.pick: Storage Gateway is the obvious choice when the requirement is tape replacement or iSCSI volumes; Azure File Sync when the estate is Windows file servers. Google Cloud has no direct product, so design around NetApp or FUSE.
rows.gotcha: Keeping on-premises workloads working while the data really lives in the cloud is a first-class product on AWS, a Windows-only feature on Azure and absent on Google Cloud. A hybrid design leaning on Tape or Volume Gateway has no like-for-like port.

rows.job: Open table formats on object storage
rows.plain: Turning piles of files in object storage into proper database-style tables that many analytics engines can read and update safely at once.

aws.name: Amazon S3 Tables
aws.note: Table buckets holding Apache Iceberg tables with automatic compaction, snapshot expiry and unreferenced-file cleanup, queried from Athena, Redshift, EMR and SageMaker Lakehouse. Intelligent-Tiering and replication arrived in late 2025.
pros: Maintenance chores like compaction are automatic
Iceberg REST endpoint works with open-source Spark and Trino
Same durability and security model as S3
cons: Iceberg only, no Delta or Hudi
Per-object monitoring and maintenance fees on top of storage
Table buckets are separate from general-purpose buckets

gcp.name: Google Cloud Lakehouse
gcp.note: Iceberg tables on Cloud Storage with a runtime catalogue, managed storage and cross-cloud federation to S3 and Azure Blob, queried from BigQuery and open engines; remote catalogues such as AWS Glue and Snowflake are still in preview. Renamed from BigLake in April 2026.
pros: BigQuery and Spark share one catalogue and one copy of data
Cross-cloud federation queries other clouds' storage in place
Fine-grained row and column security from BigQuery applies
cons: Recent rename means documentation and tooling still say BigLake
Spark, Hive and BigQuery writes through the runtime catalogue only arrived in mid-2026
Federated queries pay other clouds' egress

azure.name: Microsoft Fabric
azure.note: OneLake, the storage layer of Fabric, keeps every table as Delta Parquet and uses shortcuts to expose S3, Cloud Storage and Data Lake Storage in place. Iceberg is read through shortcuts and conversion.
pros: One logical lake for every Fabric workload and Power BI
Shortcuts virtualise other clouds without copying
Delta is native to Spark, Databricks and Power BI
cons: Delta first; Iceberg support is by translation
Capacity-unit pricing bundles storage with compute commitments
Lives inside Fabric, not the general Azure resource model

rows.pick: S3 Tables or Lakehouse are the obvious choices when Iceberg is the contract with external engines. Fabric is the obvious choice when Power BI and Delta already anchor the estate. They are not interchangeable: the table format is the lock-in.
rows.gotcha: AWS and Google Cloud standardise on Iceberg; Microsoft on Delta. Cross-cloud sharing works through catalogues and shortcuts, but writers still commit to one format. Also, BigLake became Lakehouse in April 2026, so older diagrams and IAM roles carry the old name.

rows.plain: Object storage arranged so analytics engines can treat it like folders of tables: cheap directory operations, fine permissions and formats every query tool understands.

aws.name: Amazon S3
aws.note: The lake is plain S3 with a flat namespace; directories are a naming convention. S3 Express One Zone adds directory buckets for low latency, S3 Tables adds Iceberg, and Lake Formation layers governance on top.
pros: Every analytics engine, open or commercial, reads S3 first
Storage classes cut lake cost as data ages
S3 Tables and Lake Formation are native add-ons
cons: Renaming a folder means copying every object
Directory buckets are single-zone and a separate bucket type
Governance is assembled from several services

gcp.name: Cloud Storage
gcp.note: The lake is Cloud Storage, optionally with hierarchical namespace buckets that make folders real objects with atomic renames. BigQuery reads it directly through Lakehouse tables and external tables.
pros: Hierarchical namespace gives atomic folder renames for Spark and Hadoop
BigQuery queries the lake without loading
Multi-region buckets simplify a global lake
cons: Hierarchical namespace is chosen at bucket creation only
Operation charges rise with many small files
Native tooling assumes BigQuery as the query engine

azure.name: Azure Data Lake Storage
azure.note: Gen2, a Blob Storage account with hierarchical namespace enabled, adding a real directory tree, POSIX access control lists and the ABFS driver used by Spark and Databricks. Gen1 retired in February 2024.
pros: Real directories make rename and delete cheap, not simulated
POSIX access control lists give per-folder permissions
First-class target for Databricks, Synapse and Fabric shortcuts
cons: Hierarchical namespace cannot be turned off once enabled
Some Blob features are unavailable on such accounts
Gen1 retirement forced migrations that some estates are still finishing

rows.pick: Interchangeable for a Parquet lake; choose where the query engine lives. Data Lake Storage is the obvious choice when Spark jobs depend on directory rename semantics and folder-level access control lists.
rows.gotcha: Data Lake Storage Gen2 and hierarchical Cloud Storage buckets have real directories, so renaming a partition is one operation; on S3 it is a copy of every object. Jobs that commit output by renaming folders behave very differently in cost and time.

rows.plain: Keeping a constantly updated copy of whole servers somewhere else so that, after a disaster, you press a button and they come back within minutes.

aws.name: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery
aws.note: Continuous block-level replication of on-premises, other-cloud or AWS servers into a low-cost staging area, with drills and recovery into full instances in minutes. The successor to CloudEndure Disaster Recovery.
pros: Sub-second recovery point with minute-scale recovery time
Staging area uses small instances until failover, keeping standby cheap
Cross-region and cross-cloud sources are supported
cons: Per-server hourly replication fee on top of staging storage
Agents on every source server
Failback to on-premises needs its own procedure

gcp.name: Backup and DR Service
gcp.note: Backup-based recovery: Compute Engine VMs and databases are captured into vaults and restored in another zone or region. Asynchronous Replication for Persistent Disk and Hyperdisk replicates Compute Engine disks across regions with a one-minute target recovery point; on-premises and other-cloud servers get no managed replication.
pros: Immutable vaults double as ransomware protection
Cross-region restore without a standby footprint
One service for backup and recovery reduces tooling
cons: Recovery point is the backup interval, not seconds
No continuous replication for on-premises or other-cloud servers
Restore time is bounded by re-creating disks from backup

azure.name: Azure Site Recovery
azure.note: Replication and orchestrated failover for Azure VMs between regions and for VMware, Hyper-V and physical servers into Azure. Recovery plans sequence multi-tier failover and test failovers run without disruption.
pros: Recovery plans script multi-tier failover order
Test failovers run without touching production
Per-protected-instance pricing is easy to forecast
cons: VMware replication needs an appliance and network planning
Some VM sizes, disk types and features are unsupported
Failback of physical servers is limited

rows.pick: Elastic Disaster Recovery or Site Recovery are the obvious choices when the requirement is seconds of data loss for whole servers. On Google Cloud that requirement pushes you to regional disks, application-level replication or partner tools.
rows.gotcha: Google's closest equivalent is Asynchronous Replication for Persistent Disk and Hyperdisk, Compute Engine only, with a roughly one-minute recovery point; everything else is backup and restore at the backup interval. A design certified on Site Recovery or Elastic Disaster Recovery must be re-modelled, not re-labelled.

rows.plain: A file system spread across many machines so thousands of processors can read the same training data or simulation files at once without queuing.

aws.name: Amazon FSx
aws.note: FSx for Lustre offers scratch and persistent Lustre file systems with throughput set per TiB and data repository links that hydrate from and export to S3. Amazon File Cache adds a Lustre cache over on-premises NFS and S3.
pros: Lazy-loads from S3, so the lake stays the source of truth
Scratch tier is cheap for short-lived jobs
Mature GPU cluster and EKS integrations
cons: Persistent deployments bill provisioned TiB and throughput continuously
Lustre client tuning is still your responsibility
One brand, several billing lines and limits

gcp.name: Managed Lustre
gcp.note: A managed Lustre service generally available since 30 June 2025, sized by capacity with throughput tiers per TiB and bulk import and export to Cloud Storage. Integrates with GKE and Compute Engine GPU and TPU clusters.
pros: Designed alongside AI Hypercomputer clusters and TPUs
Cloud Storage import and export are built in
Predictable per-TiB throughput tiers
cons: Young service with a smaller regional footprint
Minimum sizes push small teams to Filestore instead
Billed on provisioned capacity regardless of use

azure.name: Azure Managed Lustre
azure.note: Managed Lustre with throughput tiers per TiB and hierarchical storage management to and from Blob Storage, aimed at HPC and AI training. Azure HPC Cache, the earlier caching product, retired in September 2025.
pros: Blob integration moves cold results out automatically
Fits Azure CycleCloud and Batch HPC tooling
Throughput tiers match common HPC sizing
cons: Provisioned capacity is billed hourly whether idle or busy
HPC Cache retirement removes the lighter-weight option
Fewer regions than Blob or Files

rows.pick: Interchangeable: all three are managed Lustre with object-storage hydration and per-TiB throughput. Pick where the GPUs or TPUs are, since parallel file systems must sit in the same zone as the compute.
rows.gotcha: All three bill provisioned capacity around the clock, so a file system left running between training runs costs as much as one in use. Scratch tiers with no durability exist only on FSx for Lustre; the others need you to export and delete.

rows.plain: A cloud-hosted drop box that partners reach with the old secure file transfer protocol, with files landing straight in your object storage.

aws.name: AWS Transfer Family
