aws.note: Managed SFTP, FTPS, FTP and AS2 endpoints, plus browser-based web apps, writing into S3 or EFS. Identities come from service-managed keys, Active Directory or a custom identity provider through Lambda.
pros: Four protocols and a web portal under one service
Custom identity providers plug in existing partner credentials
Workflows can post-process files on arrival
cons: Hourly fee per protocol endpoint even when idle
Per-gigabyte upload and download charges
Static IP and VPC hosting add configuration steps

gcp.name: Cloud FTP
gcp.note: A managed SFTP endpoint launched in 2026 for moving files in and out of Cloud Storage without running your own server. Storage Transfer Service remains the tool for bulk and scheduled moves.
pros: Removes the self-hosted SFTP VM that most Google Cloud teams ran
Files land as ordinary Cloud Storage objects
IAM-native permissions rather than a separate user store
cons: Brand new, so regions, quotas and features are still thin
SFTP only, no FTPS or AS2
Little community experience to lean on

azure.name: Azure Blob Storage
azure.note: SFTP support is a feature switched on for a Blob Storage account with hierarchical namespace, using local users with SSH keys or passwords. There is no separate transfer product.
pros: No extra service to deploy or size
Files are blobs immediately, ready for Data Lake tooling
Hourly charge only while the endpoint is enabled
cons: Local users only, not Entra ID identities
Requires hierarchical namespace, which changes the account's behaviour
No FTPS, AS2 or partner-facing web portal

rows.pick: Transfer Family is the obvious choice for business-to-business exchanges that need AS2, FTPS or custom identity. For a plain SFTP drop box the three are interchangeable, with Google's offering the youngest.
rows.gotcha: On Azure the endpoint is a property of a storage account and needs hierarchical namespace, which cannot be undone; on AWS it is a separate resource with its own hourly bill. Credential models differ: Lambda-backed on AWS, local users on Azure, IAM on Google Cloud.

rows.plain: A rented, tidy filing system of linked tables, where the landlord handles backups, patches and failover so you only have to write queries.

aws.name: Amazon RDS
aws.note: Managed MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server and Db2 on instances you size, with Multi-AZ standby, read replicas and automated backups. Widest engine list of the three, including two commercial engines with licence-included pricing.
pros: Six engines including Oracle and Db2, with licence-included pricing options
Multi-AZ, read replicas and Blue/Green deployments are mature and well documented
Deep hooks into IAM, KMS, CloudWatch and Secrets Manager
cons: You pick and pay for instance sizes; idle capacity still bills
Storage, IOPS, backups and cross-AZ traffic are separate line items
Extended Support fees start once an engine version leaves standard support

gcp.name: Cloud SQL
gcp.note: Managed MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server with high-availability failover, read replicas and an Enterprise Plus edition for higher performance and near-zero-downtime maintenance. Fewer engines than RDS but the same shape: instances you size, regional by default.
pros: Enterprise Plus edition gives near-zero-downtime maintenance and faster failover
Pay-as-you-go with committed use discounts, no upfront reservation needed
Cloud SQL Auth Proxy and IAM database authentication simplify credentials
cons: Only MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server; no Oracle, MariaDB or Db2
Instance sizing is yours; there is no auto-pause for quiet databases
High availability and cross-region replicas double the compute bill

azure.name: Azure SQL Database
azure.note: The SQL Server family lives in Azure SQL Database, with Azure SQL Managed Instance for near-full engine compatibility. Open-source engines are separate products: Azure Database for PostgreSQL and Azure Database for MySQL, both flexible server; Azure Database for MariaDB retired in September 2025.
pros: Serverless tier auto-pauses, so development and bursty databases bill near zero
Hyperscale tier grows to 128 TB with fast snapshots and named replicas
Azure Hybrid Benefit reuses existing SQL Server licences, cutting cost sharply
cons: Four products with different portals, pricing units (DTU, vCore) and feature lists
Some SQL Server features need Managed Instance, at higher cost and slower provisioning
MariaDB retired in 2025 and Cosmos DB for PostgreSQL retires 2029; check lifecycles

rows.pick: Interchangeable for MySQL and PostgreSQL: pick your home cloud. Choose RDS for Oracle or Db2, and Azure for SQL Server, where Hybrid Benefit licensing and Managed Instance make it the natural home.
rows.gotcha: Same concept across all three, different bills and calendars. RDS charges Extended Support fees once an engine version leaves standard support, Cloud SQL applies maintenance windows you cannot fully disable, and Azure SQL serverless auto-pause means the first query after idle waits about a minute.

rows.plain: A familiar database with its storage rebuilt for the cloud: shared, self-healing storage under a MySQL or PostgreSQL front end, so it scales further and fails over faster.

aws.name: Amazon Aurora
aws.note: MySQL and PostgreSQL compatible engine on a shared six-copy storage layer spanning three Availability Zones, with up to 15 low-lag read replicas. Serverless v2 scales capacity in fine steps and can pause to zero; Global Database adds cross-region read replicas.
pros: Storage grows automatically to 256 TiB and survives losing two copies
Serverless v2 scales in half-ACU steps and can now scale to zero
Fast clones, Blue/Green deployments and zero-ETL to Redshift are Aurora-only conveniences
cons: Roughly 20 percent dearer than RDS for equivalent compute, plus per-million I/O charges
I/O-Optimized removes I/O charges but raises instance and storage prices
Aurora-only features are lock-in; moving to plain PostgreSQL loses them

gcp.name: AlloyDB for PostgreSQL
gcp.note: PostgreSQL-compatible engine with a disaggregated storage layer, an in-memory columnar engine for analytical queries and built-in ScaNN vector indexing. AlloyDB Omni packages the same engine to run on premises, on laptops or in other clouds.
pros: Columnar engine speeds analytical queries on the same transactional data
Omni edition runs anywhere, giving a real exit path
PostgreSQL compatibility, so most extensions and tooling work unchanged
cons: PostgreSQL only; no MySQL flavour
No serverless tier; the smallest 1 vCPU shape carries no SLA, so small production stays dear
Younger than Aurora: fewer regions and a shorter track record

azure.name: Azure SQL Database
azure.note: The Hyperscale tier of Azure SQL Database is the cloud-native shape: page servers and log service separated from compute, 128 TB, named replicas and snapshot backups. For PostgreSQL, Azure HorizonDB (preview) is the new scale-out engine with shared storage; flexible server is the conventional option.
pros: Hyperscale grows to 128 TB with backups that take seconds
Zone-redundant and named replicas scale reads without full copies
Same T-SQL, drivers and tooling as SQL Server, so migration is mostly configuration
cons: Cloud-native shape exists only for SQL Server today; HorizonDB is still preview
Leaving Hyperscale is allowed only within 45 days; after that it is an export
Per-vCore pricing with separate storage, backup and replica charges

rows.pick: Aurora if you already live on AWS and want the widest feature set; AlloyDB if analytical queries on live PostgreSQL data matter or you may need the Omni exit; Azure SQL Hyperscale only if your engine is SQL Server.
rows.gotcha: AlloyDB is the Aurora-Postgres competitor, but neither is PostgreSQL underneath: each is its own storage engine, so versions lag the community by months and Aurora-only or AlloyDB-only features (fast clones, columnar engine) vanish when you leave. Azure has no PostgreSQL twin yet; HorizonDB is preview.

rows.plain: One relational database that lives in several regions at once, accepts writes everywhere, and still gives every reader the same answer at the same moment.

aws.name: Amazon Aurora DSQL
aws.note: Serverless, PostgreSQL-compatible distributed SQL with active-active writes across Regions and no infrastructure to size, generally available since May 2025. A different animal from Aurora Global Database, which is one writer plus cross-region read replicas you promote in a failover.
pros: Active-active multi-Region writes with strong consistency, priced per request and storage
Truly serverless: no instances, patching or capacity planning
PostgreSQL wire protocol, so drivers and ORMs largely work
cons: Subset of PostgreSQL: no triggers, PL/pgSQL or temporary tables, and a 3,000 row transaction limit
Young service with a short track record and few Regions
Optimistic concurrency means contended writes fail and must be retried

gcp.name: Spanner
gcp.note: The original: horizontally scalable, strongly consistent relational database with synchronous multi-region replication built on TrueTime, offering GoogleSQL and PostgreSQL dialects plus graph, vector and full-text search in the same engine.
pros: Battle-tested at Google scale with a 99.999 percent multi-region SLA
External consistency across continents without application-level sharding
Multi-model: relational, graph, key-value, vector and search in one database
cons: Processing-unit pricing starts well above a small Cloud SQL instance
PostgreSQL interface is a dialect, not full compatibility; extensions do not exist
Schema and key design need care to avoid hotspots

azure.none: No relational service with multi-region writes. Teams use Azure SQL Database failover groups (one writer, promote on failure) or Cosmos DB where relational is negotiable.

rows.pick: Spanner when you need it today and can live on Google Cloud; Aurora DSQL when you are on AWS and can accept its PostgreSQL subset. Azure has no twin, so a multi-region relational requirement is a reason to look elsewhere.
rows.gotcha: Spanner is the headline difference: horizontally scalable, strongly consistent, global relational SQL. Aurora DSQL (2025) is AWS's first true answer; Aurora Global Database is read replicas plus a promotion, not multi-region writes. Cosmos DB has multi-region writes but is not relational.

rows.plain: A giant set of labelled boxes: give it a key, get the document back in milliseconds, at any scale, with no tables to join.

aws.name: Amazon DynamoDB
aws.note: Serverless key-value and document store with single-digit millisecond reads at any scale, on-demand or provisioned capacity, Global Tables for multi-Region active-active and Streams for change events. Items are capped at 400 KB and access patterns are designed up front around the partition key.
pros: Scales to millions of requests per second with no cluster to run
On-demand pricing, a free tier and 50 percent price cuts in late 2024
Global Tables, Streams, TTL and point-in-time recovery are built in
cons: 400 KB item limit and no joins; single-table design has a learning curve
Query flexibility is limited to key conditions and indexes you pre-declare
Hot partitions throttle; secondary indexes multiply write costs

gcp.name: Firestore
gcp.note: Serverless document database with real-time listeners, offline sync in mobile and web SDKs, and automatic indexing of every field. Firestore in Datastore mode serves server workloads; Firestore with MongoDB compatibility runs MongoDB drivers against the same engine.
pros: Live sync to mobile and web clients is unique among the three
Serverless with per-operation pricing and a generous free tier
Automatic indexes mean most queries work without planning
cons: 1 MiB document limit and a narrow query language: aggregations are count, sum, average
Per-document pricing gets dear at high write rates
Security rules and client access are a different model from server-only stores

azure.name: Azure Cosmos DB
azure.note: Globally distributed multi-model database with five tunable consistency levels, turnkey multi-region writes and a single-digit millisecond SLA. The NoSQL API is primary, with Table, Cassandra, Gremlin and MongoDB RU APIs sharing request-unit billing, while Azure Table Storage is the cheap, simple alternative.
pros: Multi-region writes and five consistency levels chosen per request
Serverless, autoscale and provisioned request units suit different load shapes
Change feed, TTL, analytical store and vector indexing are included
cons: Request-unit pricing is hard to predict; hot logical partitions throttle with 429s
20 GB per logical partition, raisable only temporarily via support, and 2 MB per item
Strong consistency and multi-region writes cannot be combined; you choose one

rows.pick: Interchangeable for a server-side key-value store: use your home cloud. Firestore is the obvious choice for a mobile or web app that needs live sync; Cosmos DB when you need multi-region writes with a consistency dial.
rows.gotcha: Firestore is a document store with live sync to mobile clients; Cosmos DB has five consistency levels and several APIs. The trap is partitioning: DynamoDB throttles hot keys, Cosmos DB caps a logical partition at 20 GB, Firestore indexes every field and bills those writes.

rows.plain: A spreadsheet with billions of rows and loose columns, built to swallow floods of incoming records such as sensor readings and find any one of them again by a single label per row.

aws.name: Amazon Keyspaces
aws.note: Serverless Apache Cassandra compatible service: CQL and existing Cassandra drivers, on-demand or provisioned capacity, multi-Region replication and no nodes to patch. It is a compatibility layer over AWS's own storage rather than Apache Cassandra, so some CQL features and tunables are missing.
pros: Serverless: no compaction, repair or node replacement to run
Existing Cassandra drivers and CQL schemas move with little change
Pay per request and storage, with optional point-in-time recovery billed on table size
cons: Not full Cassandra: user-defined functions, materialised views and some tunables are missing
Row size limit of 1 MB and per-partition throughput ceilings
Niche service with fewer Regions and a smaller community than DynamoDB

gcp.name: Bigtable
gcp.note: The original wide-column store, the design behind HBase and Cassandra, running Google's own products for two decades. Speaks the HBase API, now GoogleSQL and a Cassandra-compatible CQL client too, with autoscaling nodes and multi-cluster replication.
pros: Single-digit millisecond latency at petabyte scale, proven inside Google
Autoscaling nodes and replication across clusters in up to eight regions, one per zone
HBase API, SQL and CQL clients ease arrivals from three ecosystems
cons: Node-based pricing: at least one always-on node per cluster, even for small data
Single row key index; secondary indexes and joins are your problem
Schema design around key ordering is essential to avoid hotspots

azure.name: Azure Managed Instance for Apache Cassandra
azure.note: Real Apache Cassandra clusters run by Microsoft, with hybrid connectivity to your own on-premises rings so you can join and migrate gradually. Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra is the other option: a CQL translation layer over Cosmos DB with request-unit billing.
pros: Genuine Cassandra: full CQL, your existing tooling and hybrid ring joins
Cosmos DB alternative gives turnkey multi-region writes and autoscale
Managed patching, backups and node repair remove most toil
cons: Node-based pricing with a minimum of three nodes per data centre
You still own schema, compaction strategy and capacity planning
Two products for one job; picking wrongly means a migration later

rows.pick: Bigtable is the obvious choice for a greenfield write-heavy store on Google Cloud. Existing Cassandra users pick Azure Managed Instance to keep real Cassandra, or Keyspaces to shed operations at the cost of some CQL features.
rows.gotcha: Bigtable speaks the HBase API and now Cassandra too, but only Azure Managed Instance runs actual Cassandra. Keyspaces and Cosmos DB for Cassandra are translation layers: the CQL you write must avoid unsupported features, and consistency and pricing follow the host engine, not Cassandra.

rows.plain: A small, very fast memory sitting in front of your database, holding the answers you keep asking for so the slow store is asked less often.

aws.name: Amazon ElastiCache
aws.note: Managed Valkey, Redis OSS and Memcached, either as node clusters you size or as ElastiCache Serverless that scales per GB and request. Amazon MemoryDB (formerly MemoryDB for Redis) is the sibling for when the data must survive: multi-AZ durable log, same API.
pros: Valkey nodes run about 20 percent below Redis OSS; serverless starts at 100 MB
Serverless option removes cluster sizing and scales in seconds
MemoryDB gives Redis-compatible durability when the cache becomes the store
cons: Node clusters bill whether hot or idle; serverless bills per ECPU and GB-hour
Cross-AZ replication traffic and backups are extra
Redis Stack modules such as search and time series are absent

gcp.name: Memorystore for Valkey
gcp.note: Fully managed Valkey, Google's recommended successor to Redis, with zero-downtime scaling, multi-zone replicas and sizes from a single shard. Memorystore for Redis and Memorystore for Redis Cluster still run; Memorystore for Memcached is retiring, with new projects blocked from February 2027.
pros: Valkey tracks open-source Redis 7.2 behaviour at lower prices
Cluster scaling without downtime and a 99.99 percent SLA on multi-zone
IAM authentication and Private Service Connect fit the rest of Google Cloud
cons: Four product lines for one job, with the Memcached one ending January 2029
No serverless tier; you pick shard count and node size
Redis Enterprise features and modules are not available

azure.name: Azure Managed Redis
azure.note: Redis Enterprise run by Microsoft, generally available since May 2025, with current Redis versions, modules such as RediSearch and RedisJSON, active geo-replication and zone redundancy. Azure Cache for Redis is retiring: Enterprise tiers end March 2027, Basic, Standard and Premium in September 2028.
pros: Real Redis Enterprise: modules, active-active geo-replication and current Redis versions
SKUs from a few GB to terabytes, with zone redundancy
Successor path is clear now that Azure Cache for Redis is retiring
cons: Redis Ltd licensing keeps prices above Valkey-based rivals
Migration from Azure Cache for Redis is your project, with a 2027 or 2028 deadline
Redis modules are lock-in: Valkey elsewhere lacks them

rows.pick: Interchangeable for a plain cache: use your home cloud. Choose Azure Managed Redis if you rely on Redis Stack modules, ElastiCache Serverless if you refuse to size clusters, and MemoryDB when sessions or leaderboards must survive a node loss.
rows.gotcha: Valkey replaced Redis OSS in AWS and Google Cloud after the 2024 licence change, while Azure moved to Redis Enterprise. The forks diverge: commands and modules that work on Azure Managed Redis may not exist on Valkey, and only MemoryDB and Redis Enterprise promise durability.

rows.plain: Storage for things and the relationships between them, like a social network map, so you can ask who is connected to whom in a few hops.

aws.name: Amazon Neptune
aws.note: Managed graph database supporting property graphs (Gremlin and openCypher) and RDF (SPARQL) on the same Aurora-style storage layer, with Serverless capacity and up to 15 replicas. Neptune Analytics is the in-memory sibling for graph algorithms and vector similarity over large graphs.
pros: Both property graph and RDF in one managed service
Serverless and read replicas match the Aurora operating model
Neptune Analytics runs graph algorithms on billions of edges in seconds
cons: Instance-hour pricing with a non-trivial minimum; no scale to zero
Query languages are portable, but the storage and tuning are Neptune-specific
Single-Region writes only; Global Database is read replicas

gcp.name: Spanner Graph
gcp.note: Graph queries in GQL (the ISO graph query standard) over ordinary Spanner tables, so the same rows serve relational, graph, vector and full-text queries with Spanner's consistency and scale. There is no separate graph product to provision or synchronise.
pros: No second database: graph and relational queries hit the same data
Spanner's scale, consistency and multi-region options come for free
GQL is the ISO standard, so skills transfer as vendors adopt it
cons: Spanner's entry price applies even for a small graph
Gremlin, Cypher and SPARQL code must be rewritten in GQL
Younger than Neptune and Cosmos DB Gremlin; fewer algorithms and tooling

azure.name: Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin
azure.note: The Gremlin API of Azure Cosmos DB: property graphs stored as Cosmos DB documents, queried with Apache TinkerPop Gremlin, billed in request units, with the platform's global distribution and consistency options. It is an API surface on a document store, not a native graph engine.
pros: Turnkey global distribution and autoscale inherited from Cosmos DB
Gremlin is widely known; existing TinkerPop code largely works
Serverless request-unit billing suits small or spiky graphs
cons: Deep traversals are expensive in request units and can time out
Partitioned graphs need a partition key in every traversal
No RDF or SPARQL, and no openCypher or GQL

rows.pick: Neptune if you need RDF and SPARQL or already run Aurora. Spanner Graph if the graph is a view over data that also needs SQL. Cosmos DB for Gremlin on Azure when the graph is small or globally distributed.
rows.gotcha: Graph is a niche each cloud fills differently, and moving between them means rewriting queries, not just connection strings: Gremlin on Azure, Gremlin, openCypher or SPARQL on Neptune, GQL on Spanner. Cosmos DB's graph is a document store underneath, so deep traversals cost request units.

rows.plain: A store shaped for readings stamped with a time, such as temperatures or stock ticks, that answers questions like what happened between two and three o'clock very quickly.

aws.name: Amazon Timestream
aws.note: Two editions: Timestream for InfluxDB, a managed InfluxDB instance with the InfluxDB tooling and drivers, is the active path. Timestream for LiveAnalytics, the original serverless engine, closed to new customers in June 2025 and is in maintenance.
pros: Managed InfluxDB keeps open-source tooling, Telegraf and Grafana working unchanged
Multi-AZ deployments and automated backups without running InfluxDB yourself
Instance pricing is predictable compared with the old per-query engine
cons: The serverless LiveAnalytics edition is closed to new customers, so existing users face a migration
InfluxDB instance sizing and storage are yours to plan; no scale to zero
InfluxDB 2 instances cap ingest without sharding; only InfluxDB 3 Enterprise runs as a multi-node cluster

gcp.none: No dedicated time-series database. Teams use Bigtable for high-rate telemetry, BigQuery for analytics on it, and Cloud Monitoring for operational metrics.

azure.name: Azure Data Explorer
azure.note: Columnar analytics engine for logs, telemetry and time series, queried with Kusto Query Language, ingesting millions of events per second with time-based indexing. The same engine powers Azure Monitor logs and Eventhouse in Fabric Real-Time Intelligence; Azure Time Series Insights retired in March 2025.
pros: KQL is unusually good at time windows, series functions and anomaly detection
Same skills serve Azure Monitor, Sentinel and Fabric Real-Time Intelligence
Ingest from Event Hubs, IoT Hub and Kafka is turnkey
cons: Production clusters bill for at least two always-on engine nodes
KQL is Microsoft-only; queries do not port to SQL or PromQL
Fabric versus standalone cluster is a strategic choice Microsoft is still steering

rows.pick: Azure Data Explorer is the obvious choice when the workload is telemetry analytics over months of data. Timestream for InfluxDB when you already run InfluxDB. On Google Cloud, expect to build the shape yourself on Bigtable or BigQuery.
rows.gotcha: Azure Time Series Insights retired in 2025 and Timestream's original engine closed to new customers, so this niche is unstable. Data Explorer is an analytics engine (great for scans, poor as a hot operational store), while InfluxDB is the reverse; they are not swappable.

rows.plain: A place to run programs written for MongoDB, the popular JSON document database, without running MongoDB yourself; each cloud emulates its language on a different engine.

aws.name: Amazon DocumentDB
aws.note: MongoDB-compatible API over Aurora-style shared storage with up to 15 replicas, Global Clusters and an elastic sharded mode. Not MongoDB Inc's code, so some operators, aggregation stages and newer server features are missing.
pros: Aurora-style storage: six copies, fast failover, up to 15 read replicas
Elastic clusters shard writes to millions of operations per second
Familiar AWS operations: VPC, IAM, KMS, backups, CloudWatch
cons: Serverless since July 2025 alongside instance-hours, but the 0.5 DCU floor means no scale to zero
Trails MongoDB features; run your compatibility checks before migrating
Lock-in twice over: not MongoDB, and unrelated to Azure DocumentDB despite the name

gcp.name: Firestore with MongoDB compatibility
gcp.note: Runs MongoDB drivers and code against Firestore's serverless engine, generally available in 2025, with Firestore's multi-region replication, automatic scaling and per-operation pricing. It is a MongoDB API on Firestore, so query planning and limits are Firestore's, not MongoDB's.
pros: Serverless with per-operation billing: no instances to size
Firestore's multi-region replication and 99.999 percent SLA
Integrated with Firebase, Cloud Run and BigQuery export
cons: Newest of the three: compatibility gaps and fewer battle scars
Firestore limits apply: document size, index rules and query shapes
No MongoDB Atlas-style extras such as full-text search or charts

azure.name: Azure DocumentDB
azure.note: Renamed in November 2025 from Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore): a MongoDB-compatible service on the open-source, PostgreSQL-based DocumentDB engine that Microsoft handed to the Linux Foundation. Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (RU) remains as the request-unit, autoscale API on Cosmos DB.
pros: Open-source engine you can run yourself, a real exit path
vCore pricing is predictable and free-tier friendly compared with request units
Built-in vector search and text search for RAG on documents
cons: Two Azure products with the same job and different billing and limits
Name collision with Amazon DocumentDB; the two share nothing
PostgreSQL-based engine trails MongoDB on newer operators

rows.pick: Interchangeable only if your application uses a conservative MongoDB feature set. Otherwise the obvious choice is MongoDB Atlas on any of the three clouds; the first-party services trade fidelity for integration and billing convenience.
rows.gotcha: None of the three is MongoDB. Each speaks the wire protocol over its own engine (Aurora storage, Firestore, a PostgreSQL-based engine), so unsupported operators fail at runtime, not deploy time. Amazon DocumentDB and Azure DocumentDB are unrelated products sharing a name; do not assume portability.

rows.plain: A record book where every entry is chained to the last, so anyone can later prove nothing was altered or quietly deleted.

aws.name: Amazon QLDB
aws.note: Serverless ledger with an append-only, cryptographically verifiable journal queried in PartiQL. AWS ended the service on 31 July 2025 with no successor product; the documented path was Aurora PostgreSQL with your own hash chains and audit tables.
pros: Offered verifiable history without running a blockchain or consensus network
Serverless, priced per I/O and storage, with no cluster to size
cons: Retired 31 July 2025; nothing can be created or restored
Migration path is a hand-built ledger on Aurora PostgreSQL or Amazon Managed Blockchain
PartiQL queries and the document model do not port directly

gcp.none: Never had a ledger database. Teams build append-only tables with hash chains in Spanner or Cloud SQL, and keep audit exports in retention-locked Cloud Storage.

azure.name: Azure confidential ledger
azure.note: Tamper-proof, append-only ledger running in hardware enclaves (confidential computing), with receipts that prove an entry existed and was not changed. For data that lives in a relational database, ledger tables in Azure SQL Database and SQL Server 2022 give per-table tamper evidence instead.
pros: Only hyperscaler still selling a dedicated ledger service
Enclave-based, so even Microsoft operators cannot alter entries
SQL ledger tables add tamper evidence to existing schemas with no new store
cons: Confidential ledger is a small key-value log, not a query database
Limited regions and a per-hour instance charge regardless of use
Verification depends on Microsoft's enclave attestation chain

rows.pick: Azure is the only cloud with a first-party ledger product, so pick Azure confidential ledger or Azure SQL ledger tables if tamper evidence is a compliance requirement. Elsewhere, build hash-chained tables or use an external notary.
rows.gotcha: The ledger niche has collapsed: QLDB is gone, Google never entered, and Azure's answer is two different features. Do not confuse a ledger with a blockchain: none of these distribute trust across parties; they prove the operator's own history, which is often what auditors want.

rows.plain: A removal service for databases: copies the data into the new home, keeps the two in step while you switch over, and converts schemas between engines.

aws.name: AWS Database Migration Service
aws.note: Homogeneous and heterogeneous migration with ongoing change data capture, serverless or on replication instances you size, plus DMS Schema Conversion for engine changes. Also used as a long-running CDC pipeline to S3, Kinesis, Redshift and OpenSearch; DMS Fleet Advisor ended in May 2026.
pros: Widest source and target list, including on-premises, other clouds and streams
Serverless mode sizes itself; Schema Conversion handles Oracle and SQL Server exits
Doubles as a CDC engine, so one tool serves migration and integration
cons: Replication instances bill hourly while running, which for CDC means forever
Heterogeneous conversions still need manual fixes for procedures and triggers
Large tables and LOBs need tuning; failures are opaque without CloudWatch digging

gcp.name: Database Migration Service
gcp.note: Serverless migration of MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server into Cloud SQL and AlloyDB, with continuous replication until cutover and Gemini-assisted code conversion for Oracle. Datastream is the separate serverless change data capture service feeding BigQuery, Cloud Storage and Spanner.
pros: No charge for like-for-like migrations, and nothing to size
Continuous replication until cutover with minimal downtime
Datastream gives serverless CDC into BigQuery for analytics
cons: Targets are Google databases only; it will not move data out
Heterogeneous paths are limited to Oracle and SQL Server into PostgreSQL
Two tools (DMS and Datastream) split the job that AWS DMS does alone

azure.name: Azure Database Migration Service
azure.note: Migrates SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL and Oracle sources into Azure databases, offline or online with continuous sync until cutover, driven from Azure Migrate or the SQL migration extension in Visual Studio Code. It is a one-way, into-Azure service.
pros: Standard tier is free; Premium, for online migrations, is free for 183 days then hourly
Tight fit with Azure Migrate assessments and Azure Hybrid Benefit licensing
Online SQL Server migrations to Managed Instance are very well trodden
cons: Into Azure only; no exits or cross-cloud replication
No long-running CDC role: use Data Factory or Fabric mirroring for that
Online mode support varies by source and target pair; check the matrix

rows.pick: Interchangeable for a one-off move into your chosen cloud, and all three are free or nearly so. AWS DMS is the obvious choice when the same tool must keep replicating for years or feed non-database targets.
rows.gotcha: Same name, same job on all three, but only AWS DMS is a general replication engine run indefinitely. Google Cloud splits migration (DMS) from change data capture (Datastream); Azure DMS expects a cutover. A design that leans on DMS syncing forever does not port.

rows.plain: A search that finds things by meaning rather than exact words, by comparing lists of numbers (embeddings) that models produce for text, images or code.

aws.name: Amazon OpenSearch Service
aws.note: k-NN vector search in OpenSearch Service and OpenSearch Serverless, with hybrid keyword-plus-vector ranking, filters and Bedrock integration. Amazon S3 Vectors (GA December 2025) stores up to two billion vectors per index at object-storage prices, and pgvector on Aurora or RDS covers relational data.
pros: Hybrid search, filters and analytics in one mature engine
S3 Vectors cuts cold vector storage cost by up to 90 percent
Bedrock Knowledge Bases can target OpenSearch, S3 Vectors, Aurora or Neptune
cons: OpenSearch clusters are memory-hungry; serverless has minimum OCU charges
S3 Vectors has higher latency and suits infrequent queries, not real-time serving
Three or four options mean an architecture decision before the first embedding

gcp.name: Vector Search
gcp.note: Managed approximate nearest-neighbour index based on Google's ScaNN research, serving billions of vectors with low latency and filtering. Vector search is also built into AlloyDB (ScaNN index), Cloud SQL, Spanner, BigQuery and Firestore, so most teams keep vectors next to their data.
pros: ScaNN gives excellent recall and latency at billion-vector scale
Every Google database gained a vector index, so no separate store is required
Direct fit with Gemini embedding models and the Agent Platform
cons: Dedicated Vector Search bills for always-on index endpoints, even idle
Index rebuilds and updates are batch-oriented; streaming updates cost more
Renamed twice (Matching Engine, Vertex AI Vector Search), so samples are inconsistent

azure.name: Azure AI Search
azure.note: Managed search index with vector, keyword and hybrid retrieval, semantic reranking and integrated chunking and vectorisation, the default retriever behind Azure OpenAI and Foundry agents. Vector indexing also exists in Cosmos DB (DiskANN), Azure Database for PostgreSQL (pgvector, DiskANN) and Azure SQL Database.
pros: Best-integrated RAG retriever on Azure: hybrid search plus semantic reranker
Integrated vectorisation pipelines index blobs without your own code
DiskANN in Cosmos DB and PostgreSQL keeps vectors beside operational data
cons: Search units bill per hour whether queried or not; storage caps per tier are hard
Semantic ranker and vectorisation are extra meters
Index schema changes often require a full rebuild

rows.pick: Interchangeable: all three offer hybrid keyword-plus-vector search and a pgvector option. Azure AI Search is the obvious choice for RAG on Azure OpenAI; S3 Vectors for billions of rarely queried vectors; otherwise keep vectors in your existing database.
rows.gotcha: Vector search is a feature, not a product, and each cloud sells it four ways. All three do hybrid keyword-plus-vector retrieval, which usually beats either alone, but recall, filtering semantics and index rebuild behaviour differ per engine; benchmark before assuming results match across clouds.

rows.plain: Running Oracle's database, the incumbent in many large companies, inside a public cloud: on the cloud's own managed service or on Oracle hardware parked in its data centres.

aws.name: Oracle Database@AWS
aws.note: Oracle Exadata and Autonomous Database running on Oracle-managed hardware inside AWS data centres, generally available since July 2025, bought through AWS Marketplace and reachable with low latency from your VPC. Amazon RDS for Oracle remains the conventional managed option with licence-included and bring-your-own-licence pricing.
pros: Real Exadata performance and RAC, which RDS cannot offer
Bills through AWS and counts towards AWS commitments
Backups to S3 and integration with AWS analytics bridge the two worlds
cons: Few Regions, and dedicated Exadata infrastructure has a high entry price
Two support organisations and two consoles: Oracle runs the database, AWS the network
Oracle licensing terms still apply, including bring-your-own-licence audits

gcp.name: Oracle Database@Google Cloud
gcp.note: Oracle Exadata and Autonomous Database running on Oracle-managed infrastructure inside Google Cloud regions, generally available since September 2024, provisioned from the Google Cloud console and billed through Google Cloud. There is no Cloud SQL for Oracle, so this is the only first-party Oracle path.
pros: Only first-party Oracle on Google Cloud, next to BigQuery and Vertex AI
Provisioned from the Google Cloud console, billed on the Google invoice
Exadata performance for the workloads that cannot leave Oracle
cons: Dedicated Exadata infrastructure is a large monthly commitment
Limited regions, expanding but behind Azure
Oracle licensing and support terms remain Oracle's, not Google's

azure.name: Oracle AI Database@Azure
azure.note: The first and most widely deployed of the three partnerships, generally available since late 2023, offering Exadata Database Service, Autonomous Database and Base Database Service in Microsoft-run regions on Oracle-managed hardware. Oracle on Azure Virtual Machines is the self-managed alternative.
pros: Widest regional footprint of the three and the longest track record
Purchased through Azure Marketplace against Azure commitments
Fits Entra ID, virtual networks and Azure Monitor like a native service
cons: Exadata entry price is high; small Oracle estates are better on VMs
Oracle-run infrastructure inside Azure: two vendors, two SLAs
Licensing remains Oracle's; cost modelling needs both price lists

rows.pick: Azure if you want the widest availability and longest track record; the other two if your data platform already lives there and Oracle is the last holdout. On AWS, small Oracle estates still fit Amazon RDS for Oracle better.
rows.gotcha: The same Oracle service appears in all three clouds, but the cloud is only a landlord: Oracle patches, supports and licenses the database. Egress between the Oracle enclave and native services, region coverage and support hand-offs are what differ; check them before assuming portability.

rows.plain: A big, fast database built for asking questions across years of business data, like a library organised for research rather than daily lending.

aws.name: Amazon Redshift
aws.note: Columnar warehouse sold as provisioned RA3 clusters you size or as Redshift Serverless billed in RPU-hours. Redshift Spectrum reads S3, and zero-ETL integrations pull from Aurora, RDS and DynamoDB without pipelines.
pros: Reserved-instance pricing makes steady 24 by 7 workloads cheap
Deep S3, Glue and Lake Formation integration, plus zero-ETL sources
Postgres-flavoured SQL, familiar to most teams
cons: Cluster sizing, vacuum and distribution keys are your job on provisioned
Serverless minimum charges and 60-second billing surprise bursty users
Concurrency scaling and Spectrum bill separately

gcp.name: BigQuery
gcp.note: Fully serverless warehouse with no clusters at all: storage and compute are separate, and you pay per terabyte scanned or reserve slots. It also bundles ML, streaming inserts, Iceberg lakehouse tables and geospatial work.
pros: Zero infrastructure, from first query to petabytes
On-demand pricing is ideal for irregular workloads
Most GA features of the three, from BQML to sharing
cons: A careless SELECT star on a big table costs real money
Slot editions pricing takes effort to model
Strongly Google-shaped SQL and storage, hard to lift out

azure.name: Microsoft Fabric
azure.note: Fabric Data Warehouse is a SaaS warehouse over Delta tables in OneLake, billed through a shared Fabric capacity. Azure Synapse Analytics dedicated SQL pools are the older PaaS warehouse, still GA but no longer where features land.
pros: One capacity licence covers warehouse, Spark, real-time and Power BI
Data lands as open Delta tables, readable by any engine
Native Power BI Direct Lake mode, no import refreshes
cons: Capacity units throttle everything when one workload spikes
Younger engine, fewer tuning knobs than Synapse or Redshift
Synapse users face a migration, not an upgrade

rows.pick: Pick BigQuery when you want no infrastructure and pay per query; Redshift when you already live in S3 and want reserved-price predictability; Fabric when the audience lives in Power BI and Microsoft 365.
rows.gotcha: Redshift is provisioned clusters you size (plus Serverless); BigQuery is fully serverless and pay-per-query, so cost failures look opposite: idle clusters on AWS, runaway scans on GCP. BigQuery is often the reason companies pick GCP; Fabric bills capacity, not queries.

rows.plain: Keeping raw files in cheap storage but adding tables, permissions and a catalogue, so the pile of files behaves like a warehouse.

aws.name: AWS Lake Formation
aws.note: Permission and governance layer over S3 data registered in the Glue Data Catalog, with column, row and cell-level grants enforced by Athena, Redshift, EMR and Glue. AWS now brands the whole stack, including S3 Tables for Iceberg, as SageMaker Lakehouse.
pros: No charge of its own, you pay the engines and S3
Fine-grained grants apply consistently across AWS query engines
S3 Tables give managed Iceberg with automatic compaction
cons: Permissions layered on IAM confuse newcomers
Only governs data registered in Glue Data Catalog
SageMaker branding blurs the line with the ML service

gcp.name: Lakehouse
gcp.note: Formerly BigLake, it turns Cloud Storage files into Iceberg tables with an Iceberg REST Catalog, fine-grained security and cross-cloud federation to S3 and Azure. Knowledge Catalog supplies the discovery and governance layer above it.
pros: BigQuery security model extends to files in place
Iceberg REST Catalog is open to Spark, Trino and others
Cross-cloud tables query S3 and Azure without copying
cons: Renamed from BigLake in April 2026 after four years, so documentation and tutorials lag
Managed Iceberg tables still tie you to BigQuery for writes
Cross-cloud queries add egress and latency

azure.name: Microsoft Fabric
azure.note: OneLake is a single tenant-wide Delta lake with shortcuts to Azure Data Lake Storage, S3 and Google Cloud Storage, governed through Microsoft Purview. Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 remains the raw hierarchical object store underneath, and Azure Databricks Unity Catalog is the common alternative.
pros: One lake for the whole tenant, no per-team buckets
Shortcuts virtualise other clouds' storage without copying
Delta format is readable by Databricks and Spark
cons: OneLake storage bills separately from capacity
Shortcut reads to other clouds incur their egress
Governance split between Fabric, Purview and Unity Catalog

rows.pick: Fabric OneLake when Power BI users must reach the lake directly; Lakehouse on Google when BigQuery is already the engine; Lake Formation when you need enforceable row and column policies across Athena, Redshift and EMR.
rows.gotcha: Governing a lake means catalogue, lineage and access in one place, and each is younger and rougher than the storage it governs. Table formats differ too: AWS and Google lean Iceberg, Fabric writes Delta, so a multi-cloud lakehouse needs conversion or dual catalogues.

rows.plain: Running an ordinary SQL query straight against files sitting in storage, with no database to load them into first.

aws.name: Amazon Athena
aws.note: Trino-based serverless SQL over S3 files described in the Glue Data Catalog, billed at a flat rate per terabyte scanned, with a provisioned capacity option. Federated connectors reach other databases, and Athena for Apache Spark adds notebooks.
pros: No servers, no minimum spend, pay only per terabyte scanned
Standard Trino SQL and Iceberg support
Reads Parquet, ORC, CSV and JSON in place
cons: Per-query concurrency and timeout limits bite on big joins
Slow on unpartitioned or small-file data, and you pay for it
S3 first, other sources need connectors and Lambda costs

gcp.name: BigQuery
gcp.note: BigQuery external and Lakehouse tables query Cloud Storage, Bigtable, Drive and cross-cloud buckets with the same engine and SQL as native tables. There is no separate product because the warehouse already does it.
pros: Same SQL, IAM and pricing as the warehouse
Lakehouse tables get caching and fine-grained security
Federated queries reach Cloud SQL and Spanner
cons: External tables are slower than native storage and skip some features
Scan-based pricing still applies to file queries
Cross-cloud reads add egress

azure.name: Microsoft Fabric
azure.note: The SQL analytics endpoint queries Delta and Iceberg files in OneLake, including shortcuts to Azure Data Lake Storage, S3 and Google Cloud Storage, within your Fabric capacity. Azure Synapse Analytics serverless SQL pools are the older pay-per-terabyte equivalent.
pros: Every lakehouse gets a read-only SQL endpoint automatically
Power BI connects directly in Direct Lake mode
Synapse serverless remains for pay-per-query needs
cons: Capacity billing, not pay-per-query, unless you fall back to Synapse
Delta and Iceberg only, no raw CSV or JSON queries
Endpoint metadata sync lags writes by minutes

rows.pick: Athena is the obvious choice for occasional queries over an S3 archive with zero standing cost. On Google the question dissolves into BigQuery. On Azure, Fabric if you own capacity, Synapse serverless if you want per-query billing.
rows.gotcha: BigQuery natively queries its own storage and external data; Athena is S3-only Trino, so joining S3 to RDS needs a federated connector. Athena and Synapse serverless bill per terabyte scanned, Fabric bills capacity, so file layout drives cost on two clouds and throttling on one.

rows.plain: Renting a fleet of machines that share out one enormous data-crunching job, then handing them back when the job finishes.

aws.name: Amazon EMR
aws.note: Managed Spark, Hive, Flink, Presto and Trino in four deployment shapes: EMR on EC2 clusters, EMR on EKS inside your Kubernetes, EMR Serverless and EMR on Outposts. EMR Studio notebooks and Glue Data Catalog integration come with it.
pros: Spot instances make long batch jobs very cheap
Widest framework list of the three
Serverless option removes cluster management
cons: Cluster tuning, bootstrap actions and AMI upgrades are your job
Per-instance EMR surcharge on top of EC2
Four deployment modes with different feature sets confuse teams

gcp.name: Managed Service for Apache Spark
gcp.formerName: Dataproc and Serverless for Apache Spark
gcp.note: Unified in April 2026 from Dataproc and Serverless for Apache Spark, it runs Spark, Hadoop and Flink either as fast-starting clusters or as serverless batches, and Spark jobs can run inside BigQuery Studio. Dataproc Metastore provides the Hive metastore.
pros: Clusters start in about 90 seconds, so ephemeral is the default
Per-second billing with no surcharge on preemptible workers
Reads BigQuery and Cloud Storage natively
cons: Smaller open-source framework catalogue than EMR
Rename churn breaks tutorials and IaC module names
Serverless mode has fewer tuning options

azure.name: Azure Databricks
azure.note: First-party Databricks with Spark, Delta Lake, Unity Catalog and Photon, billed in DBUs plus VM cost. Azure HDInsight offers plain Hadoop, Spark and Kafka clusters, and Fabric Spark runs notebooks inside Fabric capacity.
pros: Most polished Spark experience, with Delta and Unity Catalog
Deep Entra ID and Azure networking integration
Serverless compute and Photon speed up SQL workloads
cons: DBU pricing on top of VMs is the priciest of the three
Unity Catalog pulls governance into Databricks, away from Purview
HDInsight is ageing and gets little investment

rows.pick: Azure Databricks when you want the best Spark experience and will pay for it. Google when clusters should be disposable. EMR when Spot pricing and framework breadth matter more than polish.
rows.gotcha: Managed Service for Apache Spark (formerly Dataproc) starts clusters quickly, encouraging ephemeral clusters, while EMR clusters take minutes, so teams leave them running idle. Databricks runs on all three clouds, and choosing it means Unity Catalog owns governance rather than the cloud's catalogue.

rows.plain: A conveyor belt for events: millions of clicks, sensor readings or orders per second arrive and are held briefly for many readers to consume in order.

aws.name: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
aws.note: Durable ordered shards you provision, or on-demand mode that scales by throughput, with up to 365 days retention. Amazon MSK covers teams that need real Kafka, and Amazon Data Firehose handles delivery to storage.
pros: On-demand mode needs no capacity planning
Native triggers for Lambda, Flink and Firehose
Enhanced fan-out gives each consumer its own throughput
cons: Shard-hour plus PUT-payload pricing is fiddly to forecast
1 MB per second per shard write limits force resharding
Proprietary API, no Kafka client compatibility

gcp.name: Pub/Sub
gcp.note: Global, serverless messaging that doubles as the event ingest layer, with BigQuery and Cloud Storage subscriptions that land data without code. Managed Service for Apache Kafka exists for Kafka-native teams, and Pub/Sub Lite is being retired in January 2027.
pros: Global endpoint, no shards, partitions or capacity to size
Pay per gigabyte, generous free tier
Direct subscriptions into BigQuery and Cloud Storage
cons: Ordering is per key and only within one publishing region, not partition-based
Per-message overhead makes tiny messages costly
Replay window is 31 days at most

azure.name: Azure Event Hubs
azure.note: Partitioned event ingest sold in Basic, Standard, Premium and Dedicated tiers, with a Kafka-compatible endpoint, Capture to storage, and a schema registry. Fabric Eventstream sits on top for no-code routing into Fabric.
pros: Kafka protocol support, existing clients just change connection strings
Capture writes to storage with no code
Dedicated tier gives single-tenant capacity
cons: Throughput units and processing units need manual scaling on lower tiers
Retention caps at 90 days, Premium and Dedicated only
Not Kafka underneath, broker-level features are missing

rows.pick: Pub/Sub when you want zero capacity planning and global reach. Event Hubs when you have Kafka clients and want a managed endpoint without running Kafka. Kinesis when Lambda and Firehose are already your downstream.
rows.gotcha: Event Hubs speaks Kafka, so Kafka clients repoint with a connection-string change, but transactions are preview-only on Premium and Dedicated and some admin APIs are missing. Kinesis and Event Hubs order within a shard or partition; Pub/Sub orders by key and scales without either.

rows.plain: Doing sums on data while it is still moving, such as averaging sensor readings every minute, instead of waiting to analyse it later.

aws.name: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
aws.note: Runs Apache Flink applications, in Java, Python or Flink SQL notebooks, billed per Kinesis Processing Unit hour. The old SQL-only flavour shut down in January 2026, so Flink is now the only engine.
pros: Real open-source Flink, code ports on and off AWS
Reads Kinesis, MSK and Kafka sources natively
Studio notebooks lower the entry bar
cons: KPU-hour billing runs whether events arrive or not
Flink operations, checkpoints and version upgrades are still your problem
SQL-only users lost their simpler option in 2026

gcp.name: Dataflow
gcp.note: Managed Apache Beam that runs the same pipeline code in streaming or batch mode, autoscaling workers and shuffling in a separate service. Prebuilt templates cover Pub/Sub to BigQuery and similar common paths.
pros: One programming model for batch and streaming
Autoscaling and dynamic work rebalancing are automatic
Dozens of Google-maintained templates need no code
cons: Beam has a smaller community than Flink or Spark
Streaming Engine and worker costs are hard to predict
Beam abstraction hides some Flink-level controls

azure.name: Azure Stream Analytics
azure.note: SQL-like streaming queries over Event Hubs and IoT Hub, billed per streaming unit, with outputs to Power BI, SQL and storage. Fabric Real-Time Intelligence, with Eventstream and KQL Eventhouse, is where Microsoft now invests for streaming analytics.
pros: Declarative SQL with windows, no cluster or code
Direct output to Power BI for live dashboards
Simple per-streaming-unit pricing
cons: Proprietary query language, nothing ports off Azure
No user-defined operators beyond JavaScript and C# functions
Feature investment has moved to Fabric Real-Time Intelligence

rows.pick: Dataflow when your team writes pipelines in code and wants batch and streaming unified. Managed Flink when portability of Flink jobs matters. Stream Analytics or Fabric when a SQL query into a Power BI dashboard is the goal.
rows.gotcha: Only AWS runs unmodified open-source Flink; Dataflow needs Beam, and Stream Analytics needs its own SQL, so a streaming job is the least portable piece of an analytics stack. Exactly-once semantics also differ, so check duplicate handling before trusting counts.

rows.plain: The plumbing that copies data from many systems, cleans and reshapes it, and drops it into the warehouse on a schedule.

aws.name: AWS Glue
aws.note: Serverless Spark and Python ETL jobs, a visual Glue Studio, crawlers, and the Glue Data Catalog in one service, billed per DPU-hour. Zero-ETL integrations into Redshift and OpenSearch increasingly replace hand-written jobs.
pros: Catalogue, crawlers and jobs come in one service
Serverless, per-second DPU billing with no cluster
Zero-ETL from Aurora, RDS and DynamoDB into Redshift
cons: Cold start of about a minute per job
DPU minimum charges make many small jobs expensive
Spark under the hood, so debugging needs Spark skills

gcp.name: Dataflow
gcp.note: Google splits the job: Dataflow for coded pipelines, Cloud Data Fusion for graphical CDAP pipelines, Dataform for SQL transformations inside BigQuery, Datastream for change data capture and BigQuery Data Transfer Service for SaaS loads. Most teams land data raw and transform in BigQuery SQL.
pros: Each tool is fit for purpose rather than one Swiss Army knife
ELT in BigQuery SQL with Dataform is cheap and simple
Templates cover common sources with no code
cons: Five products to learn, licence and monitor
Data Fusion instances bill hourly whether pipelines run or not
No single catalogue tied to the pipelines, that is Knowledge Catalog

azure.name: Azure Data Factory
azure.note: Visual pipelines with over a hundred connectors, Mapping Data Flows for Spark transformations, and self-hosted integration runtimes that reach on-premises sources. Fabric Data Factory carries the same model inside Fabric capacity.
pros: Largest connector catalogue, including SAP and on-premises
Self-hosted runtime bridges to private networks without VPNs
Low-code, business analysts can build pipelines
cons: Per-activity and per-DIU-hour billing is opaque
Mapping Data Flows cold start and bill Spark minutes
Two Data Factories now, Azure and Fabric, with different feature sets

rows.pick: Data Factory when sources are on-premises or SAP-heavy and builders are analysts. Glue when everything already sits in AWS and you want catalogue plus jobs together. Google when you are happy to land raw and transform in BigQuery SQL.
rows.gotcha: GCP splits ETL across several tools; Glue bundles catalogue and ETL, so a Glue migration to Google is a redesign, not a port. Everywhere, the trend is zero-ETL and mirroring: check whether your source has a native integration before writing any pipeline.

rows.plain: The conductor that decides which data jobs run when, waits for dependencies, retries failures and shows you what happened overnight.

aws.name: Amazon MWAA
aws.note: Managed Apache Airflow environments in your VPC, sized small to large and billed per environment-hour plus workers. Step Functions and Glue workflows are the AWS-native alternatives for simpler dependency graphs.
pros: Genuine Airflow, DAGs move to any other Airflow
Runs inside your VPC with IAM integration
Step Functions exists for lighter, serverless orchestration
cons: Smallest environment still costs hundreds of dollars a month idle
Airflow version upgrades lag and need environment recreation
Scheduler tuning and plugin packaging are on you

gcp.name: Managed Service for Apache Airflow
gcp.note: Cloud Composer renamed in April 2026, it runs Airflow on GKE with autoscaling workers and a Google-maintained Airflow build. Workflows is the lighter serverless option for step chains without Airflow.
pros: Autoscaling workers and per-vCPU billing on the current generation
Prebuilt operators for BigQuery, Dataflow and Spark
Workflows covers simple serverless chains cheaply
cons: An always-on environment is never cheap
Rename means docs, IaC and operator names are in flux
Older environment generations are on a retirement clock

azure.name: Azure Data Factory
azure.note: Data Factory pipelines are the mainstream Azure orchestrator, with triggers, dependencies and monitoring built in, and its own Airflow option, Workflow Orchestration Manager, is deprecated and closed to new instances. Apache Airflow jobs inside Fabric Data Factory give teams a managed Airflow when portability matters.
pros: No idle environment charge, pay per pipeline run
Visual dependency graphs, monitoring and alerts included
Fabric offers managed Airflow when DAG portability is needed
cons: Pipeline JSON is proprietary, nothing ports off Azure
Complex branching and dynamic DAGs are awkward compared with Airflow
Fabric Airflow needs Fabric capacity

rows.pick: If your DAGs are already Airflow, AWS and Google are interchangeable managed hosts. Azure is the odd one: pick Data Factory when you want to avoid running an always-on scheduler, and accept the different model.
rows.gotcha: Managed Airflow on AWS and GCP; Azure pushes Data Factory instead, which is a different model rather than a port. Managed Airflow environments also bill 24 hours a day, so a team with three nightly jobs may pay more for the conductor than the orchestra.

rows.plain: A searchable index of every dataset the organisation owns, who owns it, where it came from and who may use it, like a library catalogue for data.

aws.name: Amazon DataZone
aws.note: Business catalogue with domains, publish-and-subscribe access workflows and glossaries, now surfaced as SageMaker Catalog inside SageMaker Unified Studio. The Glue Data Catalog remains the technical metastore underneath that every AWS engine reads.
pros: Subscription workflow automates Lake Formation grants
Glue Data Catalog is free at small scale and Hive-compatible
Now bundled into SageMaker Unified Studio
cons: Two catalogues, technical and business, to keep aligned
Rebranding to SageMaker Catalog confuses search and support
Lineage and quality features are thinner than Purview

gcp.name: Knowledge Catalog
gcp.note: Renamed from Dataplex Universal Catalog in April 2026, it catalogues BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Spanner and Gemini Enterprise assets with lineage, data quality and a business context graph aimed at AI agents. The legacy Data Catalog shut down in June 2026.
pros: Automatic discovery of BigQuery and Cloud Storage assets
Lineage and quality scans built in
Metadata exposed to agents through MCP and search
cons: Three names in five years, tooling and docs lag
Weak coverage of non-Google sources
Governance policies still enforced elsewhere, in IAM and BigQuery

azure.name: Microsoft Purview
azure.note: Unified data governance spanning Azure, Fabric, Microsoft 365, SQL Server, S3 and SaaS sources, with scanning, classification, lineage, sensitivity labels and compliance in one portal. It replaced Azure Data Catalog in May 2024.
pros: Broadest source coverage, including Microsoft 365 and multicloud
Sensitivity labels flow from documents to datasets
Compliance and data governance in one licence conversation
cons: Pricing spans capacity units, scans and M365 licences
Sprawling product, several portals merged over time
Governance in Fabric and Databricks still partly separate

rows.pick: Purview is the obvious pick when the estate includes Microsoft 365 and on-premises SQL Server. Knowledge Catalog when almost everything lives in BigQuery. DataZone when you need governed self-service access to Lake Formation data.
rows.gotcha: Each catalogue indexes its own cloud well and others poorly, so multi-cloud governance usually means Purview or a third party such as Collibra or Unity Catalog. Watch the names: Google's has been renamed twice and AWS folded DataZone into SageMaker, so searches return stale guidance.

rows.plain: Turning tables of numbers into charts and dashboards that managers can click through, and now asking questions in plain language.

aws.name: Amazon Quick
aws.note: QuickSight became Amazon Quick Suite in October 2025 and Amazon Quick in April 2026, merging dashboards, the SPICE in-memory engine, Q Business-style research and automation agents into one suite. Per-user and capacity pricing, with embedding for customer-facing apps.
pros: Cheapest per-reader pricing of the three
SPICE caches data, so dashboards stay fast off Redshift and Athena
Embedding is pay-per-session, good for SaaS products
cons: Smaller visual and modelling toolkit than Power BI or Looker
Two renames in a year, docs and connectors in flux
Semantic layer is thin, logic lives in each analysis

gcp.name: Looker
gcp.note: Enterprise BI with LookML, a governed semantic model queried live against BigQuery and other databases, priced per platform and per user. Data Studio, briefly Looker Studio and renamed back in April 2026, is the free and Pro self-service dashboard tool.
pros: Governed metrics defined once in LookML
Live query, no extracts to refresh
Data Studio is free and connects to hundreds of sources
cons: LookML needs developers, not analysts
Platform licence is expensive for small teams
Data Studio lacks governance and enterprise features

azure.name: Power BI
azure.note: The market-leading BI tool, sold per user or through Fabric capacity, with Direct Lake reads from OneLake, Copilot natural-language reporting and deep Excel and Teams integration. Power BI Embedded serves customer-facing apps.
pros: Included in many Microsoft 365 E5 licences
Direct Lake mode queries Fabric data without imports
Largest community, training and connector ecosystem
cons: Desktop authoring is Windows only
Premium features need Fabric capacity, F64 for free viewers
DAX and tabular modelling have a real learning curve

rows.pick: Power BI when the audience already lives in Microsoft 365. Looker when governed, consistent metrics across teams matter more than cost. Quick when you want cheap readers and embedded dashboards on AWS data.
rows.gotcha: Power BI is the reason many organisations land on Azure; Looker is a full BI platform owned by Google. Each BI tool works best against its own warehouse, so BI choice quietly decides warehouse choice, and QuickSight's rename to Quick broke old links.

rows.plain: An index built for finding needles in text, whether a product in a catalogue or one error in a billion log lines, in milliseconds.

aws.name: Amazon OpenSearch Service
aws.note: Managed OpenSearch clusters and OpenSearch Serverless for full-text search, log analytics dashboards and vector search, with OpenSearch Ingestion pipelines and zero-ETL from S3 and DynamoDB. Amazon CloudSearch is closed to new customers.
pros: Real OpenSearch, compatible with most Elasticsearch tooling
Serverless option removes shard and node sizing
Zero-ETL from S3, DynamoDB and Security Lake
cons: Clusters need sizing, shard planning and index lifecycle care
Serverless can scale to zero OCUs when idle, but avoiding cold starts means a paid minimum
Costly for long log retention compared with object storage

gcp.name: Cloud Logging
gcp.note: Cloud Logging with Log Analytics covers the log half on a BigQuery engine, but Google has no first-party Elasticsearch or OpenSearch. Product search means Elastic Cloud from Marketplace or Agent Search, formerly Vertex AI Search.
pros: Log Analytics queries logs with SQL at BigQuery scale
No clusters to size for logs
Agent Search gives managed semantic search over documents
cons: No first-party Elasticsearch or OpenSearch
Logging ingestion pricing climbs fast above the free allotment
Product search means a partner bill and a second console

azure.name: Azure AI Search
azure.note: Managed search index with full-text, vector and hybrid retrieval, sold in Dedicated tiers (a consumption-based Serverless model is in preview) and used heavily as the RAG store for Azure OpenAI apps. Azure Data Explorer handles the log analytics half with KQL, as in Azure Monitor.
pros: Best-integrated vector store for Azure OpenAI RAG builds
Data Explorer plus KQL is superb for telemetry analytics
Tier pricing is predictable
cons: Not Elasticsearch, no Lucene query DSL or Kibana ecosystem
Tier limits on index size and replicas force a new service, except between Basic and Standard
Two products, AI Search and Data Explorer, for one OpenSearch

rows.pick: OpenSearch Service is the obvious choice when you already run Elasticsearch or Kibana workflows. Azure AI Search when building RAG on Azure OpenAI. On Google, accept Elastic Cloud from Marketplace or reshape the problem around BigQuery and Agent Search.
rows.gotcha: GCP has no first-party Elasticsearch, which is a genuine gap if search is central to the product. Azure splits the job in two, and only AWS gives one engine for both search and logs, so OpenSearch dashboards do not port to either rival.

rows.plain: Letting another company or team query your data in place, without emailing a copy, and sometimes only in aggregate so nobody sees the raw rows.

aws.name: AWS Data Exchange
aws.note: Marketplace for subscribing to third-party datasets delivered into S3, Redshift, APIs or, in preview, Lake Formation, with billing through your AWS account. AWS Clean Rooms adds privacy-preserving joint analysis, and Redshift datashares cover internal live sharing.
pros: Thousands of commercial datasets billed on the AWS invoice
Clean Rooms supports differential privacy and cryptographic computing
Redshift datashares are live and cross-account
cons: Deliveries are S3 or Redshift centric, consumers must be on AWS
Clean Rooms bills per query and per collaboration
Three products for one job

gcp.name: BigQuery
gcp.note: BigQuery sharing, formerly Analytics Hub, publishes datasets as listings that other projects and organisations subscribe to as live linked datasets, with no copies. BigQuery data clean rooms add aggregation and privacy rules on top.
pros: Zero-copy, live sharing inside the warehouse
Public and commercial listings alongside your own
Clean rooms are a feature, not a separate bill
cons: Consumers must be BigQuery users
Subscriber queries bill the subscriber, pricing surprises follow
Exchange marketplace is smaller than AWS

azure.name: Azure Data Share
azure.note: Snapshot sharing of storage, SQL and Synapse data with external organisations, with invitation and tracking; in-place sharing exists only for Azure Data Explorer. Fabric external data sharing now offers live OneLake shortcuts across tenants and is where Microsoft's investment goes.
pros: Snapshot shares work with any Azure storage consumer
Fabric external sharing is live and zero-copy across tenants
Purview tracks the shared assets
cons: Snapshot model means stale copies and storage cost
Clean rooms lag: Azure Confidential Clean Rooms is still in limited preview
Two overlapping mechanisms, Data Share and Fabric sharing

rows.pick: BigQuery sharing is the simplest when both parties use BigQuery. AWS when you buy commercial data or need clean rooms with cryptographic guarantees. Azure only for tenant-to-tenant Fabric sharing.
rows.gotcha: Sharing only works within a cloud: a BigQuery listing cannot be subscribed to from Redshift, and Redshift datashares stop at the AWS border. Cross-cloud sharing still means Iceberg or Delta files in a bucket with an agreed catalogue, or a commercial platform.

rows.plain: Someone else runs the Kafka brokers your applications already speak to, so you keep the protocol and drop the 3 a.m. disk alerts.

aws.name: Amazon MSK
aws.note: Managed Apache Kafka in three shapes: provisioned brokers you size, Express brokers with faster scaling and cheaper storage, and MSK Serverless. MSK Connect runs Kafka Connect, and tiered storage offloads old segments to S3.
pros: Real Apache Kafka, every client and Connect plugin works
Express brokers scale in minutes and cut storage cost
IAM authentication removes credential management
cons: Provisioned clusters need broker sizing and partition planning
Serverless caps throughput and partitions per cluster
Broker replication is free but client cross-zone traffic bills, and version upgrades are manual

gcp.name: Managed Service for Apache Kafka
gcp.note: Launched in 2024, it runs Kafka clusters with automatic rebalancing, Kafka Connect connectors and IAM or SASL authentication. Pub/Sub remains the Google-native path, and Pub/Sub Lite is retiring in January 2027.
pros: Genuine Kafka for lift-and-shift of existing streaming apps
Automatic broker rebalancing and patching
Kafka Connect for BigQuery, Cloud Storage and Pub/Sub
cons: Youngest of the three, fewer regions and features
No serverless tier, clusters bill all day
Google's own guidance still favours Pub/Sub

azure.name: Azure Event Hubs
azure.note: Event Hubs exposes a Kafka-compatible endpoint on Standard tier and above, so producers and consumers connect with a connection-string change, but the brokers are Event Hubs, not Kafka. Azure HDInsight offers real Kafka clusters for teams that need broker-level features.
pros: No brokers to run, Kafka clients just repoint
Same service doubles as the general event ingest layer
HDInsight Kafka exists when full compatibility is needed
cons: Not Kafka underneath: transactions preview-only on Premium and Dedicated, compaction tier-limited, no broker plugins
Kafka Connect needs self-hosting; Kafka Streams is preview-only on Premium and Dedicated
HDInsight is ageing and gets little investment

rows.pick: MSK is the mature default when you need real Kafka on a hyperscaler. Google's service is the choice for Kafka apps moving to GCP without rewriting to Pub/Sub. Event Hubs when protocol compatibility is enough and you want zero brokers.
rows.gotcha: Event Hubs speaks Kafka without being Kafka, usually a benefit until you need a broker-level feature such as a custom Connect plugin, or a tier-gated one such as transactions, preview-only on Premium and Dedicated. Consumer offsets, ACLs and topic configs translate imperfectly between the three.

rows.plain: A chute at the end of the conveyor belt that batches events into files or tables in storage, with no code written by you.

aws.name: Amazon Data Firehose
aws.note: Renamed from Kinesis Data Firehose in February 2024, it buffers streams from Kinesis, MSK or direct puts and lands them in S3, Redshift, OpenSearch, Iceberg tables, Splunk and HTTP endpoints. Lambda transforms and Parquet conversion happen in flight.
pros: Fully serverless, billed per gigabyte ingested
Converts to Parquet and partitions dynamically on the way in
Widest destination list, including third-party tools
cons: Latency follows your buffer interval, 0 to 900 seconds; even zero buffering takes about five seconds
Format conversion and VPC delivery bill extra
Yet another Kinesis-family name to keep straight

gcp.name: Pub/Sub
gcp.note: Pub/Sub export subscriptions write directly to BigQuery tables or Cloud Storage files with schema mapping and no code, replacing many simple Dataflow templates. Anything needing transformation still goes through Dataflow.
pros: A subscription setting, no extra service or bill
BigQuery subscriptions stream straight into the warehouse
Cloud Storage writes in Avro or text with time-based files
cons: No in-flight transformation, Dataflow is needed for that
Only BigQuery and Cloud Storage as destinations
Schema mismatches route messages to a dead-letter topic silently

azure.name: Azure Event Hubs
azure.note: Event Hubs Capture writes Avro files to Blob Storage or Data Lake Storage on a time or size window with no code; Parquet output needs a Stream Analytics no-code editor job. Fabric Eventstream extends this into OneLake, Eventhouse and Fabric tables with light transformation.
pros: Capture is a checkbox on the hub, no extra service
Parquet output and Delta Lake via Eventstream
Eventstream adds no-code filtering and routing
cons: Capture bills an hourly fee per throughput unit on Standard
Only storage destinations without Fabric
Eventstream requires Fabric capacity

rows.pick: The three are interchangeable for landing events as files in storage. Firehose is the obvious pick when the destination is OpenSearch, Splunk or an HTTP endpoint; the other two only reach their own storage and warehouse.
rows.gotcha: Teams choose Kinesis Data Streams when Firehose alone would do, and pay for shards they never read. Buffering windows differ, so near-real-time on one cloud is a minute of latency on another; check the minimum before promising dashboards freshness.

rows.plain: One workshop for the whole machine-learning job: notebooks to explore data, big machines to train models, and a counter that serves predictions.

aws.name: Amazon SageMaker AI
aws.note: Notebooks, training jobs, HyperPod clusters for large-scale training, a model registry and hosted endpoints, assembled as separate parts. The wider Amazon SageMaker brand now also covers the lakehouse and Unified Studio for data and analytics.
pros: Deepest menu of instance types, including Trainium and Inferentia for cheaper training and inference
HyperPod runs multi-week cluster training with automatic checkpoint recovery
Every piece is scriptable and fits teams already living in IAM and S3
cons: Many services under one name; the learning curve is steep and the console sprawls
Idle notebooks bill per instance-hour unless you set lifecycle rules
Ground Truth, Clarify, Debugger and Studio Lab moved to maintenance, announced 30 June 2026 and effective 30 July 2026

gcp.name: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform
gcp.note: The renamed Vertex AI: Workbench and Colab Enterprise notebooks, Managed Training, Pipelines, Inference endpoints, Model Garden and the agent tooling under one console and one API surface. Reorganised agent-first in April 2026.
pros: Most unified of the three: training, tuning, serving and agents share one project and IAM
TPU access alongside GPUs, often the cheaper route for very large models
Direct BigQuery integration for features and training data
cons: Rename churn: tutorials, SDKs and package names still say Vertex AI
Newer accelerators and Gemini variants reach fewer regions than the console implies
Custom training quotas are low by default and take time to raise

azure.name: Azure Machine Learning
azure.note: Workspaces, compute clusters, AutoML, pipelines and managed online endpoints for classical and deep learning. Generative AI work has moved to Microsoft Foundry and the SDKs were consolidated into azure-ai-projects, so two portals now share the job.
pros: Strongest AutoML and low-code designer for teams without ML engineers
Managed endpoints and Entra ID permissions map neatly onto existing Microsoft estates
Prompt flow and Foundry tie generative work into the same workspace
cons: Two products for one job: Azure Machine Learning for classical ML, Foundry for generative
SDK v1 support ended June 2026, forcing rewrites of older pipelines
Compute quotas per region are tight; GPU capacity often needs a support ticket

rows.pick: Choose by where the data already lives and which cloud runs production: all three train and serve the same frameworks. Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform is the most unified, SageMaker AI the most tunable, Azure Machine Learning the best AutoML.
rows.gotcha: AWS and Azure split classical ML from generative AI into separate products (SageMaker AI versus Bedrock, Azure Machine Learning versus Foundry); Google folds both into one platform. Budget two consoles, two permission models and two SDKs on AWS and Azure.

rows.job: Foundation model API and model hub
rows.plain: Rent the big pre-trained models for chat, images and embeddings through one pay-per-use door, billed per token (the word fragments a model counts), instead of running them yourself.

aws.name: Amazon Bedrock
aws.note: One API over Anthropic, Amazon Nova, Meta, Mistral, Cohere and, since June 2026, OpenAI frontier models, with knowledge bases, guardrails and fine-tuning attached. Marketplace-style: pick a model and pay per token or provision throughput.
pros: Widest third-party model choice of the three, with Anthropic and OpenAI side by side
Provisioned throughput and batch inference give predictable cost for heavy loads
Cross-region inference routes around capacity shortages automatically
cons: Newest model versions often reach Bedrock weeks after the vendors' own APIs
Per-model quotas and regional availability vary widely; check before designing
Invocation logging and private endpoints add cost and set-up for regulated use

gcp.name: Model Garden
gcp.note: The catalogue inside Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform: Gemini and Gemma first, plus Anthropic Claude, Meta Llama, Mistral and hundreds of open models to call as a service or deploy. Gemini is also sold directly through the Gemini API for smaller teams.
pros: Gemini models arrive here first, with the longest context windows and native multimodal input
Open models deploy onto TPUs or GPUs you control, with one-click endpoints
Context caching and batch prediction cut token bills for repeated prompts
cons: Two doors to Gemini (Agent Platform and the Gemini API) with different quotas, auth and billing
Partner model availability is region-bound and sometimes US-only
Committed-use discounts require forecasting token volume up front

azure.name: Foundry Models
azure.note: The Foundry catalogue of OpenAI, Microsoft, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, xAI and open models, deployed through one endpoint with pay-per-token or dedicated capacity. Azure OpenAI in Foundry Models is no longer the only cloud home for GPT models; Bedrock added them in June 2026.
pros: First hyperscaler with first-party OpenAI models under enterprise terms, though Bedrock now sells them too
Provisioned throughput units and data-zone deployments make regulated use predictable
Model router picks a cheaper model per request automatically
cons: Serverless and provisioned model lists differ by region; availability tables need checking
Quotas per region and subscription are tight; capacity for new GPT releases is rationed
Frequent renames and API versions leave samples and SDKs inconsistent

rows.pick: Need GPT models under enterprise terms: Foundry Models. Want Claude, Nova, Llama and OpenAI behind one bill: Bedrock. Building on Gemini or open models on TPUs: Model Garden. Otherwise interchangeable; the model matters more than the door.
rows.gotcha: Same model, different behaviour: quotas, context limits, regions and version cadence differ per cloud, and request and response schemas are not portable. Write an adapter layer from day one or a model switch becomes a rewrite.
