rows.plain: A managed place to build an AI assistant that acts through tools, then host it, scale it and watch it work: a serviced office for software workers.

aws.name: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
aws.note: Modular services for agents built with any framework: Runtime for hosting, Memory, Gateway for tools, Identity, Policy, Code Interpreter, Browser and Evaluations, with Strands Agents as the open-source SDK. The older Bedrock Agents Classic entered maintenance mode on 30 July 2026.
pros: Runs agents from any framework (Strands, LangGraph, CrewAI) against any model
Session isolation per user in Runtime: eight hours on microVMs, 14 days on runtime instances
Each module is billed separately, so you pay only for the parts you adopt
cons: Assembly required: several services to wire together before a first production agent
Bedrock Agents Classic, the earlier managed agents, is in maintenance with migrations pending
Consumption pricing across modules is hard to forecast at scale

gcp.name: Agent Runtime
gcp.note: The hosting half of the Agent Platform: deploy agents written with the open-source Agent Development Kit (Python, Java, Go) or other frameworks; it scales them, keeps sessions and runs jobs of up to seven days. Agent Studio and the Agents CLI handle build and deploy.
pros: Agent Development Kit and Runtime are designed together; the deploy path is one command
Seven-day asynchronous runs, second only to AgentCore runtime instances at 14 days
Sessions, Memory Bank, sandboxes and evaluation live in the same platform
cons: Two renames in a year (Agent Engine, then Runtime) break tutorials and package names
Pricing per vCPU-hour and GiB-hour of active runtime is easy to underestimate
Best experience assumes Gemini; other models work with fewer integrations

azure.name: Foundry Agent Service
azure.formerName: Azure AI Foundry Agent Service (earlier Azure AI Agent Service)
azure.note: Managed agents with threads, tools (Azure AI Search, Bing grounding, Logic Apps, functions, MCP servers) and built-in tracing, wired into Foundry Models and governed by Foundry Control Plane. Hosted agents let you bring your own container; Microsoft Agent Framework is the open-source SDK.
pros: Ready-made connectors to Microsoft 365, Logic Apps and most enterprise SaaS
Threads, tracing and evaluation are on by default with no extra services
Same identity, network and compliance controls as the rest of Azure
cons: Assistants API retired in August 2026, forcing migrations onto the newer API
Hosted agents are generally available, but protocols such as A2A v0.3 remain in preview
Private networking set-up needs several Azure resources and careful RBAC

rows.pick: Deep Microsoft 365 or Dynamics estate: Foundry Agent Service. Gemini-centred and wanting the simplest build-to-deploy path: Agent Runtime with ADK. Mixed frameworks and models, or long sessions with strict per-user isolation: AgentCore. Otherwise interchangeable.
rows.gotcha: Execution limits and state models differ: AgentCore sessions last eight hours on microVMs or 14 days on runtime instances, Agent Runtime jobs up to seven days, Foundry threads persist but each run is short. Shape long-running, multi-step designs around these limits rather than porting them.

rows.plain: Giving each AI agent its own badge, a guarded door for its tool calls, and a register so the organisation knows which agents exist and may do what.

aws.name: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
aws.note: Gateway turns APIs, Lambda functions and MCP servers into governed agent tools; AgentCore Identity issues agent credentials and brokers OAuth to third-party services; AgentCore Policy enforces Cedar rules on tool calls. All three are modules of Bedrock AgentCore.
pros: Gateway converts existing APIs into MCP tools without rewriting them
Identity vaults user tokens and handles OAuth flows on the agent's behalf
Policy rules written in Cedar are testable and auditable like IAM
cons: Agents remain IAM roles at heart; there is no first-class agent principal type
AgentCore Registry catalogues agents, MCP servers and tools, but is newer than rival registries
Each module bills per request, so chatty agents multiply costs

gcp.name: Agent Gateway
gcp.note: Agent Identity makes an agent a SPIFFE-based IAM principal with attested credentials; Agent Gateway is the network choke point applying IAM, policy and Model Armor to agent and MCP traffic; Agent Registry catalogues agents, tools and MCP servers. All reached GA in 2026.
pros: Agents are true IAM principals, so existing policies and audit logs just work
Gateway inspects prompts with Model Armor inline, not as a separate call
Registry gives one inventory of agents and MCP servers across projects
cons: All three shipped in 2026; patterns and third-party tooling are immature
Gateway sits in the network path, adding latency and a single point of misconfiguration
Tightly bound to Google IAM; agents on other clouds cannot use it

azure.name: Microsoft Entra Agent ID
azure.note: Every agent from Foundry or Copilot Studio gets an Entra identity with conditional access, lifecycle and access reviews like a user. Foundry Control Plane adds a registry, policy and observability for agents wherever they run, and API Management acts as the tool gateway.
pros: Agents governed with the same conditional access and access reviews as staff
Automatic registration for Foundry and Copilot Studio agents; nothing to wire
Works for agents outside Azure through the Entra identity model
cons: Extending Conditional Access to agents needs Microsoft Agent 365 licences, so sprawl becomes a licensing question
Tool gateway is API Management, a separate product with its own bill
Registry is Foundry-centric; third-party agents need manual onboarding

rows.pick: If governance means treating agents like employees with conditional access and reviews, Entra Agent ID leads. If it means network enforcement and prompt inspection at one choke point, Agent Gateway. AgentCore suits teams exposing existing APIs as tools.
rows.gotcha: The word identity means three things: on Azure an agent is a directory object, on Google an IAM principal with SPIFFE credentials, on AWS still an IAM role plus brokered OAuth tokens. Audit, revocation and cost models all follow from that choice.

rows.plain: A bouncer on both doors of the model: it blocks harmful or off-topic requests going in and leaks, hallucinations or abuse coming out.

aws.name: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
aws.note: Configurable policies for content, denied topics, word lists, PII masking, prompt-attack detection and contextual grounding checks against hallucination, applied to Bedrock models or, through the ApplyGuardrail API, any model. Automated Reasoning checks add formal verification of policy claims.
pros: Works on any model via ApplyGuardrail, not only Bedrock-hosted ones
Grounding and Automated Reasoning checks catch factual drift, not just toxicity
Priced per thousand text units per policy, so light use is cheap
cons: Each policy type bills separately; enabling everything multiplies cost per call
Image checks and some languages lag the English text filters
Adds a few hundred milliseconds per checked call on synchronous paths

gcp.name: Model Armor
gcp.note: A Security Command Center service, also sold standalone, that screens prompts and responses for injection, jailbreaks, sensitive data, malicious links and unsafe content, callable as an API or enforced inline on Agent Gateway. Owned by the security team rather than the ML team.
pros: Cloud-agnostic REST API: screen traffic to models on any provider
Inline enforcement on Agent Gateway needs no code changes in agents
Sensitive Data Protection templates reuse existing DLP rules
cons: Pricing per token screened stacks on top of model tokens
No hallucination or grounding check; it is a safety filter, not a fact-checker
Security-team ownership can slow iteration for application teams

azure.name: Content Safety in Foundry Control Plane
azure.note: Harm categories with severity levels for text, image and video, Prompt Shields for jailbreak and indirect injection, groundedness detection and protected-material checks, exposed as an API and as content filters on every Foundry model deployment. Content Moderator retires in March 2027.
pros: Filters are on by default on Foundry deployments; safety is the baseline, not an add-on
Groundedness detection with correction can rewrite ungrounded answers
Custom categories train from your own examples in hours
cons: Lowering default filters needs an approval process for some scenarios
Billed per thousand records on top of model tokens
Rename churn (Content Safety, then Foundry Control Plane) confuses documentation

rows.pick: Interchangeable for basic harm filtering. Bedrock Guardrails when you need hallucination and reasoning checks; Model Armor when the security team must own screening across clouds; Content Safety when default-on filtering with an approval trail matters.
rows.gotcha: Default posture differs: Azure filters every Foundry deployment unless you opt out, Google's adjustable Gemini filters default to off (core-harm protections excepted) and AWS filters nothing until a guardrail is attached. Porting an app without recreating the guardrails silently changes what users can say.

rows.plain: Marking the AI's homework: scoring answers for accuracy, tone and safety, and checking an agent chose the right tools, before and after release.

aws.name: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations
aws.note: AgentCore Evaluations scores agent trajectories with built-in and custom LLM-judge evaluators, online against live traces or offline; Bedrock Evaluations covers model and RAG evaluation with human or automated judges. SageMaker AI adds classical metrics and Clarify, now in maintenance.
pros: Online evaluation samples live AgentCore traces, not just test sets
Bedrock Evaluations compares models side by side on your own prompts
Custom evaluators are plain prompts; no new framework to learn
cons: Split across Bedrock, AgentCore and SageMaker; three consoles for one discipline
Judge-model tokens are billed like any other inference
Human evaluation workflows thinned since Augmented AI moved to maintenance

gcp.name: Gen AI evaluation service
gcp.note: Part of Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform: pointwise and pairwise LLM-judge metrics, computation metrics, rubric-based and agent-trajectory evaluation, with results stored in experiments and surfaced in Agent Studio. The Agents CLI runs the same evaluations in CI.
pros: Agent trajectory metrics (tool choice, order, precision) out of the box
Pairwise autoraters against Gemini baselines, with adaptive rubrics
Evaluations run from the Agents CLI, so they fit pull-request checks
cons: The judge is Gemini; judging Gemini with Gemini needs second opinions
Priced per thousand characters judged; large suites cost real money
Documentation still mixes Vertex AI and Agent Platform names

azure.name: Foundry Control Plane
azure.note: Evaluations, monitoring and tracing for models and agents, GA since March 2026: built-in quality, safety and agent evaluators (intent resolution, tool-call accuracy, task adherence), a red-teaming agent, and continuous evaluation on production traces. Results feed Foundry's governance views.
pros: Red-teaming agent automates adversarial testing before release
Continuous evaluation on live traffic with alerts in Azure Monitor
One place covers models, agents and the safety filters together
cons: Evaluators default to Azure OpenAI judges; other judges need extra deployment
Evaluation runs consume model quota alongside production
Portal-first; the SDK lags the UI on newer evaluators

rows.pick: All three score models and agents; pick the one where your agents run, because online evaluation depends on that platform's traces. Foundry Control Plane is the most complete single view; Google's has the best CI story.
rows.gotcha: Scores do not transfer: each cloud's judge model, rubric wording and metric names differ, so a 0.8 groundedness here is not a 0.8 there. Keep a small cloud-neutral golden set and re-baseline before comparing providers.

rows.plain: Ready-made eyes for software: spot objects, faces, text and unsafe content in photos and video without training anything yourself.

aws.name: Amazon Rekognition
aws.note: Pre-trained image and video analysis: labels, faces, text, content moderation and Custom Labels, with streaming video events now closed to new customers. Lookout for Vision and Panorama have been retired, leaving Rekognition and Bedrock multimodal models as the AWS vision story.
pros: Face liveness and identity verification are mature and widely deployed
Stored-video analysis continues; streaming via Kinesis Video Streams is existing customers only
Custom Labels trains a detector from a few hundred images
cons: Per-image and per-minute pricing climbs fast on video
Face features carry legal and ethical constraints in several jurisdictions
Edge appliance path ended with Panorama in May 2026

gcp.name: Cloud Vision API
gcp.note: Labels, OCR, faces, landmarks, logos and safe-search for images, with Video Intelligence for video shots, labels and text. Agent Platform Vision (was Vertex AI Vision) for streaming pipelines shuts down on 30 September 2026 after deprecation in June; Gemini multimodal now handles much of this.
pros: Best-in-class OCR and handwriting across scripts, including Indic languages
Free monthly tier of 1,000 units per feature
Gemini can replace fixed features with open-ended questions about an image
cons: Agent Platform Vision ends September 2026; streaming pipelines must move to Vision API or Gemini
No face identification, only detection, by policy
Video Intelligence is priced per minute per feature; multiple features multiply cost

azure.name: Azure Vision in Foundry Tools
azure.note: Image Analysis, OCR (Read), spatial analysis and video retrieval, with Azure AI Face as a separate limited-access API and Azure AI Video Indexer for media insights. Custom Vision and the legacy Image Analysis API retire in September 2028.
pros: Read OCR is strong on printed and handwritten documents and forms
Video Indexer extracts transcripts, faces and topics in one job
Face API includes liveness with limited-access controls for regulated use
cons: Face API requires an approved use-case application
Custom Vision is retiring; custom detectors move to Foundry models
Feature sets differ between API versions; migrations are regular

rows.pick: Interchangeable for labels and OCR. Rekognition for face verification and liveness at scale, Cloud Vision for OCR in many scripts, Azure for video insights via Video Indexer. Increasingly the real choice is a multimodal model prompt instead.
rows.gotcha: Face recognition is policy-gated differently: Google detects faces but will not identify them, Azure needs an approved application, AWS allows it under usage terms. A face-matching design ports cleanly to only one of the three.

rows.plain: A transcriber and a voice actor on tap: turn recordings or live audio into text, and text into natural-sounding speech, billed by audio length or characters.

aws.name: Amazon Transcribe
aws.note: Streaming and batch speech to text with speaker labels, custom vocabularies, PII redaction and call analytics; Amazon Polly provides neural and generative text to speech. Amazon Nova speech models and Connect Customer reuse both for contact centres.
pros: Call analytics and medical transcription variants with redaction built in
Polly generative voices are among the most natural at low price
Deep integration with Connect Customer and Kinesis for live audio
cons: Two separate services and bills for the two directions
Streaming quotas per account need raising for large call centres
Fewer languages for streaming than for batch

gcp.name: Speech-to-Text
gcp.note: Chirp models for streaming and batch recognition across more than 125 languages, with Text-to-Speech offering WaveNet, Neural2, Studio and Gemini-based voices. Gemini Live in the Agent Platform now provides end-to-end voice conversations.
pros: Broadest language coverage, strong on Indian and Southeast Asian languages
Gemini native audio lets one model listen and speak without a pipeline
Speaker diarisation and word timestamps included in the price
cons: Two products and price sheets, and a third path via Gemini Live
Model versions (v1, v2, Chirp 2, Chirp 3) have different feature sets
Data-residency options for speech are narrower than for text

azure.name: Azure Speech in Foundry Tools
azure.note: One service for speech to text, text to speech with neural and custom voices, speech translation, speaker recognition and avatars, plus the Voice Live API for real-time agents. Custom Neural Voice is limited-access.
pros: Single service and bill for both directions, plus live translation
Custom Neural Voice and avatars for branded voices, under approval
Containers let speech run on-premises for data residency
cons: Custom voice needs a use-case application and consent recordings
Concurrency limits per resource are low; scale means several resources
The newer Voice Live API is billed differently from classic speech

rows.pick: Interchangeable for plain dictation and voice-out. Azure Speech when you want one service and on-premises containers; Speech-to-Text for the widest language list; Transcribe plus Polly when audio already flows through Connect Customer or Kinesis.
rows.gotcha: Billing units differ: audio is rounded per second, per 15 seconds or per minute depending on cloud and model, and voices bill per character or per million characters. A cost model built on one cloud can be off by a third on another.

rows.plain: Instant translation between languages for text and whole documents, charged per million characters, like a metered interpreter.

aws.name: Amazon Translate
aws.note: Neural translation for text and documents across 75-plus languages, with custom terminology, active custom translation and batch jobs from S3. Bedrock models increasingly handle nuanced translation with context.
pros: Custom terminology and parallel data adapt output to your domain
Batch translation of whole S3 buckets
Free tier of two million characters a month for the first year
cons: Smaller language list than the other two
Formality control only for some languages
No real-time speech translation; combine with Transcribe and Polly

gcp.name: Cloud Translation
gcp.note: Basic and Advanced editions covering nearly 200 languages, document translation preserving layout, glossaries, custom models and a Gemini-based translation LLM option. Adaptive translation learns from a handful of examples.
pros: Largest language list, including many low-resource languages
Layout-preserving document translation for PDF and Office formats
Adaptive translation with few examples instead of full model training
cons: Basic and Advanced editions have different APIs and prices
Custom models bill for training and hosting
Gemini-based translation is priced differently from the standard model

azure.name: Azure Translator in Foundry Tools
azure.note: Text and document translation across 100-plus languages, transliteration, dictionary lookup and Custom Translator for domain models, with speech translation living in Azure Speech. Containers allow on-premises translation.
pros: Document translation keeps formatting for Office, PDF and HTML
Custom Translator builds domain models from your parallel data
On-premises container option for sovereign environments
cons: Custom Translator training and hosting are billed separately
The move into Foundry Tools has scattered the documentation
Speech translation is a different service and bill

rows.pick: Interchangeable for common language pairs. Cloud Translation for rare languages and Gemini-quality output, Translator for on-premises containers and Office documents, Translate when the text already sits in S3 and a batch job suffices.
rows.gotcha: Free tiers and character counting differ, and custom-model quality depends on how much parallel text you hold. The newer trap is comparing these against a general LLM, which translates better with context but offers no glossary guarantees.

rows.plain: Turning scanned forms, invoices and contracts into structured fields, tables and text that software can use, without a human retyping them.

aws.name: Amazon Textract
aws.note: OCR plus forms, tables, queries and signatures from documents, with specialised APIs for invoices, receipts and identity documents. Bedrock multimodal models and Comprehend cover the classify-and-understand step beyond extraction.
pros: Queries API extracts fields by asking a question, no template needed
Asynchronous jobs handle multi-thousand-page PDFs
Pay per page with separate prices per feature, so OCR-only is cheap
cons: No fully custom models; Custom Queries adapters trained on your documents only sharpen query accuracy
Feature prices stack: forms plus tables plus queries per page
Human review path weakened as Augmented AI moved to maintenance

gcp.name: Document AI
gcp.note: Pre-trained processors for invoices, receipts, identity documents, contracts and more, a Custom Extractor trained from a few labelled samples, and layout parsing that feeds RAG chunking. Gemini underpins the newer processors.
pros: Custom Extractor learns new document types from around ten examples
Layout Parser output drops straight into RAG pipelines
Processor versions are pinned, so behaviour does not shift under you
cons: Pricing per page differs sharply between OCR and specialised processors
Processor quotas per project are modest and take time to raise
Custom processors bill for hosting even when idle

azure.name: Azure Document Intelligence in Foundry Tools
azure.formerName: Azure AI Document Intelligence (earlier Form Recognizer)
azure.note: Read, Layout and prebuilt models for invoices, receipts, identity documents, tax and health forms, plus custom extraction and classification models trained from a few samples. Azure Content Understanding extends the idea to audio, video and images for agents.
pros: Prebuilt models for many regional tax and identity forms
Custom models train from five labelled documents in the Studio
Container option runs extraction inside your own network
cons: Two overlapping products now: Document Intelligence and Content Understanding
Custom neural models bill for training hours
Regional availability of newer model versions lags

rows.pick: Interchangeable for invoices and receipts. Document AI when you must train custom extractors quickly, Document Intelligence for regional tax forms and on-premises containers, Textract when documents already land in S3 and ad hoc queries suffice.
rows.gotcha: Only Google and Azure train custom extractors; on AWS a novel document type means Textract plus an LLM you prompt yourself. Field names, confidence scales and table schemas match nowhere, so downstream parsers get rewritten on every move.

rows.plain: Pre-built text analysis: pull out names, places and dates, judge sentiment, classify topics or summarise, without training a model.

aws.name: Amazon Comprehend
aws.note: Entities, key phrases, sentiment, language detection, PII detection, topic modelling and custom classifiers, with Comprehend Medical for clinical text. Many teams now do the same with a Bedrock prompt.
pros: PII detection and redaction at scale over S3 batches
Custom entity and classification models without ML expertise
Comprehend Medical extracts conditions, medications and codes
cons: Per-unit pricing across many APIs adds up on long text
Custom model endpoints bill by the hour while provisioned
Feature development has slowed as LLMs absorb the use cases

gcp.name: Cloud Natural Language
gcp.note: Entity analysis, sentiment, syntax, content classification and entity sentiment for text, priced per thousand-character unit. Gemini in the Agent Platform is now Google's recommended route for custom or nuanced text understanding.
pros: Syntax and dependency parsing still unmatched among the three
Free tier of 5,000 units per month per feature
Content classification spans more than a thousand categories
cons: No custom model training in the API itself
Feature set is frozen; new work goes to Gemini
No PII redaction; that is Sensitive Data Protection, a separate product

azure.name: Azure Language in Foundry Tools
azure.note: Core capabilities are PII and language detection, named entity recognition and Text analytics for health; conversational language understanding, question answering, sentiment, key phrases, summarisation and custom classification are legacy. QnA Maker retired in October 2025 and LUIS in March 2026, both folded in here.
pros: Conversational language understanding and question answering in the same service
Summarisation and health text analytics without extra products
Custom models train in Language Studio with small labelled sets
cons: LUIS and QnA Maker migrations were forced on customers
Per-record pricing across many features is complex
Custom models bill for training and deployment slots

rows.pick: Interchangeable for sentiment and entities. Azure Language when a chatbot needs intent classification and question answering in one place; Comprehend for PII redaction over S3; Cloud Natural Language for syntax parsing. For anything nuanced, a foundation model prompt now wins.
rows.gotcha: These APIs are frozen or shrinking on all three clouds as LLM prompts absorb the job, so treat them as cheap, deterministic filters rather than the core of understanding. The retired Azure services show how fast the ground shifts.

rows.plain: The chat or phone assistant customers talk to for bookings, support or FAQs, built from dialogue flows or generative prompts and plugged into channels.

aws.name: Amazon Lex
aws.note: Intent and slot-based voice and chat bots with generative fallbacks and Bedrock-powered conversational FAQ, feeding Amazon Connect Customer, the contact centre suite formerly called Amazon Connect. Nova Act and AgentCore cover deeper agentic customer flows.
pros: Native telephony through Connect Customer with one billing relationship
Streaming voice with barge-in and sentiment on the same call
Bedrock intents reduce hand-built dialogue trees
cons: Lex alone lacks channels; you build the web or messaging front end
Pricing per request plus Connect per-minute charges stack on voice
Flow-based bots and generative fallbacks feel like two products

gcp.name: Customer Experience Agent Studio
gcp.note: The 2026 ADK-based platform for customer-facing agents, sitting alongside Conversational Agents (Dialogflow CX) with flows and playbooks, Dialogflow ES for simple bots, Agent Assist and Google Cloud CCaaS for the full contact centre.
pros: Playbooks and ADK agents mix deterministic flows with generative behaviour
Google Cloud CCaaS provides telephony and routing when needed
Evaluation and simulation tooling for customer agents built in
cons: Four overlapping products; choosing between them is a project in itself
Studio launched in 2026, so migration paths from Dialogflow are fresh
Per-session and per-request pricing differ between editions

azure.name: Microsoft Copilot Studio
azure.note: Low-code agent builder with generative answers, topic flows, multi-agent orchestration and computer-using agents, publishing to Teams, web, WhatsApp and telephony; Azure AI Bot Service remains the code-first layer for Bot Framework bots. Licensed via Microsoft 365 prepaid packs or pay-as-you-go on an Azure subscription.
pros: Publishes to Teams and Microsoft 365 with no extra channel work
Model choice across OpenAI and Anthropic since September 2025
Business users build; developers extend through Foundry Agent Service
cons: Copilot Credits come as Microsoft 365 packs or pay-as-you-go on Azure, two billing routes to reconcile
Bot Framework and Bot Service feel legacy and are thinly updated
Telephony needs Dynamics 365 Contact Center or a partner

rows.pick: Contact centre with phone lines: Lex with Connect Customer, or Google Cloud CCaaS. Internal or Teams-facing assistants: Copilot Studio. Google's Customer Experience Agent Studio is strongest for generative customer agents with built-in evaluation.
rows.gotcha: Only AWS bills the bot and the telephony on one cloud invoice; Copilot Studio is a Microsoft 365 licence and Google splits CCaaS from the agent platform. Channel integration, not dialogue design, is where migrations break.

rows.plain: Letting staff and apps ask questions of the company's own documents and systems, with the AI answering from what it finds rather than from memory.

aws.name: Amazon Quick
aws.formerName: Amazon Q Business (succeeded), Amazon QuickSight, Amazon Quick Suite
aws.note: The employee-facing assistant and BI suite that absorbed Amazon Q Business: connectors to SharePoint, Salesforce and S3, chat over documents, dashboards and automation. For developer-built RAG, Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases (fully managed since March 2026) replaces Amazon Kendra, closed to new customers in July 2026.
pros: Suite bundles search, chat, BI and automation on one per-user price
Bedrock Knowledge Bases handle chunking, embeddings and vector storage for you
Dozens of connectors with document-level permissions
cons: Kendra and Q Business are both retiring; existing customers face migrations
Per-user pricing makes broad rollout expensive compared with usage-based search
Quick is BI-flavoured; pure search teams may find it heavy

gcp.name: Gemini Enterprise
gcp.note: Employee-facing app to find, chat with and build agents over company data via connectors to Workspace, Microsoft 365, Salesforce and more. Developers build the same on Agent Search (was Vertex AI Search) and RAG Engine inside the Agent Platform.
pros: Google-quality ranking over data stores with permission-aware results
Agent Search doubles as the grounding tool for custom agents
Gemini Enterprise ships prebuilt agents such as Deep Research
cons: Per-seat licensing for Gemini Enterprise on top of usage-based Agent Search
Two renames (Agentspace, Vertex AI Search) in twelve months
Connectors to non-Google systems are less mature than to Workspace

azure.name: Azure AI Search
azure.note: The index behind most Azure RAG builds: hybrid keyword, vector and semantic ranking, integrated vectorisation and agentic retrieval, now wrapped by Foundry IQ as a managed knowledge layer for agents. The employee-facing equivalent is Microsoft 365 Copilot, licensed outside Azure.
pros: Most-used vector and hybrid index for custom RAG, with mature SDKs
Foundry IQ handles chunking, indexing and retrieval planning
Integrated vectorisation pipelines skip custom embedding code
cons: Search units bill per hour whether or not queries arrive
The employee assistant, Microsoft 365 Copilot, is a separate licence, not an Azure service
Index size and vector limits per tier force tier upgrades

rows.pick: Employees wanting a ready assistant over Google Workspace: Gemini Enterprise; over Microsoft 365: Microsoft 365 Copilot; AWS shops with BI needs: Amazon Quick. Developers building custom RAG most often pick Azure AI Search or Bedrock Knowledge Bases.
rows.gotcha: The three sit at different layers: Quick and Gemini Enterprise are per-seat employee apps, Azure AI Search is a per-hour index most custom RAG builds use as their vector store. Match layers before comparing price, and expect the AWS retirements to force a redesign.

rows.plain: A pair programmer inside the editor and terminal that completes code, explains it, and increasingly takes on whole tasks on its own.

aws.name: Kiro
aws.note: Agentic IDE and CLI built around specs, hooks and steering files, with Kiro Autonomous Agent working asynchronously as a virtual developer. Amazon Q Developer's IDE plugins and subscriptions end in April 2027, leaving Kiro as the coding tool and Q Developer as the console assistant.
pros: Spec-driven workflow suits teams wanting requirements and design before code
Autonomous Agent runs tasks from issue to pull request without babysitting
Kiro CLI replaced the Q Developer CLI, so terminal and IDE share one agent
cons: Young product with fast-changing pricing tiers
AWS-centric MCP servers and skills; less value outside AWS
Q Developer's deadline forces a tooling change on existing users

gcp.name: Gemini Code Assist
gcp.note: Completion, chat and agent mode in IDEs and terminal, in Standard and Enterprise editions with private-repository customisation; the free individual tier ended 18 June 2026. Antigravity, the agent-first IDE, CLI and SDK where agents write, run and test code, now hosts free and consumer use.
pros: Enterprise tier customises on your own codebase with intellectual-property indemnity
Antigravity gives a full agent-first IDE, not just a plugin
Free and consumer use lives on in Antigravity; Code Assist is Standard and Enterprise only
cons: Two products (Code Assist and Antigravity) with unclear boundaries
Gemini CLI consumer tiers stopped serving; scripts needed updating
Best model access assumes Gemini; no Anthropic or OpenAI choice

azure.name: GitHub Copilot
azure.note: Completion, chat, coding agent and agent mode across VS Code, JetBrains and the GitHub web, with model choice across OpenAI, Anthropic and Google models. Sold by GitHub per seat with premium request quotas, and the de facto default on any cloud.
pros: Model choice across vendors inside one subscription
Coding agent works from GitHub issues to pull requests where code already lives
Most mature enterprise controls: policies, audit, intellectual-property indemnity
cons: Premium request quotas make heavy agent use cost extra
Tied to GitHub for the best features; Azure DevOps gets less
Not an Azure service: billed and governed through GitHub

rows.pick: Most teams pick GitHub Copilot regardless of cloud because the code is on GitHub. Kiro appeals to spec-first AWS teams; Gemini Code Assist and Antigravity to Google-centred shops, with free use now living in Antigravity.
rows.gotcha: Rapid churn is the trap: Amazon Q Developer plugins end April 2027, Gemini CLI consumer tiers ended June 2026 and Duet AI is two renames back. Standardise on the assistant, not the cloud, and budget for a tooling swap every eighteen months.

rows.plain: The 'you might also like' engine: ranking products or content for each visitor from their behaviour, as a managed service instead of a data-science team.

aws.name: Amazon Personalize
aws.note: Real-time recommenders trained from your interaction, item and user data with ready recipes for e-commerce and media, plus batch inference and generative themes. Long-lived and stable while rivals retired theirs.
pros: Recipes for user personalisation, similar items and rankings with no ML work
Real-time event ingestion updates recommendations within seconds
Batch and streaming inference on the same trained solution
cons: Campaign endpoints bill per provisioned transactions per second while idle
Training costs per data hour add up on frequent retrains
Cold-start quality depends heavily on item metadata quality

gcp.name: AI Commerce Search
gcp.note: Retail-focused product search and recommendations trained on catalogue and event data, using Google Search ranking technology. General recommendation outside retail moves to BigQuery ML matrix factorisation or custom models on the Agent Platform.
pros: Search and recommendations share one catalogue and event stream
Google ranking quality with revenue-optimised objectives
Usage-based pricing per thousand predictions, nothing provisioned
cons: Retail-only shape; media or content recommendations fit awkwardly
Three renames since 2020 complicate documentation
Event volume minimums before models reach quality

azure.none: Azure AI Personalizer retires on 1 October 2026 with no successor; teams train recommenders in Azure Machine Learning or rank with Foundry Models.

rows.pick: Personalize is the obvious managed choice for non-retail or mixed catalogues; AI Commerce Search for retailers wanting search and recommendations together. On Azure, plan to build.
rows.gotcha: Two of three clouds have retired or narrowed their recommenders, so the managed-service approach carries platform risk. Data schemas (items, users, events) are not portable either; keep raw events in your own store so a switch is a retrain, not a rebuild.

rows.plain: Predicting next month's demand, traffic or revenue from past numbers, with the statistics handled for you.

aws.name: Amazon SageMaker AI
aws.note: Amazon Forecast closed to new customers in July 2024; SageMaker Canvas (no-code) and SageMaker Autopilot time-series jobs inherited the recipes, alongside Bedrock and Nova for narrative forecasts. The path is now a general ML platform, not a dedicated service.
pros: Canvas gives analysts a no-code forecasting flow with what-if analysis
Same platform hosts custom models when the recipes fall short
No separate service to learn or govern
cons: Forecast users must migrate; recipes moved but the APIs did not
Canvas sessions and Autopilot jobs bill by the hour
No ready API endpoint; deployment is your job

gcp.name: BigQuery
gcp.note: BigQuery ML forecasts in SQL with ARIMA_PLUS and the TimesFM foundation model behind AI.FORECAST, so data never leaves the warehouse. The Agent Platform hosts TimesFM and custom models when SQL is not enough.
pros: Forecast in one SQL statement over data already in BigQuery
TimesFM zero-shot forecasting needs no training step
Billed as BigQuery compute; no separate service
cons: Tied to BigQuery; data elsewhere must be loaded first
Less control over model internals than a notebook workflow
Slot or byte pricing surprises on large backfills

azure.name: Azure Machine Learning
azure.note: AutoML forecasting trains and compares many models, with deep-learning options and hierarchical forecasts, deployed to managed endpoints. AI Anomaly Detector and Metrics Advisor retire on 1 October 2026, so Azure Machine Learning is the remaining path.
pros: AutoML handles feature engineering, lags and holiday calendars
Endpoints and monitoring in the same workspace
Fabric notebooks can call the same models over OneLake data
cons: Compute for AutoML sweeps bills per node-hour
Two retiring adjacent services force migrations
Requires a workspace and some ML literacy

rows.pick: If the history already sits in BigQuery, BigQuery ML is the obvious choice. Otherwise all three route you to a general ML platform; pick the one your data team already uses.
rows.gotcha: Dedicated forecasting services are dying on all three clouds (Amazon Forecast, Anomaly Detector, Metrics Advisor), so designs should assume a general platform. Foundation-model forecasting such as TimesFM shifts the cost model from training hours to per-query compute.

rows.plain: The specialised engines that make training and running models affordable: NVIDIA GPUs everywhere, plus each cloud's own chips at a discount.

aws.name: AWS Trainium
aws.note: Custom training and inference chips (Trainium2, Trainium3 UltraServers GA December 2025, Inferentia) sold as EC2 Trn and Inf instances and through SageMaker HyperPod, alongside the P and G series NVIDIA GPU instances. Elastic Inference has been discontinued, closed to new customers since April 2023.
pros: Trainium and Inferentia undercut GPU prices by a wide margin for supported models
EC2 UltraClusters and HyperPod for very large training jobs
Capacity Blocks reserve GPUs for a defined window
cons: Trainium needs the Neuron SDK; not every framework or kernel is supported
Latest NVIDIA generations are often scarce and region-limited
Custom chip lock-in: Neuron-compiled models do not move

gcp.name: Cloud TPU
gcp.note: Google's tensor processors (Trillium, Ironwood, and eighth-generation TPU 8t and 8i announced in 2026) for training and serving, alongside Cloud GPUs on Compute Engine, GKE and Cloud Run, packaged with networking and storage as AI Hypercomputer and scheduled by Cluster Director.
pros: TPU pods offer the best price-performance for large JAX and PyTorch training
GPUs attach to Cloud Run for serverless inference
AI Hypercomputer bundles storage and networking tuned for accelerators
cons: TPUs favour JAX and XLA; some PyTorch code needs rework
TPU availability is concentrated in a few regions
Reservations or committed use are effectively required for large jobs

azure.name: Azure Virtual Machines
azure.note: NVIDIA GPUs through the ND and NC series (H100, GB200 and successors) on Virtual Machines, AKS, Batch and CycleCloud, with Azure Machine Learning and Foundry on top. Azure Maia, Microsoft's own accelerator, serves first-party models and is not sold as a VM size.
pros: Early access to each NVIDIA generation at OpenAI-partnership scale
InfiniBand-connected ND clusters for large distributed training
Same quota and reservation model as the rest of Azure
cons: No customer-rentable custom chip; GPU pricing has no in-house alternative
GPU quota is tight and approval-gated in most regions
Newest sizes arrive in a handful of US regions first

rows.pick: Training very large models: TPUs or Trainium give the cheapest price per token if your stack supports them. Anything else, or portable code: NVIDIA GPUs on any cloud, chosen by where you can actually get quota.
rows.gotcha: Custom chips are a one-way door: Neuron-compiled and TPU-compiled models do not move between clouds, whereas CUDA code does. The real constraint in 2026 is quota and capacity, not list price, so design for the accelerator you can obtain.

rows.plain: A notebook the agent keeps between conversations, so it remembers your preferences and past facts instead of starting from zero every time.

aws.name: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory
aws.note: Short-term session memory plus long-term strategies (summaries, user preferences, semantic facts and, since December 2025, episodic memory) that AgentCore extracts from conversations and retrieves by namespace. Works with any framework, hosted on or off AgentCore.
pros: Built-in extraction strategies; no embedding pipeline to build
Namespaces separate memory per user, tenant or agent
Usable from agents running outside AgentCore Runtime
cons: Billed per event stored and per retrieval, hard to forecast for chatty agents
Extraction runs asynchronously; facts appear seconds later
Memory schema is AgentCore-specific, so exports are manual

gcp.name: Memory Bank
gcp.note: Managed long-term memory in the Agent Platform that extracts user context from sessions, consolidates it and recalls it by scope, with memory profiles GA in July 2026 for per-user personas. Integrates natively with ADK and Agent Runtime sessions.
pros: Native ADK integration; one flag turns memory on
Consolidation merges and updates facts instead of appending forever
Memory profiles let one agent hold distinct user personas
cons: Extraction uses Gemini and is billed as tokens
Tightly bound to Agent Platform sessions; other runtimes integrate by hand
Deletion and residency controls are newer than the rest of IAM

azure.none: No standalone memory service: Foundry Agent Service keeps threads and long-term memory is preview-only, so teams persist facts in Cosmos DB or Azure Managed Redis.

rows.pick: Memory Bank if you build with ADK, AgentCore Memory if you need memory for agents hosted anywhere. On Azure, build it yourself for now.
rows.gotcha: Memory is not portable: each service extracts different fact types with its own schema and retrieval semantics, so an agent moved between clouds forgets everything. Keep raw transcripts in your own store as the source of truth.

rows.plain: A locked, disposable room where an agent can run the code it wrote or drive a web browser without touching your real systems.

aws.name: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
aws.note: AgentCore Code Interpreter runs agent-written Python, JavaScript or TypeScript in isolated sessions, and AgentCore Browser provides managed headless browsers with session recording. Amazon Nova Act adds a model and SDK for reliable browser automation.
pros: Code Interpreter and Browser bill per second for CPU and memory used, no infrastructure
Browser sessions record and replay for audit
Nova Act specialises in dependable web-form automation
cons: Sandbox images are fixed; custom dependencies need workarounds
Session lifetimes and concurrency quotas cap long jobs
Three products for one idea, each with its own pricing

gcp.name: Agent Sandbox
gcp.note: Hardened gVisor-based sandboxes on GKE, plus code execution, shell and computer-use sandboxes in the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform for running agent code and driving desktops; launch stages vary, so check before relying on GA. Cloud Run Sandboxes are in preview for the serverless route.
pros: Kernel-level isolation via gVisor with GKE-native scaling
Computer Use sandbox gives agents a full desktop, not just a browser
Warm pools cut start latency for interactive agents
cons: The GKE flavour means running a cluster; the serverless path is still preview
New in 2026; tooling and examples are thin
Priced as GKE or Agent Platform compute, so idle pools cost

azure.name: Azure Container Apps
azure.note: Dynamic sessions give Hyper-V isolated code interpreter or custom container sandboxes allocated from a warm pool in under a second, the natural home for Foundry agents' code execution. Copilot Studio adds computer-using agents for desktop and browser tasks.
pros: Hyper-V isolation per session with a pooled, sub-second allocator
Custom container sessions run any runtime you package
Same Container Apps environment and networking as your other services
cons: Session pools bill for the ready pool, not only active sessions
Browser automation lives in Copilot Studio, a Microsoft 365 licence
Regional availability of session pools lags Container Apps generally

rows.pick: Interchangeable for running snippets of agent-written code. Google when agents need a full desktop; Azure when you already run Container Apps or Foundry agents; AWS when browser automation and recording matter most.
rows.gotcha: Isolation technology differs (gVisor on Google, Hyper-V on Azure, isolated containers on AWS), and so do session lifetimes and what counts as billable time. A design that lets agents keep state in the sandbox between turns hits a different lifetime cap on each cloud.

rows.plain: Your own fenced-off network inside the cloud, like the internal wiring of an office building: you divide it into smaller address blocks (subnets), and peering wires two such networks together.

aws.name: Amazon VPC
aws.note: A regional network you carve into zonal subnets with route tables, security groups, stateless network ACLs and gateways. Peering, Transit Gateway and PrivateLink join VPCs together, and VPC IPAM tracks address ranges across accounts.
pros: Finest-grained controls of the three: security groups, network ACLs, per-subnet routing, flow logs
Security groups can reference other groups, so rules follow identity rather than IP ranges
The VPC itself is free; you pay only for gateways, endpoints and addresses
cons: Regional, so multi-region estates mean many VPCs stitched by peering or Transit Gateway
Public IPv4 addresses have billed by the hour since 2024
CIDR planning across accounts is your problem; overlaps block peering later

gcp.name: Virtual Private Cloud
gcp.note: A single global network with regional subnets, so VMs in different regions talk privately without peering. Firewall rules and routes are network-wide and match by tag or service account, and Shared VPC lets one host project serve many service projects.
pros: One network spans every region; no cross-region peering or transit hub to build
Shared VPC centralises networking under one host project while teams keep their own projects
Regional subnets are zone-agnostic, so zone failures need no subnet redesign
cons: Global scope means a wrong route or firewall rule has worldwide blast radius
VPC Network Peering is non-transitive and quota-bound; many networks push you to Network Connectivity Center
Every new project gets a permissive default network that organisation policy must disable

azure.name: Azure Virtual Network
azure.note: A regional network whose subnets span all availability zones, with zone placement chosen per resource. Network security groups attach to subnets or NICs, VNet peering including global peering links networks, and Azure Virtual Network Manager handles fleets of them.
pros: Subnets span the region, so zone placement is a per-VM decision, not a subnet redesign
Global VNet peering connects regions directly without a hub
Virtual Network Manager applies connectivity and security rules across hundreds of VNets
cons: Regional, so hub-and-spoke or Virtual WAN is needed at scale
Peering traffic is billed in both directions
Firewall, Bastion, VPN Gateway and many PaaS services each demand a dedicated subnet, eating address space

rows.pick: Interchangeable as a concept, and the rest of your stack decides. GCP's global VPC removes cross-region plumbing for multi-region systems; AWS gives the finest-grained controls for regulated designs; Azure's region-wide subnets simplify zone placement.
rows.gotcha: The single biggest structural difference: AWS and Azure networks are regional; a GCP VPC is global. Subnets differ again: an AWS subnet lives in one availability zone, Azure and GCP subnets span the whole region, with the zone chosen per resource.

rows.plain: A traffic director that spreads incoming requests across many servers and stops sending to any that fall ill, like a restaurant host seating diners across tables.

aws.name: Elastic Load Balancing
aws.note: One family with three regional balancers: Application Load Balancer for layer 7, Network Load Balancer for layer 4 with static IPs, and Gateway Load Balancer for inserting third-party appliances. Every one is regional and spans zones; global entry needs Route 53 or Global Accelerator.
pros: Native targets for Auto Scaling, ECS, EKS and Lambda
Network Load Balancer gives static IPs and very high throughput
Gateway Load Balancer is unique: transparent insertion of firewalls and other appliances
cons: Regional only; cross-region needs Route 53 or Global Accelerator on top
Capacity-unit pricing is hard to forecast and one balancer per microservice adds up
Application Load Balancer has no static IP without Global Accelerator in front

gcp.name: Cloud Load Balancing
gcp.note: A single product family covering global and regional, external and internal, application and network balancing on Envoy-based proxies. The global external Application Load Balancer gives one anycast IP across all regions, and Cloud CDN and Cloud Armor attach to it directly.
pros: One anycast IP fronts backends in many regions with no extra product
Cloud CDN, Cloud Armor and Certificate Manager plug straight in
First five forwarding rules share one flat hourly charge, cheap for many small services
cons: Global balancers require Premium Tier networking, priced above Standard Tier
Many variants (global, regional, classic, passthrough, proxy) with different feature sets confuse newcomers
Regional proxy balancers need a proxy-only subnet reserved in each region

azure.name: Azure Load Balancer
azure.note: Azure splits the job by layer and scope: Load Balancer for zone-redundant layer 4, Application Gateway for regional layer 7 with WAF, Front Door for the global layer 7 door. Application Gateway V1 retired in April 2026; V2 is the only current tier.
pros: Standard Load Balancer is cheap, zone-redundant and handles internal and public traffic
Application Gateway bundles WAF and integrates with AKS via Application Gateway for Containers
Front Door covers global routing, caching and WAF in one bill
cons: Three products, three configuration models and three bills for one job
Application Gateway V2 carries a fixed hourly floor plus capacity units, expensive for small workloads
Cross-region Load Balancer is layer 4 only; Basic Load Balancer retired September 2025

rows.pick: GCP is the obvious choice when you want one anycast IP fronting backends in several regions. AWS when you need transparent appliance insertion or static-IP layer 4 at scale. Azure when regional layer 7 with WAF and AKS integration matters.
rows.gotcha: Azure splits by scope as well as layer: Front Door is the global layer 7 door, Application Gateway the regional layer 7 one, Load Balancer the layer 4 one. GCP does all of it with one global family, and AWS balancers are regional only.

rows.plain: One fixed address advertised from every corner of the world, so users land on the nearest healthy entrance, like a single phone number routed to the closest branch.

aws.name: AWS Global Accelerator
aws.note: Two static anycast IPs that carry TCP and UDP over the AWS backbone to load balancers, instances or Elastic IPs in several regions. It works at layer 4 with health-checked failover in seconds, with no caching, TLS termination or WAF.
pros: Static IPs survive endpoint changes, ideal for customer allowlists
Handles non-HTTP traffic such as gaming, VoIP and MQTT
Failover between regions in seconds using its own health checks
cons: Fixed hourly fee plus a premium data transfer rate on every byte
No layer 7 features; HTTP workloads usually want CloudFront instead or as well
Endpoints must be AWS resources; it cannot front on-premises or other clouds

gcp.name: Cloud Load Balancing
gcp.note: There is no separate product: a global external Application Load Balancer or proxy Network Load Balancer already advertises one reserved anycast IP from every Google edge with Premium Tier. Cloud Armor and Cloud CDN ride on the same front end.
pros: No extra service or fee beyond the load balancer itself
The anycast address is a reserved static IP you own
WAF and CDN attach to the same global front
cons: Premium Tier networking only, so no cheaper Standard Tier option
Only HTTP(S), TCP proxy and SSL proxy go global; UDP stays regional among GA products, with a global passthrough option in preview
Anycast is a property of the balancer, not attachable to arbitrary endpoints

azure.name: Azure Front Door
azure.note: A global layer 7 entry with anycast, split TCP, TLS termination, caching and WAF in Standard and Premium tiers. For non-HTTP traffic the cross-region Load Balancer offers a global layer 4 address, and Front Door classic retires in 2027.
pros: TLS termination, WAF and caching come with the anycast front
Premium tier reaches origins over Private Link with no public exposure
Health probes and priority or weighted origin groups give simple failover
cons: HTTP and HTTPS only; no TCP or UDP passthrough
Premium carries a monthly base fee of several hundred dollars before traffic
Front-end IPs are shared, so origin allowlists must use service tags instead of IPs

rows.pick: AWS Global Accelerator is the choice for non-HTTP traffic that needs fixed IPs. Azure Front Door when you want anycast, WAF and caching in one HTTP product. On GCP, you already have it if you use a global load balancer.
rows.gotcha: Global Accelerator is layer 4 with no caching or WAF; Front Door is layer 7 only; GCP's anycast is a property of its load balancer, not a product. Only AWS and GCP give you a dedicated static anycast IP, Front Door's addresses are shared.

rows.plain: The internet's address book, turning a memorable name into a machine address and, optionally, steering each user to the closest or healthiest copy of your site.

aws.name: Amazon Route 53
aws.note: Public and private hosted zones, domain registration, hybrid resolution through Route 53 Resolver, and the richest routing policy set: weighted, latency, geolocation, geoproximity, failover, IP-based and multivalue, all health-checked. Amazon Application Recovery Controller, formerly under the Route 53 brand, adds routing controls for failover.
pros: DNS, domain registration, hybrid resolvers and traffic steering in one service
Health-checked routing policies cover latency, geography and failover without another product
99.99 percent monthly uptime SLA per hosted zone on the authoritative service
cons: Per zone, per query, per health check and per Resolver endpoint hour: many small line items
Traffic Flow policies, optional for geoproximity, cost 50 dollars per policy record per month
Resolver endpoints bill per elastic network interface per hour, whether busy or idle

gcp.name: Cloud DNS
gcp.note: Managed public and private zones on Google's anycast servers with DNSSEC, forwarding and peering zones for hybrid, and routing policies for weighted, geolocation and failover answers. Private zones bind to the global VPC, and Cloud Domains handles registration separately.
pros: Private zones attach to a global VPC once, covering every region
Cheap per zone and per million queries with a 100 percent SLA
Forwarding and peering zones make hybrid resolution declarative
cons: Routing policies and health checks are narrower than Route 53's
Domain registration lives in a separate service, Cloud Domains
Inbound and outbound server policies are per VPC and easy to misconfigure in Shared VPC

azure.name: Azure DNS
azure.note: Azure DNS hosts public zones and Private DNS zones that link to VNets and can auto-register VM records; DNS Private Resolver covers hybrid forwarding. Traffic steering is a separate product, Azure Traffic Manager, with priority, weighted, performance, geographic, multivalue and subnet routing.
pros: Private DNS zones auto-register VMs from linked VNets
Traffic Manager probes endpoints in any cloud or on-premises, not just Azure
Very low per-zone and per-query pricing
cons: Two products, Azure DNS and Traffic Manager, for what Route 53 does in one
No routing policies in Azure DNS itself; every steering need means Traffic Manager
Domain registration is not part of Azure DNS; App Service Domains covers a subset

rows.pick: Route 53 is the obvious choice when you want DNS-level traffic steering with health checks inside one service. For plain zone hosting the three are interchangeable: all anycast, all cheap, all with private zones for internal names.
rows.gotcha: Route 53's routing-policy set (geoproximity and so on) is richer; on Azure any steering lives in Traffic Manager, not Azure DNS, and Cloud DNS policies are narrower. Private zones attach to VPCs on AWS, one global VPC on GCP, and per-VNet links on Azure.

rows.plain: A worldwide network of caches that keeps copies of your images, videos and pages close to users, like stocking local warehouses instead of shipping from one factory.

aws.name: Amazon CloudFront
aws.note: A global CDN with edge compute (CloudFront Functions and Lambda@Edge), Origin Shield, signed URLs and tight S3 and Application Load Balancer integration, protected by AWS WAF and Shield. Each distribution carries its own behaviours and cache policies.
pros: One terabyte of egress free every month
Edge compute is built in, from tiny CloudFront Functions to Lambda@Edge
Origin access control keeps S3 buckets private behind the CDN
cons: Behaviours, cache and origin request policies are fiddly to configure and debug
Invalidations cost after the first thousand paths a month
Configuration changes take minutes to propagate to every edge

gcp.name: Cloud CDN
gcp.note: Not a standalone distribution but a checkbox on a backend of the global external Application Load Balancer, using its anycast IP and Cloud Armor policies. Media CDN is a separate product for very large video streaming and download workloads.
pros: Enabled per backend on the load balancer you already have; nothing extra to deploy
Shares the balancer's anycast IP, certificates and Cloud Armor policy
Media CDN offers a purpose-built tier for streaming at scale
cons: Requires a global external Application Load Balancer on Premium Tier
Edge compute relies on Service Extensions, far younger than Lambda@Edge
Media CDN is a separate product with its own configuration model and pricing

azure.name: Azure Front Door
azure.note: Front Door Standard and Premium are Azure's CDN, combining caching, a rules engine, global routing and WAF, with Private Link to origins on Premium. Azure Content Delivery Network classic is retiring: the Edgio flavour ended in 2025 and Microsoft classic retires in September 2027.
pros: CDN, global load balancing and WAF on one profile and one bill
Premium reaches origins privately over Private Link
Rules engine handles redirects, header rewrites and cache overrides without code
cons: Monthly base fee per profile before any traffic, steep on Premium
No edge compute comparable to Lambda@Edge or CloudFront Functions
Classic CDN and Front Door classic customers face a forced migration by 2027

rows.pick: CloudFront when you need edge compute or serve heavily from S3, helped by the free terabyte. Cloud CDN if you already front with a global load balancer. Front Door when one product for CDN, WAF and global routing suits you.
rows.gotcha: Cloud CDN attaches to the global load balancer rather than existing as its own distribution, and Lambda@Edge-style compute is a separate concern there (Service Extensions or Cloud Run patterns). On Azure the standalone CDN is retiring, so CDN now means Front Door, a global balancer.

rows.plain: A private side door that lets your network reach a cloud service or another company's service without touching the public internet, like a corridor between two offices.

aws.name: AWS PrivateLink
aws.note: Interface endpoints place an elastic network interface with a private IP in your subnets, fronting AWS services, Marketplace SaaS or your own service behind a Network or Gateway Load Balancer. Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free and route-based; cross-region endpoints arrived in 2024.
pros: Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB cost nothing
Cross-account and, since 2024, cross-region connections without peering
Private DNS makes the service's normal hostname resolve to the endpoint
cons: Interface endpoints bill per hour per zone plus per gigabyte; many services across VPCs add up
Producers must front their service with a Network or Gateway Load Balancer
Endpoint policies are coarse compared with IAM on the service itself

gcp.name: Private Service Connect
gcp.note: Endpoints are internal forwarding rules that reach Google APIs or a producer's service attachment, with the producer side NATed so no routes or address ranges are exchanged. Private Google Access and private services access (VPC peering) are older siblings still in use.
pros: One endpoint can reach the whole bundle of Google APIs
Global access lets an endpoint in one region serve clients in every region of the VPC
Producer-side NAT means consumer and producer address ranges may overlap
cons: Producers need an internal load balancer, a service attachment and a dedicated NAT subnet
Three overlapping mechanisms (Private Service Connect, Private Google Access, private services access) confuse designs
Per-endpoint hourly plus per-gigabyte charges, like the others

azure.name: Azure Private Link
azure.note: A Private Endpoint is a NIC with a private IP in your VNet fronting an Azure PaaS resource, partner service or your own Private Link Service behind a Standard Load Balancer. Private DNS zones map each service's public name to the private address.
pros: Covers almost every Azure PaaS service, including storage and databases
Front Door Premium and API Management can use it to reach private origins
Per-endpoint hourly plus per-gigabyte pricing with no per-zone multiplier
cons: Every PaaS resource needs its own endpoint and matching private DNS zone; dozens of zones
Network security groups on private endpoints require explicit opt-in
Private Link Service producers must sit behind a Standard Load Balancer

rows.pick: Interchangeable: all three are the same pattern, a consumer-side endpoint fronting a producer service with no route exchange. Choose whichever cloud hosts the consuming network; producers selling across clouds simply publish on all three.
rows.gotcha: Azure draws a line between Private Endpoint (a private IP in your VNet) and Service Endpoint (a routing shortcut), and they are not interchangeable. AWS separates free gateway endpoints from paid interface endpoints, and GCP has Private Google Access as a route-based alternative.

rows.plain: A leased private cable from your own data centre straight into the cloud, bypassing the public internet for steadier speed and lower transfer bills.

aws.name: AWS Direct Connect
aws.note: Dedicated ports of 1, 10, 100 and 400 Gbps or partner-hosted connections from 50 Mbps, split into private, transit and public virtual interfaces. Direct Connect Gateway reaches VPCs in many regions from one port, and MACsec encrypts dedicated links.
pros: Up to 400 Gbps dedicated, matching the largest ports on Google Cloud and Azure
Direct Connect Gateway serves every region from one physical connection
Cheaper data transfer out than internet egress
cons: Port hours bill from provisioning, weeks before traffic flows
The 99.99 percent SLA needs redundant connections at two sites; a single link gets 95 percent
Hosted connections have no native encryption; you layer VPN or MACsec

gcp.name: Cloud Interconnect
gcp.note: Dedicated Interconnect at 10, 100 or 400 Gbps, Partner Interconnect from 50 Mbps to 50 Gbps, and Cross-Cloud Interconnect to other providers, all terminating in VLAN attachments with BGP on Cloud Router. Because the VPC is global, one attachment can reach every region.
pros: One attachment reaches all regions of a global VPC with global dynamic routing
Cross-Cloud Interconnect extends the same product to other clouds
99.99 percent SLA topology is documented and achievable with four attachments
cons: Dedicated ports start at 10 Gbps, then 100 and 400; anything smaller means a partner
BGP through Cloud Router is mandatory; no static-route shortcut
VLAN attachments bill hourly on top of port and egress charges

azure.name: Azure ExpressRoute
azure.note: Provider circuits from 50 Mbps to 10 Gbps or ExpressRoute Direct at 10, 100 or 400 Gbps, with private peering into VNets and Microsoft peering for Microsoft 365 and PaaS. Each VNet needs an ExpressRoute gateway or Virtual WAN hub; Global Reach links your sites.
pros: Microsoft peering carries Microsoft 365 and public PaaS traffic privately
Metered or Unlimited egress plans let heavy movers fix their transfer bill
Global Reach joins your data centres through Microsoft's backbone
cons: A gateway per VNet with its own SKU pricing, or a Virtual WAN hub
Standard circuits cap linked VNets; cross-geography needs the Premium add-on
Three bills: the circuit, the gateway and the connectivity provider

rows.pick: Interchangeable: dedicated fibre from a carrier or colocation site into the cloud, in all three. The choice follows where your data centre and colocation partner already have presence and which cloud holds the bulk of your traffic.
rows.gotcha: Dedicated and Partner Interconnect mirror Direct Connect tiers, and all three pair with VPN or MACsec for encryption. Scope differs: one GCP attachment reaches every region of a global VPC, AWS needs a Direct Connect Gateway, Azure a gateway per VNet or Virtual WAN.

rows.plain: An encrypted tunnel over the ordinary internet that joins your office or laptop to your cloud network, like a sealed pipe running through a public street.

aws.name: AWS Site-to-Site VPN
aws.note: Managed IPsec with two tunnels per connection at 1.25 Gbps each, or 5 Gbps as large bandwidth tunnels, terminating on a virtual private gateway or Transit Gateway where ECMP adds throughput. AWS Client VPN is the separate OpenVPN-based service for people.
pros: Simple per-connection hourly price; Transit Gateway ECMP scales throughput across tunnels
Accelerated Site-to-Site VPN cuts jitter by entering the AWS backbone near the user
Client VPN plugs into IAM Identity Center, SAML and Active Directory
cons: Standard tunnels cap at 1.25 Gbps, large bandwidth tunnels at 5 Gbps; beyond that means ECMP
Client VPN bills per associated subnet hour plus per connection hour, expensive for many users
Two products, two consoles and two bills for site and user access

gcp.name: Cloud VPN
gcp.note: HA VPN gives a 99.99 percent SLA with two interfaces, BGP through Cloud Router and about 3 Gbps per tunnel, landing directly in the global VPC; Classic VPN lingers for static routing. There is no first-party client VPN for individual users.
pros: HA VPN's 99.99 percent SLA is the strongest of the three
One gateway serves every region because the VPC is global
Per-tunnel hourly pricing with no gateway SKU ladder
cons: No managed client VPN; user access goes through Identity-Aware Proxy or third parties
BGP via Cloud Router is mandatory for HA VPN
Classic VPN is deprecated for dynamic routing and offers no SLA uplift

azure.name: Azure VPN Gateway
azure.note: One gateway resource handles site-to-site IPsec and point-to-site user access (OpenVPN, IKEv2, SSTP with Entra ID authentication), sized by zone-redundant SKUs from VpnGw1AZ to VpnGw5AZ, the older VpnGw1 to VpnGw5 SKUs being retired, with active-active mode. It lives in a dedicated GatewaySubnet.
pros: Point-to-site with Entra ID sign-in is included, up to ten thousand clients on the top SKU
Zone-redundant SKUs and active-active mode without a second product
Site and user access on one gateway and one bill
cons: Deployment often takes 45 minutes or more, and SKU changes are disruptive
Hourly SKU charge whether idle or busy, plus egress
Throughput and tunnel counts are SKU-bound; growth means resizing

rows.pick: For IPsec to your own data centre the three are interchangeable. For people connecting from laptops, Azure includes point-to-site, AWS sells Client VPN separately, and GCP has nothing, which pushes you towards zero-trust access instead.
rows.gotcha: IPsec to your own data centre works in all three; the differences are throughput tiers and BGP setup. HA VPN needs BGP and lacks client VPN, AWS caps tunnels at 1.25 Gbps (5 Gbps for large bandwidth ones), and Azure ties everything to gateway SKUs.

rows.plain: A central junction that connects dozens of separate networks and offices so any of them can reach the others through one place, like a railway hub.

aws.name: AWS Transit Gateway
aws.note: A regional hub with attachments for VPCs, VPNs, Direct Connect and appliances, route tables for segmentation and inter-region peering, scaling to thousands of attachments. AWS Cloud WAN layers a global, policy-driven core network with segments on top of the same technology.
pros: Proven at very large scale with thousands of attachments and route-table segmentation
Cloud WAN turns multi-region hub meshes into one declarative policy
Attaches VPN, Direct Connect, Network Firewall and third-party appliances
cons: Every packet through the hub pays a per-gigabyte processing fee plus per-attachment hours
Regional; inter-region peering must be built and paid for
Route table sprawl needs discipline or automation

gcp.name: Network Connectivity Center
gcp.note: A hub with spokes: VPC spokes for transitive routing between networks, and hybrid spokes for VLAN attachments, VPN tunnels and router appliances, including other clouds. Cloud WAN (2025) builds an enterprise WAN on the same hub, while plain VPC Network Peering serves simple cases.
pros: Often unnecessary: a global VPC already spans regions, and Shared VPC spans teams
VPC spokes give transitive routing without a hub appliance; spokes bill hourly, hub traffic per GiB
Hybrid spokes accept partner router appliances for SD-WAN
cons: Younger, with fewer segmentation controls than Transit Gateway route tables
VPC Network Peering, the simpler alternative, is non-transitive and quota-bound
Per-spoke hourly charges plus data, and topology choices are hard to reverse

azure.name: Azure Virtual WAN
azure.note: Microsoft-managed hubs per region that terminate ExpressRoute, site-to-site and point-to-site VPN, route between spoke VNets and transit hub-to-hub across regions. A Secured Virtual Hub adds Azure Firewall; the self-managed alternative is hub-and-spoke peering with Azure Virtual Network Manager.
pros: Hub-to-hub transit across regions is managed for you
ExpressRoute, VPN, point-to-site and Firewall terminate in one hub
Routing intent gives a simple inspect-everything policy
cons: Hub hours, per-gigabyte hub processing and gateway scale units stack into a large bill
Less control than a hand-built hub, and limited third-party appliance choice
Basic SKU lacks VNet transit; Standard is the real product

rows.pick: Transit Gateway for dozens of AWS accounts and VPCs. Virtual WAN when branch, ExpressRoute and VPN aggregation across regions is the job. On GCP, start with Shared VPC and add Network Connectivity Center only for hybrid or multi-VPC needs.
rows.gotcha: Because GCP VPCs are global, much of what Transit Gateway solves does not exist there; Network Connectivity Center handles hybrid hub-and-spoke. Beware the name clash: AWS Cloud WAN and Google Cloud WAN are different products, and Azure Virtual WAN is different again.

rows.plain: A shared exit door that lets servers with no public address reach the internet for updates and downloads while nothing outside can call them back.

aws.name: NAT Gateway
aws.note: A managed, zonal by default (a regional mode since late 2025 spans zones automatically) gateway inside Amazon VPC that scales from 5 to 100 Gbps, with public and private modes. Resilience means one gateway per availability zone with matching route tables, and S3 or DynamoDB traffic should bypass it through free gateway endpoints.
pros: Fully managed, no instance to patch or size
Private NAT mode handles overlapping ranges between VPCs
Scales automatically to 100 Gbps per gateway
cons: Per-gigabyte processing fee on top of hourly, a notorious bill driver
Zonal: one per zone for resilience, or pay cross-zone charges and risk an outage
Sending S3 traffic through it instead of a gateway endpoint wastes money

gcp.name: Cloud NAT
gcp.note: Regional NAT configured on Cloud Router and enforced in the software-defined network, so there is no appliance in the path and nothing to size or fail over. Ports are allocated per VM, statically or dynamically, and Private NAT and hybrid NAT variants exist.
pros: Distributed enforcement means no bandwidth chokepoint and no single point of failure
Regional scope covers every zone with one configuration
Logging and per-VM port allocation are built in
cons: Port exhaustion planning is your job; too few ports per VM drops connections
Billed per VM hour up to thirty-two VMs then flat, plus per gigabyte
One gateway covers one region of one VPC; multi-region means several

azure.name: Azure NAT Gateway
azure.note: A regional, subnet-attached gateway with up to sixteen public IPs, 64,512 SNAT ports each and 50 Gbps, solving the port exhaustion that plagued Load Balancer outbound rules. new virtual networks created with API versions after 31 March 2026 get no default outbound access, while existing ones keep it.
pros: Attaches to subnets with one click and takes precedence over other outbound paths
Up to sixteen IPs gives over a million SNAT ports
Hourly plus per gigabyte, with no per-VM element
cons: A gateway is zonal or non-zonal, so zone-resilient outbound takes deliberate design
Cannot mix with Basic Load Balancer or Basic public IPs
Another hourly resource that small landing zones used to get implicitly for free

rows.pick: Interchangeable and mandatory: any private server that pulls updates needs one in every cloud. Design differs, not choice: one per zone on AWS, one per region on GCP, one per set of subnets on Azure.
rows.gotcha: Cloud NAT is not an appliance in your path; it is configured on the router, so nothing to size or fail. AWS NAT Gateway is zonal by default, one per zone, with a regional mode since late 2025. Azure has removed default outbound access for new virtual networks, while existing networks keep it, so an explicit NAT gateway is now the correct pattern.

rows.plain: The bouncer for your network: rules that decide which traffic may enter or leave each server, plus a heavier inspection point for anything suspicious.

aws.name: AWS Network Firewall
aws.note: A managed stateful firewall and intrusion prevention system using Suricata-compatible rules, deployed as endpoints per availability zone with TLS inspection, and centrally governed by AWS Firewall Manager. Beneath it sit stateful security groups on interfaces and stateless network ACLs on subnets.
pros: Suricata rule compatibility makes existing signatures portable
Firewall Manager pushes rules across every account in the organisation
Security groups referencing groups give identity-style micro-segmentation
cons: Endpoints bill per hour per zone plus per gigabyte, costly for small estates
Routing gymnastics: firewall subnets, ingress route tables and symmetric return paths
Network ACLs exist only on AWS, so designs leaning on them do not port

gcp.name: Cloud NGFW
gcp.note: A distributed firewall enforced at every VM rather than an appliance: hierarchical policies at organisation and folder level, network policies, and rules matched by tag or service account. Essentials, Standard and Enterprise tiers add threat intelligence, geo rules and Palo Alto-powered intrusion prevention.
pros: No chokepoint or bandwidth ceiling; enforcement scales with the VMs
Hierarchical policies give organisation-wide rules teams cannot override
Service-account matching ties rules to workload identity
cons: Enterprise intrusion prevention needs firewall endpoints billed per zone hour plus per gigabyte
URL filtering needs the Enterprise tier; explicit-proxy egress control still means Secure Web Proxy
Legacy VPC firewall rules and newer policies coexist; migration is manual

azure.name: Azure Firewall
azure.note: A managed stateful firewall in a dedicated subnet, usually a hub, with Basic, Standard and Premium SKUs; Premium adds TLS inspection, IDPS and URL filtering, and Azure Firewall Manager applies hierarchical policy. Beneath it, network security groups filter at subnet or NIC.
pros: Premium bundles TLS inspection, IDPS and Microsoft threat intelligence
FQDN tags and application rules simplify allow-lists for Windows Update and Azure services
Firewall Manager gives parent-child policy across hubs
cons: Hourly base fee plus per gigabyte makes it the priciest item in a small landing zone
Needs a dedicated /26 subnet and, for forced tunnelling, a management subnet
NSGs at subnet and NIC are both evaluated; a rule must pass both

rows.pick: Interchangeable as a pattern: a managed inspection appliance for egress filtering and layer 7 rules above the basic firewall. GCP stands out for distributed enforcement with no appliance to size; Azure Premium when Microsoft threat intelligence and TLS inspection matter.
rows.gotcha: All three basic layers are stateful, but AWS security groups attach to the interface, GCP rules are network-wide matched by tag or service account, and Azure NSGs attach to subnet or NIC or both, when both must allow. Stateless network ACLs are AWS-only.

rows.plain: A filter in front of your website that blocks hacking attempts and floods of junk traffic before they reach your servers, like a security screen at the entrance.

aws.name: AWS WAF
aws.note: Web ACLs attach per resource to CloudFront, Application Load Balancers, API Gateway and Verified Access, with managed rule groups, rate limits, CAPTCHA, Bot Control and AI-bot access monetisation; WAF Classic support ended 30 September 2025. AWS Shield adds DDoS protection, free Standard and paid Advanced.
pros: Protects regional resources directly, not just the CDN edge
Marketplace and AWS managed rule groups plus a rich nested rule language
Shield Advanced brings a response team and cost protection during attacks
