cons: Priced per web ACL, per rule, per million requests, with Bot Control extra
Shield Advanced costs three thousand dollars a month on a one-year commitment
Web ACLs are regional or CloudFront-scoped, so policies are duplicated per region

gcp.name: Google Cloud Armor
gcp.note: Security policies attach to backend services of Google load balancers, giving one policy at a global anycast front with preconfigured OWASP rules, rate limiting, Adaptive Protection against DDoS and bot management via Fraud Defense. Standard is pay-per-use; Enterprise is a subscription with bill protection.
pros: One policy protects a global front instead of one per region
Adaptive Protection learns traffic baselines and proposes rules automatically
Enterprise tier includes DDoS bill protection and response support
cons: Only works behind Google load balancers; nothing for arbitrary VMs or other clouds
Enterprise is a subscription tier priced per protected resource, not pay-as-you-go
Rule language is less expressive than AWS WAF's nested statements

azure.name: Azure Web Application Firewall
azure.note: WAF policies attach to Front Door (global edge) or Application Gateway V2 (regional), with Microsoft-managed OWASP rulesets, bot manager, custom and rate-limit rules. Azure DDoS Protection is separate: free infrastructure protection, IP Protection per address or Network Protection per subscription.
pros: Front Door Premium bundles the managed WAF rules into its price
DDoS IP Protection gives a per-address entry point far cheaper than the full plan
Microsoft maintains the default rulesets and bot signatures
cons: WAF exists only on Front Door and Application Gateway; nothing for Load Balancer or API Management
On Application Gateway the WAF adds capacity-unit cost and latency
DDoS Network Protection costs roughly three thousand dollars a month per plan of 100 public IPs

rows.pick: All three cover OWASP rules. Cloud Armor when you want a single policy at one global front; AWS WAF when regional load balancers or API Gateway need direct protection. Paid DDoS tiers buy response support and bill protection, not detection.
rows.gotcha: Request inspection at the edge, but attachment differs: Cloud Armor and Front Door WAF attach to the global load balancer, AWS WAF attaches per resource. Basic DDoS protection is included everywhere; the paid tier buys response support and a bill guarantee during an attack.

rows.plain: A managed front desk for your programming interfaces that checks callers' credentials, limits how often they call, and forwards requests to the right backend.

aws.name: Amazon API Gateway
aws.note: Three flavours: REST APIs with usage plans, keys, caching and a WAF; cheaper, faster HTTP APIs; and WebSocket APIs for live two-way connections. All pay per million requests and plug into Lambda, IAM and Cognito, and private APIs can stay inside your VPC.
pros: Pure per-request pricing with no hourly floor
Deep hooks into Lambda, IAM, Cognito and Step Functions
WebSocket APIs and private APIs come in the same service
cons: REST and HTTP API feature split confuses; many features exist on only one
Ten megabyte payload cap; 29 second default timeout, raisable only for Regional and private REST APIs
Built-in portals and products are recent additions; monetisation still needs partner tooling

gcp.name: API Gateway
gcp.note: An Envoy-based gateway configured from an OpenAPI 2.0, 3.0 or 3.1 spec for Cloud Run, Cloud Run functions and App Engine backends, paying per call. Apigee is Google's heavy enterprise suite with portal, monetisation, analytics and MCP exposure; Apigee hybrid runs in your own Kubernetes.
pros: Cheap per-call pricing and fully serverless
Apigee offers the most complete API management of any cloud
Apigee hybrid keeps the runtime in your own clusters
cons: API Gateway takes OpenAPI 2.0, 3.0 and 3.1 but only serverless backends, with no WebSockets
Apigee is expensive, with environment and organisation fees before traffic
Three overlapping products (Cloud Endpoints, API Gateway, Apigee) to choose between

azure.name: Azure API Management
azure.note: A full suite with XML policies, developer portal, products and subscriptions, self-hosted gateway and AI gateway policies such as token limits and semantic caching for LLM backends. Tiers run from serverless Consumption through Basic, Standard and Premium, with v2 tiers adding scaling and VNet integration.
pros: Portal, products, subscriptions and policies in one product from the start
AI gateway policies meter and cache calls to LLM backends
Consumption tier gives a per-call entry with no hourly fee
cons: Premium units run near three thousand dollars a month for VNet injection and multi-region
Classic tier scaling and configuration changes take fifteen minutes or longer
XML policy language is powerful but nobody enjoys it

rows.pick: For a thin front on serverless functions all three have a cheap per-call option. For an API programme with portal, products and monetisation, Apigee and API Management are the heavyweights; AWS's portal is new and monetisation still needs a partner.
rows.gotcha: Apigee is a much heavier enterprise API-management suite than the gateways. The name API Gateway means different things: AWS's is full-featured, Google's is a thin OpenAPI front for serverless backends. Azure has only the suite, so its cheap option is a tier, not a product.

rows.plain: Tools that record who talked to whom inside your network and test whether a path is actually open, like CCTV and a walk-through for your wiring.

aws.name: VPC Flow Logs
aws.note: Flow Logs capture accepted and rejected connection metadata per VPC, subnet or interface into CloudWatch Logs or S3; Reachability Analyzer and Network Access Analyzer prove or disprove paths from configuration. Traffic Mirroring copies packets, and CloudWatch Network Monitor probes hybrid links.
pros: Flow logs are unsampled and can include path and traffic metadata
Reachability Analyzer explains exactly which rule blocks a path
Traffic Mirroring gives full packets when metadata is not enough
cons: Several separate tools with no single network console
Log volume from busy VPCs drives CloudWatch or S3 and Athena costs
Reachability Analyzer is billed per analysis and covers only configuration, not live probes

gcp.name: Network Intelligence Center
gcp.note: One console for Network Topology, Connectivity Tests (configuration analysis plus live probes), Performance Dashboard, Firewall Insights, Network Analyzer and Flow Analyzer. VPC Flow Logs are sampled per subnet and land in Cloud Logging.
pros: Network Analyzer flags misconfigurations automatically at no charge
Connectivity Tests combine configuration analysis with live data-plane probes
Topology view spans the whole global VPC
cons: Flow logs are sampled by default, so counts are estimates
Log ingestion bills through Cloud Logging and can dwarf the network spend
Flow Analyzer and Firewall Insights are newer and less mature than the topology views

azure.name: Azure Network Watcher
azure.note: A per-region service with VNet flow logs, Traffic Analytics, Connection Monitor, IP flow verify, next hop, NSG diagnostics, packet capture and topology. NSG flow logs are retiring on 30 September 2027 and cannot be created since June 2025; VNet flow logs replace them.
pros: Packet capture on VMs is built in, no mirroring setup
Connection Monitor probes on-premises and other-cloud endpoints too
Traffic Analytics turns flow logs into maps and top-talker views
cons: NSG flow logs are retiring, forcing a migration to VNet flow logs
Traffic Analytics needs Log Analytics ingestion, billed per gigabyte
Tools are scattered across blades and a per-region Network Watcher instance

rows.pick: Interchangeable at the basic level: flow logs to a log store plus a reachability test tool in each cloud. GCP's Network Analyzer and Connectivity Tests are the most automatic; Azure's built-in packet capture is the easiest deep dive.
rows.gotcha: GCP flow logs are sampled while AWS and Azure logs are complete, so volume, cost and accuracy differ. Azure NSG flow logs retire in September 2027 and new work must use VNet flow logs. AWS needs Traffic Mirroring for packets; Azure captures them natively.

rows.plain: A safe way for administrators to open a terminal or desktop on a server that has no public address, without running your own jump box.

aws.name: AWS Systems Manager
aws.note: Session Manager opens shells and port forwards to instances running the SSM Agent with an instance role, with no inbound ports and sessions logged to S3 or CloudWatch. EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint adds agentless SSH and RDP through a VPC endpoint.
pros: Free; no bastion host or hourly resource
IAM controls who reaches which instance, with full session logging
No inbound ports, security group rules or public IPs
cons: Needs the SSM Agent, an instance role and reachability to SSM endpoints
Port forwarding requires the CLI session plugin on every admin machine
EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint is one per VPC with limited concurrency

gcp.name: Identity-Aware Proxy
gcp.note: IAP TCP forwarding tunnels SSH and RDP from gcloud or the console to VMs with no external IP, gated by IAM and a firewall rule for Google's proxy range. OS Login maps SSH keys to IAM identities.
pros: Free, with browser SSH built into the console
IAM roles per VM decide who may tunnel
OS Login removes shared SSH keys
cons: Tunnels are bandwidth-limited, unsuitable for bulk file transfer
A firewall rule for the proxy range must be added to every network
RDP needs a local tunnel command before the client connects

azure.name: Azure Bastion
azure.note: A managed jump host in a dedicated AzureBastionSubnet offering browser or native-client RDP and SSH to VMs in the VNet and peered VNets, with Developer, Basic, Standard and Premium SKUs; Premium adds session recording. Entra ID and Key Vault credentials are supported.
pros: No agent on the VM and painless Windows RDP
Serves an entire hub and its peered spokes from one host
Premium adds session recording for audit
cons: Hourly charge per host, over a hundred dollars a month even on Basic
Developer SKU is free but single-VM and limited to some regions
Needs a dedicated /26 subnet in the VNet

rows.pick: Use the built-in path in every cloud and stop giving servers public addresses. Systems Manager and Identity-Aware Proxy are free and identity-driven; Azure Bastion is a paid resource, worth it for Windows-heavy estates that live in RDP.
rows.gotcha: Shell access with no public IP and no bastion to patch should be the default in every new build. The trap is Azure: Bastion bills per hour, so teams skip it and open RDP to the internet; the Developer SKU removes that excuse.

rows.plain: A dedicated private connection running directly between two different cloud providers, so data moves between them without crossing the public internet.

aws.name: AWS Interconnect - multicloud
aws.note: A managed, high-bandwidth private link from AWS to other clouds ordered from the AWS side, announced in preview on 30 November 2025 with Google Cloud as launch partner and extended to Azure through the joint Microsoft offering in 2026. No colocation cross-connect to arrange.
pros: No colocation cage or carrier contract; ordered like any other AWS resource
Both cloud providers manage their ends of the link
Designed to pair with Cross-Cloud Interconnect and Azure Multicloud Interconnect
cons: Preview: limited regions, bandwidth options and no production SLA yet
Egress is still billed by both clouds
New enough that tooling and reference architectures are thin

gcp.name: Cross-Cloud Interconnect
gcp.note: Cloud Interconnect's multicloud option: Google provisions 10 or 100 Gbps links (400 Gbps to AWS and Oracle Cloud) at colocation sites to AWS, Azure, Oracle Cloud or Alibaba Cloud, generally available since 2023. You still order the far-side Direct Connect or ExpressRoute port yourself.
pros: Generally available with an SLA when deployed in redundant pairs
Reaches four other clouds, not just one partner
Data Transfer Essentials waives transfer fees for qualifying EU and UK multicloud workloads
cons: Minimum 10 Gbps, expensive for modest cross-cloud traffic
You still buy and manage the other cloud's circuit and gateway
Limited to specific colocation facilities where both clouds are present

azure.name: Azure Multicloud Interconnect
azure.note: A joint Microsoft and AWS offering in public preview since August 2026 that provisions managed private, high-throughput connectivity between Azure and AWS with no colocation involvement. It is the Azure-side counterpart of AWS Interconnect.
pros: Managed at both ends; no carrier or colocation contract
Ordered and monitored from the Azure portal
Fits alongside ExpressRoute in an existing hub design
cons: Preview and AWS-only so far; no Google or Oracle path
Two providers, two bills and egress on both sides
Regions and bandwidth tiers are limited during preview

rows.pick: Cross-Cloud Interconnect is the only generally available option, obvious whenever Google is one end. For AWS to Azure the managed pair is in preview, so production designs join Direct Connect and ExpressRoute at a shared colocation site, or use VPN.
rows.gotcha: Every option bills egress on both sides, so the link saves latency and carrier fees, not transfer charges. Cross-Cloud Interconnect still needs you to order the far-side Direct Connect or ExpressRoute. On AWS, Interconnect means multicloud; on Google, Interconnect also means on-premises.

rows.plain: A phone book that services update themselves so other services can look up where a healthy copy is running right now.

aws.name: AWS Cloud Map
aws.note: A registry of namespaces, services and instances discovered by DNS through Route 53 private zones or by API call, with health checks, used by ECS service discovery. New work increasingly leans on ECS Service Connect and VPC Lattice instead.
pros: DNS or API lookup from the same registry
Native ECS integration registers tasks automatically
Health-checked entries drop unhealthy instances
cons: Per registered resource per month plus per million discovery calls and Route 53 queries
Being overtaken by Service Connect and VPC Lattice for new designs
No portability; the API is AWS-specific

gcp.name: Service Directory
gcp.note: A managed registry of namespaces, services and endpoints with IAM, queried by API or exposed through Cloud DNS private zones, and able to register Private Service Connect endpoints. Adoption is modest; most teams rely on Kubernetes DNS or Cloud Run URLs.
pros: Cheap and IAM-governed
Cloud DNS integration exposes entries to anything that speaks DNS
Registers Private Service Connect endpoints for cross-project discovery
cons: Few native integrations register endpoints for you
Low adoption means fewer examples and tooling
Cross-project use needs careful IAM on namespaces

azure.none: No standalone registry: teams use Private DNS zone auto-registration, Kubernetes DNS in AKS or Container Apps' built-in service names.

rows.pick: Mostly matters on AWS, where Cloud Map underpins ECS service discovery. Elsewhere Kubernetes DNS or the platform's own service names do the job, so this row is rarely a deciding factor.
rows.gotcha: On AWS and GCP the registry surfaces through the DNS service, so private zone design is the real integration point. Azure's auto-registration only records VMs, not PaaS endpoints, so private endpoints need their own zones. Kubernetes DNS works identically everywhere.

rows.plain: The rulebook that says which people and programs may do which actions on which resources, like a building's badge system with a different badge per door.

aws.name: AWS Identity and Access Management
aws.note: Users, roles and JSON policy documents that allow or deny actions on resources, with permission boundaries and conditions. Roles are assumed for short-lived credentials, and IAM Access Analyzer checks who can reach what.
pros: Free, and the most expressive policy language of the three
Conditions can key on tags, source VPC endpoint, MFA and time
Roles give every workload short-lived credentials without stored keys
cons: JSON policies are verbose and easy to get subtly wrong
No inheritance: every account needs its own roles and policies
Managed policy size and attachment limits bite large teams

gcp.name: Identity and Access Management
gcp.note: Binds a principal to a role at organisation, folder, project or resource, and the grant inherits downward. Predefined roles are fine-grained, custom roles and deny policies fill gaps, and IAM Conditions add context such as time.
pros: Grant once at a folder and every project beneath inherits it
Hundreds of predefined roles map closely to real duties
Policy Intelligence tools are free and recommend role trims
cons: Basic roles Owner, Editor and Viewer are dangerously broad
Service account keys are the classic leaked credential
Deny policies and conditions are newer and less familiar to teams

azure.name: Microsoft Entra ID and Azure RBAC
azure.note: Entra ID holds the identities; Azure RBAC assigns a role to a principal at management group, subscription, resource group or resource, inheriting downward. Two separate role systems exist: Entra directory roles and Azure resource roles.
pros: Same directory as Microsoft 365, so users and groups already exist
Privileged Identity Management gives just-in-time elevation
Conditional Access enforces device and location rules on every sign-in
cons: Two role systems confuse newcomers: directory roles versus resource roles
Conditional Access needs P1 and PIM needs P2 licences per user
Role assignments per subscription are capped, which large estates hit

rows.pick: Interchangeable for basic grants. Azure is the obvious choice when the workforce already lives in Microsoft 365. AWS suits teams who need condition-rich policies and accept the verbosity.
rows.gotcha: GCP and Azure attach a principal to a role at a scope and inherit downward; AWS writes JSON policy documents instead, more expressive and easier to get wrong. Porting an AWS design means rethinking, not translating, each policy.

rows.plain: One login for staff that opens every cloud account and app they are allowed into, like a single office pass that works on every floor.

aws.name: AWS IAM Identity Center
aws.note: Maps users and groups from its own store or an external identity provider to permission sets across all accounts in an organisation. It also fronts SAML applications and issues short-lived CLI credentials.
pros: Free; permission sets replace hand-built roles in every account
SCIM sync from Okta, Entra ID or Google Workspace
Trusted identity propagation carries the user into Redshift, Athena and Q
cons: One organisation instance per management account, in a primary region though replicable to others since 2026
Not a general identity provider for non-AWS apps at scale
Adding a second directory means another federation layer

gcp.name: Cloud Identity
gcp.note: The user and group directory shared with Google Workspace, with SSO, device management and MFA. Workforce Identity Federation lets an external identity provider's users reach Google Cloud without creating Google accounts at all.
pros: Free edition covers directory, SSO and basic MFA
Workforce Identity Federation avoids duplicating users into Google
Groups are first-class IAM principals across the hierarchy
cons: Premium features such as device management are per user per month
Federated workforce identities lack support in some console features
Teams outside Workspace find the admin console unfamiliar

azure.name: Microsoft Entra ID
azure.note: The tenant directory behind Microsoft 365 and Azure, with SSO to thousands of gallery apps, Conditional Access, MFA and passwordless. It is a full identity provider rather than a bridge to one.
pros: Already present wherever Microsoft 365 is in use
Largest SaaS app gallery and richest Conditional Access engine
Entra ID Governance adds access reviews and lifecycle workflows
cons: Real controls sit in P1 and P2 tiers, priced per user
Tenant design is hard to change after the fact
Sign-in and audit logs need export to keep beyond 30 days

rows.pick: Azure whenever the organisation runs on Microsoft 365: the directory already exists. Otherwise all three simply federate to Okta, Entra or Google Workspace, and the choice hardly matters.
rows.gotcha: Entra ID is the same directory as Microsoft 365, which is why identity so often decides that an enterprise goes to Azure. IAM Identity Center and Cloud Identity are bridges into one cloud, not company-wide identity providers.

rows.plain: The account system for your own customers: sign up, log in, reset password, social login, kept deliberately separate from the staff directory.

aws.name: Amazon Cognito
aws.note: User pools hold customer accounts with hosted managed login, social and SAML federation, MFA and passwordless; identity pools swap tokens for temporary AWS credentials. Lite, Essentials and Plus tiers price the feature set.
pros: Generous free monthly active users on the entry tier
Identity pools hand mobile apps scoped AWS credentials directly
Lambda triggers customise every step of the flow
cons: User pools are regional, with no global replication
Advanced features such as threat protection sit in the pricier tier
Hosted UI customisation has long been the top complaint

gcp.name: Identity Platform
gcp.note: Firebase Authentication with enterprise extras: SAML and OIDC federation, multi-tenancy, MFA and an SLA. The same SDKs serve web, iOS and Android, so mobile teams often start on Firebase and upgrade.
pros: Firebase SDKs make mobile sign-in trivial
Multi-tenancy for platforms serving many customer organisations
Per monthly active user, with a sizeable free tier
cons: SMS second factor is billed per message and adds up
Fewer hooks for custom flows than Cognito triggers
Admin experience split between Firebase and Cloud consoles

azure.name: Microsoft Entra External ID
azure.note: A separate external tenant for customers and partners with branded sign-up, social and enterprise federation, MFA and native authentication SDKs. Azure AD B2C stopped selling to new customers in May 2025 and this is its successor.
pros: Per monthly active user with a generous free band
Custom URL domains and native mobile authentication
Same Conditional Access and identity protection engine as the workforce tenant
cons: No Identity Experience Framework: B2C custom policies do not port
Migration from B2C is a rebuild, not an upgrade
Younger feature set than B2C in places

rows.pick: Interchangeable for a standard web login. Mobile-first teams lean to Identity Platform for the Firebase SDKs; teams already on Azure AD B2C must plan a move to External ID rather than assume continuity.
rows.gotcha: Customer identity is kept deliberately separate from workforce identity in all three, so do not put staff in Cognito or customers in Entra ID. Cognito's regional user pools also mean a multi-region app needs its own replication strategy.

rows.plain: The rules head office sets that no team can override, such as which regions or services may be used, applied across every account at once.

aws.name: AWS Organizations
aws.note: Groups accounts into organisational units with consolidated billing. Service control policies cap what identities in an account may do, resource control policies cap what resources may accept, and Control Tower wraps both into a landing zone.
pros: Accounts are hard blast-radius boundaries; SCPs make them safe to delegate
Consolidated billing and shared savings plans across accounts
Control Tower automates the landing zone and drift detection
cons: SCPs only restrict; they never grant, and debugging denials is painful
Account creation and closure are heavyweight, slow operations
Policy size and count limits per organisational unit

gcp.name: Resource Manager
gcp.note: The organisation, folder and project hierarchy, with Organization Policy constraints applied at any level and inherited downward. Constraints are boolean or list rules, with custom constraints and a dry-run mode.
pros: Projects are lightweight, so one per workload is normal
Folders let policies and IAM flow down naturally
Dry-run shows what a constraint would break before enforcing
cons: Constraints only cover what Google has modelled; gaps exist
Billing accounts sit outside the hierarchy and confuse newcomers
Deleted projects linger 30 days, which surprises cost reports

azure.name: Azure Policy with management groups
azure.note: Management groups nest subscriptions up to six levels; Azure Policy assigns definitions at any level with deny, audit, append, modify or deploy-if-not-exists effects and remediation tasks. Azure Landing Zones provide the reference layout.
pros: Policy can deny, audit and auto-remediate, not only block
Built-in initiatives map to CIS, NIST and ISO controls
Free; compliance dashboard across the whole estate
cons: Compliance evaluation lags 15 to 30 minutes, with a full re-evaluation only every 24 hours
Subscription is billing and quota boundary, resource group is lifecycle: two things to design
Deleting a resource group deletes everything inside, instantly

rows.pick: Azure Policy is the obvious choice when you want guardrails that fix drift, not merely forbid. AWS suits organisations that want hard account isolation; GCP suits those who create many small projects.
rows.gotcha: Three weights of boundary: an AWS account is heavyweight, a GCP project light, and Azure splits the job between subscription (billing and quota) and resource group (lifecycle). SCPs only deny, Organization Policy can enforce or audit in dry-run mode, and only Azure Policy also remediates.

rows.plain: A locked safe that holds encryption keys and does the locking and unlocking for you, so the keys themselves never leave the safe.

aws.name: AWS Key Management Service
aws.note: Customer managed keys in FIPS-validated HSMs, used by envelope encryption across nearly every AWS service, with key policies, grants and configurable automatic rotation, yearly by default, plus on-demand rotation. AWS CloudHSM offers dedicated single-tenant clusters and AWS Payment Cryptography covers card PIN workloads.
pros: Every AWS service integrates; one key policy gates access
Multi-Region keys and External Key Store for sovereignty cases
Cheap per key, with per-request billing that scales down
cons: Per-request charges surprise chatty workloads such as S3 with SSE-KMS
Key policies are yet another JSON document to get right
CloudHSM is billed per HSM-hour and you run the cluster

gcp.name: Cloud Key Management Service
gcp.note: Software, HSM and external protection levels behind one API, so Cloud HSM is a checkbox rather than a cluster. Cloud EKM keeps keys with an outside provider, and Autokey creates customer-managed keys automatically as resources are made.
pros: HSM-backed keys without operating an HSM cluster
Autokey removes the manual key-per-resource chore
Key destruction has a mandatory delay, protecting against mistakes
cons: Per key version per month, so unrotated old versions keep billing
Fewer services support customer-managed keys than on AWS
EKM adds latency and an external dependency to every decrypt

azure.name: Azure Key Vault
azure.note: One service for keys, secrets and certificates, with soft-delete and purge protection. Managed HSM adds a single-tenant FIPS 140-3 Level 3 pool, Azure Cloud HSM (2025) gives customer-owned clusters, and Dedicated HSM retires in July 2028.
pros: Keys, secrets and certificates in one place with one access model
Per-operation pricing; an idle vault costs almost nothing
Managed HSM is fully managed yet single-tenant
cons: Per-vault throughput limits; busy apps need several vaults
Managed HSM is billed per hour per pool and is expensive
Two permission models, access policies and RBAC, confuse migrations

rows.pick: Interchangeable for encrypting cloud storage and databases. GCP is the obvious choice when you want HSM-backed keys without running anything; Azure when one service for keys, secrets and certificates simplifies the estate.
rows.gotcha: Key Vault covers secrets, keys and certificates in one service; on AWS that is KMS plus Secrets Manager plus ACM, and on GCP KMS plus Secret Manager plus Certificate Manager. Vault throughput limits also force a sharding decision AWS never asks.

rows.plain: A safe for passwords, API keys and tokens that programs fetch at run time, so nothing sensitive is written into code or config files.

aws.name: AWS Secrets Manager
aws.note: Versioned secrets encrypted with KMS, with built-in rotation for RDS, Redshift and DocumentDB and Lambda-driven rotation for anything else. Systems Manager Parameter Store is the cheaper sibling for configuration and simple secrets.
pros: Managed rotation for database credentials out of the box
Cross-region replication and resource policies for sharing
Parameter Store standard tier is free for non-rotating values
cons: Monthly charge per secret, plus per API call
Rotation for non-AWS systems means writing and running a Lambda
Two services for one job invites inconsistent usage

gcp.name: Secret Manager
gcp.note: Versioned secrets with automatic or user-chosen replication, IAM at secret level and CMEK support. Rotation is a schedule that publishes a Pub/Sub message; you write the rotation itself.
pros: Simple model: one service, secret-level IAM, versions
Automatic multi-region replication by default
Cheap per active version per location
cons: No built-in rotation logic, only a reminder event
Charges per replication location, so global secrets multiply cost
Fewer managed services read secrets natively than on AWS

azure.name: Azure Key Vault
azure.note: Secrets live alongside keys and certificates in the same vault, fetched with managed identities and referenced directly from App Service, Functions and Container Apps. Rotation is event-driven through Event Grid and your own function.
pros: No per-secret monthly fee, only per operation
Managed identity references in App Service need no code
One access model for secrets, keys and certificates
cons: Rotation is do-it-yourself with Event Grid and Functions
Per-vault throttling; hot secrets need caching in the app
Vault-per-app sprawl is common and hard to inventory

rows.pick: AWS is the obvious choice when you need managed rotation of database credentials. Otherwise the three are interchangeable: store, version, fetch with a workload identity, and never in environment variables.
rows.gotcha: Azure puts secrets, keys and certificates in one service; on AWS that is Secrets Manager, KMS and ACM. Only AWS rotates credentials for you; on GCP and Azure rotation is an event you must handle, so budget the code.

rows.plain: The identity papers a website shows to prove it is genuine, issued and renewed for you, plus a private issuing office for your internal systems.

aws.name: AWS Certificate Manager
aws.note: Issues and auto-renews public certificates for load balancers, CloudFront and API Gateway, and since 2025 can issue exportable public certificates for a fee. AWS Private Certificate Authority runs internal CAs for services, devices and Kubernetes.
pros: Public certificates are free and renew themselves while DNS validation stands
Private CA integrates with ACM, EKS and IoT for issuance
Renewal failures surface as events you can alarm on
cons: Free certificates cannot leave AWS; exportable ones are charged
Private CA carries a fixed monthly fee per CA
Only works with integrated services, not arbitrary EC2 software

gcp.name: Certificate Manager
gcp.note: Google-managed or self-managed certificates for external and internal load balancers, with DNS authorisation and certificate maps for many domains. Certificate Authority Service runs private CAs for internal PKI and workload certificates.
pros: Google-managed certificates renew without any action
Certificate maps handle thousands of customer domains on one balancer
Certificate Authority Service offers DevOps and Enterprise CA tiers
cons: Tied to load balancers; nothing for a VM running its own server
Charges per certificate beyond the free allowance
Private CA billing per certificate issued adds up for short-lived certs

azure.name: Azure Key Vault certificates
azure.note: Stores certificates and automates renewal with DigiCert and GlobalSign as integrated issuers; otherwise you import and renew yourself. App Service managed certificates give free basic certificates for web apps, and there is no managed private CA for workload certificates, and Microsoft Cloud PKI covers only Intune-managed devices.
pros: Certificates sit with the keys and secrets that protect them
App Service managed certificates are free and automatic
Integrated public CAs renew without human steps
cons: No managed private CA; teams run their own or buy one
Non-integrated issuers mean manual renewal reminders
App Service certificates exclude wildcards and cannot be exported

rows.pick: Interchangeable for public certificates on a load balancer, all free and self-renewing. AWS or GCP is the obvious choice when you need a managed private CA; Azure has no equivalent.
rows.gotcha: Free managed certificates in all three, renewed as long as validation stays in place. On Azure the certificate is a Key Vault object shared with keys and secrets, so vault access control decides who can read your private keys.

rows.plain: A guard who checks every door is locked and watches the cameras for intruders, then puts the worst problems at the top of one list.

aws.name: AWS Security Hub
aws.note: Since December 2025 the name belongs to a unified risk-analytics service correlating findings from Amazon GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie and AWS Security Hub CSPM, the renamed original posture checker. Detectors are enabled underneath but billed through consolidated Security Hub plans.
pros: Correlation ranks exposures rather than listing thousands of findings
GuardDuty analyses CloudTrail, DNS and flow logs with no agents
Organisation-wide delegated administrator view across accounts
cons: Per-resource Essentials pricing folds in GuardDuty, Inspector and CSPM; out-of-plan capabilities still bill separately
The 2025 rename makes older runbooks and documentation ambiguous
AWS-only; no view of other clouds without a third party

gcp.name: Security Command Center
gcp.note: Standard and Premium tiers combine misconfiguration findings, threat detection and attack path simulation, with Google's Wiz acquisition feeding the Security Operations side. The Enterprise tier, the only one covering AWS and Azure, shuts down on 21 May 2027 and moves customers to Premium.
pros: Standard tier is free at organisation level
Enterprise brings multicloud posture and case management, but only until its May 2027 shutdown
Attack paths and toxic combinations explain why a finding matters
cons: Premium pricing by usage is hard to forecast
Enterprise is a sales-led subscription, not self-serve
Threat detection depth trails the posture side

azure.name: Microsoft Defender for Cloud
azure.note: Foundational posture for free, Defender CSPM for attack paths and agentless scanning, and per-workload Defender plans for servers, containers, databases, storage and app services. Connectors extend it to AWS and GCP.
pros: Free posture tier and a regulatory compliance dashboard
Native AWS and GCP connectors for one multicloud view
Alerts flow straight into Sentinel and Defender XDR
cons: Per-plan pricing sprawls; storage and database plans surprise
Agentless features need Defender CSPM, itself per resource per hour
Recommendation noise is high without careful exemptions

rows.pick: Defender for Cloud is the obvious choice for a multicloud estate with a Microsoft SOC; Security Command Center Enterprise competes there only until its May 2027 shutdown. Single-cloud teams simply enable their native stack.
rows.gotcha: Each cloud's detector sees only its own logs, and the labels have moved: Defender doubles as the posture tool, which AWS splits into Security Hub CSPM, GuardDuty and Inspector. Since December 2025 AWS Security Hub means the new correlation layer; the old checker is Security Hub CSPM.

rows.plain: The control room that collects every security log in one place, searches across them and raises the alarm when a pattern looks like an attack.

aws.name: Amazon Security Lake
aws.note: Normalises CloudTrail, VPC flow, Route 53, Security Hub and third-party logs into OCSF Parquet in your own S3 buckets for Athena, OpenSearch or a partner SIEM to query. Amazon Detective adds graph-based investigation of GuardDuty findings.
pros: Open schema and your own buckets; no SIEM lock-in
Cheap storage; pay normalisation per GB then S3 rates
Subscribers such as Splunk and Sentinel read it directly
cons: No detections, rules or case management of its own
You still need a SIEM or OpenSearch on top
Detective is priced per GB ingested and is AWS-only

gcp.name: Google Security Operations
gcp.note: SIEM, SOAR and Mandiant threat intelligence on Google's search infrastructure, with a year of hot retention and YARA-L detection rules. Sold in Standard, Enterprise and Enterprise Plus packages rather than per gigabyte.
pros: Retention and search speed at petabyte scale without tuning
Flat packaging removes the ingest-volume anxiety
Curated detections and Mandiant intelligence included
cons: Separate tenant and console from the Cloud console
Enterprise sales motion; not something a small team switches on
YARA-L is its own rule language to learn

azure.name: Microsoft Sentinel
azure.note: Cloud-native SIEM and SOAR built on Log Analytics with KQL queries, analytics rules, playbooks in Logic Apps and hundreds of connectors. A data lake tier arrived in 2025 for cheap long-term retention and graph queries.
pros: Office 365 audit logs and Defender alerts ingest free; raw Defender and Entra logs are paid
KQL is the same language as Monitor and Data Explorer
Commitment tiers and the data lake tier cut ingestion bills
cons: Per-GB analytics ingestion balloons without tiering
Workspace design decisions are hard to undo
Best value only inside a Microsoft-heavy estate

rows.pick: Sentinel is the obvious choice for a Microsoft-centred SOC; Google Security Operations for teams wanting flat pricing and Mandiant intelligence. AWS teams pick a SIEM and feed it from Security Lake.
rows.gotcha: Sentinel and Google Security Operations are full SIEMs; AWS offers no first-party SIEM, only a normalised lake plus Detective. An AWS design must budget for a third-party SIEM or OpenSearch, and the operations effort that goes with it.

rows.plain: A sniffer dog that finds personal or secret data hiding in your files and databases, and a tool that blacks it out before anyone else sees it.

aws.name: Amazon Macie
aws.note: Scans S3 buckets for personal, financial and credential data with managed and custom identifiers, with automated discovery that samples the estate continuously. It reports findings to Security Hub; it does not mask or transform data.
pros: Automated discovery samples every bucket continuously, billed per object monitored and gigabyte analysed
Findings integrate with Security Hub and EventBridge
Managed identifiers cover common regulated data types
cons: S3 only; nothing for RDS, DynamoDB or Redshift
Full scans are billed per GB and get expensive
Discovery only: no masking, tokenisation or redaction

gcp.name: Sensitive Data Protection
gcp.note: Inspects, classifies and de-identifies data in Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Cloud SQL and arbitrary content through an API, with masking, tokenisation and format-preserving encryption. Discovery profiles map sensitive data across the organisation.
pros: De-identification and re-identification, not just findings
Works on streaming text and images through the API
Discovery profiles cover BigQuery, Cloud SQL and Storage
cons: Per-GB inspection pricing is steep at data lake scale
API quotas and latency need designing around
Over 200 infoTypes tempt broad scans that flood results

azure.name: Microsoft Purview Information Protection
azure.note: Sensitivity labels, classifiers and DLP policies across Microsoft 365, endpoints and, through the Purview data map, Azure storage and databases. Strongest on documents and email; formerly Microsoft Information Protection, which itself absorbed the older Azure Information Protection.
pros: Labels travel with documents and encrypt them wherever they go
One policy engine across Office, Teams, endpoints and SharePoint
Trainable classifiers for organisation-specific content
cons: Real capability needs Microsoft 365 E5 or add-on licences
Raw cloud storage scanning is weaker than Google's
Sprawls across Purview portals that keep reorganising

rows.pick: Sensitive Data Protection is the obvious choice when you must mask or tokenise data in pipelines. Purview wins for documents and email in a Microsoft 365 estate. Macie is for S3 hygiene only.
rows.gotcha: Finding personal data you did not know you were storing. Google's tool is the most developed of the three and the only one that transforms data; Macie only reports, and Purview's strength is Office content, not buckets.

rows.plain: The signed visitors' book that records who did what to your cloud, when and from where, so you can investigate later or satisfy an auditor.

aws.name: AWS CloudTrail
aws.note: Records every API call as an event: management events free, data events for S3, Lambda and DynamoDB charged per volume, delivered to S3 with integrity validation. CloudTrail Lake entered maintenance in March 2026, closed to new customers from 31 May, so querying returns to Athena.
pros: One free copy of management events in every account
Organisation trails collect all accounts into one bucket
Log file integrity validation satisfies auditors
cons: Data events are billed per hundred thousand and pile up
Delivery lags by several minutes; not a real-time control
CloudTrail Lake maintenance leaves querying to you

gcp.name: Cloud Audit Logs
gcp.note: Admin Activity and System Event logs are always on and free, retained 400 days; Data Access logs are off by default outside BigQuery and billed as Cloud Logging ingestion when enabled. Aggregated sinks route them organisation-wide.
pros: Admin activity logged everywhere without configuration or cost
Same Logging pipeline and Log Analytics as application logs
Aggregated sinks export the whole organisation to BigQuery
cons: Data Access logs off by default; enabling them costs real money
Per-GiB ingestion pricing for the interesting logs
Access Transparency for Google staff access is a separate feature

azure.name: Azure Activity Log
azure.note: Subscription-level control-plane events kept 90 days for free and exported through diagnostic settings to Log Analytics, Storage or Event Hubs. Entra ID sign-in and audit logs are separate streams with their own export, and resource logs cover the data plane.
pros: Free 90-day history in every subscription
Diagnostic settings export at management group scale
KQL in Log Analytics unifies activity, resource and Entra logs
cons: Three separate log families to wire up and retain
Control plane only; data-plane access needs per-resource logs
Entra logs keep only 7 to 30 days without export

rows.pick: Interchangeable in purpose. The choice is made by the platform you are on; the real decision is whether to pay for data-plane logs, which every provider makes optional and expensive.
rows.gotcha: Same purpose: admin and data access audit. But defaults differ: AWS and GCP log management actions everywhere for free, Azure splits identity from resource logs, and every provider leaves data-plane events off until you pay for them.

rows.plain: Running code inside a sealed box in the processor so that even the cloud provider's own staff and software cannot see the data while it is in use.

aws.name: AWS Nitro Enclaves
aws.note: Carves an isolated, network-less enclave out of a parent EC2 instance, reachable only over a local socket, with signed attestation documents that KMS can require before releasing keys. Confidential VMs with AMD SEV-SNP are also available on selected instance families.
pros: No extra charge; part of the parent instance
KMS attestation conditions bind keys to measured code
Nitro Enclaves are available in most regions
cons: You build the enclave image and proxy everything over vsock
No persistent storage or networking inside the enclave
Developer experience is the roughest of the three

gcp.name: Confidential Computing
gcp.note: Confidential VMs on AMD SEV, SEV-SNP and Intel TDX, Confidential GKE Nodes, and Confidential Space for multi-party workloads that share data under attestation. Enabling it is largely a checkbox on the VM.
pros: Turn it on per VM with no code changes
Confidential Space solves multi-party clean-room cases
Confidential GPUs for sensitive model inference
cons: Premium on the VM price and fewer machine types
Attestation only proves the VM, not your application, unless you use Space
Regional availability of newer hardware lags

azure.name: Azure confidential computing
azure.note: Confidential VM sizes on AMD SEV-SNP and Intel TDX, confidential containers on AKS and Container Instances, Azure Attestation for verifying enclaves, and Azure confidential ledger built on it. The broadest set of confidential offerings of the three.
pros: Widest range: VMs, containers, ledger, SQL Always Encrypted enclaves
Azure Attestation is a managed verification service
Confidential VM disks and OS encryption are handled for you
cons: Confidential SKUs are region-limited and cost a premium
Three hardware models, SGX enclaves plus SEV-SNP and TDX VMs, with different programming
Attestation policy authoring is its own skill

rows.pick: Azure or GCP is the obvious choice when you want confidential VMs with no code change. Nitro Enclaves suit a small, sensitive component such as key handling, not lifting whole applications.
rows.gotcha: Nitro Enclaves isolate a slice of one instance and demand you write for it; GCP and Azure encrypt whole VMs with a checkbox. Most teams actually need customer-managed keys and good IAM, so confirm the threat model first.

rows.plain: A fence around your cloud storage and APIs so that even someone holding a valid key cannot copy data out to a project you do not own.

aws.note: No single product. A data perimeter is composed from VPC endpoint policies, service control policies, resource control policies and conditions such as source VPC endpoint and organisation identifiers on every resource policy.
pros: No extra charge beyond the VPC endpoints you already run
Resource control policies apply to resources organisation-wide
Every control is plain IAM, so no new service to learn
cons: Dozens of policies to keep consistent across services
Each service's resource policy has its own quirks
Testing a change is slow and false denials are common
aws.none: Composed from VPC endpoint policies, SCPs and resource control policies; teams follow the AWS data perimeter pattern instead of a product.

gcp.name: VPC Service Controls
gcp.note: Draws a service perimeter around projects so Google APIs such as Storage and BigQuery only accept calls from inside it, with ingress and egress rules for exceptions. Access Context Manager adds device and location conditions; dry-run mode previews the blast radius.
pros: One perimeter protects every supported API at once
Dry-run logs violations before enforcing
Blocks exfiltration even by a compromised credential
cons: Breaks legitimate flows in Cloud Build, Dataflow and third-party tools
Debugging a violation is notoriously painful
Some services are unsupported or only partly covered

azure.name: Network Security Perimeter
azure.note: Network Security Perimeter draws a logical isolation boundary around PaaS resources, with inbound and outbound access rules that stop data exfiltration. Private endpoints and Azure Policy still cover services it does not support; Azure Enclave (preview) is a separate managed isolated-environment offering.
pros: One perimeter resource with inbound and outbound rules replaces per-resource firewall settings
Generally available and first-party; the closest Azure has to VPC Service Controls
Private endpoints and Azure Policy still cover services outside its supported list
cons: Only a subset of PaaS resource types can join a perimeter so far
Network-level only; it does not make the identity-aware checks VPC Service Controls does
Private DNS and endpoint sprawl remain for services outside the perimeter

rows.pick: VPC Service Controls is the obvious choice when the requirement is a hard perimeter around data services. Network Security Perimeter gets Azure close for supported services; on AWS the same outcome is a programme of policy work.
rows.gotcha: Azure's Network Security Perimeter is the closest one-service equivalent to VPC Service Controls; only AWS composes it from policies. Google's perimeter is identity-aware, so a stolen key cannot copy data out; AWS and Azure lean on network and policy and need more pieces.

rows.plain: Letting staff reach internal apps from anywhere by checking who they are and how healthy their device is on every request, instead of a VPN.

aws.name: AWS Verified Access
aws.note: Fronts internal HTTP and TCP applications with a policy evaluated per request against identity from IAM Identity Center or an OIDC provider and device posture from partners such as CrowdStrike and Jamf. Policies are written in Cedar.
pros: No VPN client for browser apps; per-request policy
Cedar policies are testable and version-controlled
Logs every access decision to CloudWatch or S3
cons: Priced per application-hour plus data, which multiplies with app count
Device posture depends on third-party agents
Younger and less proven than the other two

gcp.name: Chrome Enterprise Premium
gcp.note: Google's own zero-trust model sold as a per-user licence that adds threat and data protection in Chrome. Identity-Aware Proxy is the free enforcement point in front of load balancers, App Engine and VMs, and Access Context Manager supplies device and location rules.
pros: Identity-Aware Proxy is free for GCP-hosted apps
Longest track record: Google has run this model internally for years
IAP TCP forwarding gives SSH and RDP with no public IPs
cons: Premium licence per user per month for the browser controls
Strongest when users are on Chrome and managed devices
Apps outside Google Cloud need a connector

azure.name: Microsoft Entra Private Access
azure.note: Part of Global Secure Access with Entra Internet Access, it tunnels traffic from a client agent to private apps through connectors, applying Conditional Access per app or per network segment. It succeeds Application Proxy and replaces VPNs.
pros: Conditional Access policies apply per app, including legacy protocols
Same identities, devices and Intune compliance as the rest of Entra
Covers any TCP or UDP app, not just HTTP
cons: Client agent required on every device
Per-user licence on top of P1
Connector servers to deploy and patch

rows.pick: Entra Private Access is the obvious choice for a Microsoft-managed device fleet. Identity-Aware Proxy wins for apps already on Google Cloud at zero cost. Verified Access fits AWS-only estates with a partner device agent.
rows.gotcha: Identity-Aware Proxy lets staff reach apps and servers with no door open to the internet at all, and it is free; Verified Access bills per application-hour and Private Access per user. The pricing model, not the security model, usually decides.

rows.plain: Where the auditor's paperwork comes from: the provider's own certificates, and tools that gather proof that your setup meets a standard.

aws.name: AWS Artifact
aws.note: Free on-demand downloads of AWS SOC, ISO, PCI and regional attestation reports, plus acceptance of agreements such as the BAA. AWS Audit Manager, which automated evidence collection for your own controls, closed to new customers in April 2026.
pros: Free, immediate access to every AWS third-party report
Agreements accepted once at organisation level
Security Hub CSPM standards fill part of the evidence gap
cons: Covers AWS's compliance, not yours
Audit Manager retiring leaves evidence collection to partners
Reports carry NDA terms that slow sharing with auditors

gcp.name: Audit Manager
gcp.note: Assesses workloads against frameworks such as ISO 27001, SOC 2 and CIS, generating evidence reports you can hand to auditors. Compliance Reports Manager provides Google's own certifications and Assured Workloads builds regulated environments.
pros: Evidence collection aimed at your controls, not just Google's
Assured Workloads enforces data residency and personnel controls
Google's reports are free to download
cons: Young service with a short framework list
Assured Workloads restricts which services you may use
Evidence is Google Cloud only

azure.name: Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager
azure.note: Scores your posture against hundreds of regulatory templates across Microsoft 365 and Azure and tracks improvement actions with evidence. Microsoft's own audit reports come from the Service Trust Portal, and Defender for Cloud's regulatory dashboard covers Azure resources.
pros: Widest template library, covering global and sector regulations
Spans Microsoft 365 and Azure in one score
Service Trust Portal reports are free
cons: Premium templates carry a separate licence
Scores reward ticking actions, which can flatter reality
Split between Purview, Defender and the Trust Portal

rows.pick: Interchangeable for downloading the provider's certificates. For evidence about your own controls, Azure has the widest template set; GCP has a native tool; AWS teams now rely on Security Hub CSPM and partner platforms.
rows.gotcha: Worth knowing before someone asks for SOC 2 on a Friday. Provider reports prove the cloud is compliant, not that your workload is, and with AWS Audit Manager retiring only GCP and Azure still gather that second kind of evidence first-party.

rows.plain: Tools that answer who can actually reach this resource, which permissions have gone unused, and ask managers to reconfirm access on a schedule.

aws.name: IAM Access Analyzer
aws.note: A feature of IAM that finds resources shared outside your organisation, reports unused roles, keys and permissions, validates policies and generates least-privilege policies from CloudTrail activity. There is no first-party access review workflow.
pros: External access findings are free and organisation-wide
Generates a scoped policy from real CloudTrail usage
Custom policy checks run in CI before deployment
cons: Unused access analysis is billed per role and user per month
No periodic access review or approval workflow
AWS-only view; nothing for SaaS or other clouds

gcp.name: Policy Intelligence
gcp.note: Policy Analyzer answers who has what access, Policy Troubleshooter explains a denied request, and IAM Recommender proposes role trims from 90 days of usage. Policy Simulator previews a change before applying it.
pros: Free across the organisation
Recommender surfaces removals with usage evidence attached
Troubleshooter turns a permission denied into a clear reason
cons: Recommendations need someone to act; no enforcement loop
No access review workflow for managers
Analysis covers Google Cloud resources only

azure.name: Microsoft Entra ID Governance
azure.note: Access reviews, entitlement management access packages and lifecycle workflows for joiners, movers and leavers, sitting on Entra ID P2 and Privileged Identity Management. Entra Permissions Management, the multicloud permissions analyser, retired in November 2025.
pros: Real review campaigns with manager sign-off and auto-removal
Access packages bundle groups, apps and SharePoint sites
Covers SaaS and Microsoft 365 as well as Azure
cons: Per-user licence on top of P2
No multicloud permission analysis since Permissions Management retired
Configuration is elaborate; small teams underuse it

rows.pick: Entra ID Governance is the obvious choice when you need recurring access reviews with sign-off. For pure permission trimming inside one cloud, the free AWS and GCP analysers are enough.
rows.gotcha: Answering who can actually reach this resource is a harder question than it sounds in every cloud. AWS and GCP analyse; only Azure runs the human review loop. Multicloud permission analytics went with Entra Permissions Management in 2025, so plan a third party.

rows.plain: A hosted copy of the classic Windows directory that older servers and applications insist on, run and patched by the cloud instead of you.

aws.name: AWS Directory Service
aws.note: AWS Managed Microsoft AD runs real domain controllers in your VPC in Standard or Enterprise editions, with trusts to on-premises forests and seamless domain join for EC2, RDS and FSx. AD Connector proxies to an existing directory; Simple AD is closed to new customers.
pros: Genuine Active Directory with schema extensions and group policy
Trusts and multi-region replication for hybrid estates
Native integration with RDS for SQL Server and FSx
cons: Hourly per domain controller pair, plus additional controllers
You still manage users, OUs and policy inside it
No domain admin: some tooling assumes rights you do not have

gcp.name: Managed Service for Microsoft Active Directory
gcp.note: Highly available domain controllers in a Google-managed project peered to your VPC, with trusts to on-premises domains and automatic patching. Used for Windows VMs, Cloud SQL for SQL Server and legacy applications that need Kerberos or LDAP.
pros: Multi-region domains with Google-run patching and backups
Trusts to existing forests keep one identity source
Cloud SQL for SQL Server can join it
cons: Hourly per domain and per extra region
Delegated admin only; no schema changes without a request
Smaller Windows ecosystem on GCP means fewer integrations

azure.name: Microsoft Entra Domain Services
azure.note: Projects your Entra ID tenant into a managed domain with LDAP, Kerberos, NTLM and group policy, synchronised one way from Entra. It is not a full forest: no domain admin, no schema extension, and hashes must sync from Entra.
pros: Users and groups already exist in Entra; nothing to migrate
Fixed hourly SKUs by object count
Domain join for Azure VMs and Azure Files with Kerberos
cons: One-way sync only; changes made in the domain are not reflected back
No schema extension, no domain admin, no trusts in lower SKUs
Password hash sync must be enabled, a policy hurdle in some firms

rows.pick: AWS and GCP run a real forest for you, so they suit lifting an existing domain. Entra Domain Services is the obvious choice when identities already live in Entra and apps just need LDAP or Kerberos.
rows.gotcha: Entra Domain Services is a projection of Entra ID, not Active Directory: no schema changes, no domain admin, one-way sync. An application that extends the schema must go to AWS or GCP managed AD or self-host; forest trusts need the Enterprise SKU.

rows.plain: Software assistants that read alerts, model threats and test your systems the way a junior analyst would, then hand a human the summary.

aws.name: AWS Security Agent
aws.note: A frontier agent, previewed in December 2025 and generally available since March 2026, that performs threat modelling, reviews pull requests and runs penetration tests, with findings routed into Security Hub. It now sits within AWS Continuum, which extends to finding, validating and remediating vulnerabilities.
pros: Penetration testing on demand without scheduling a vendor
Threat models generated from design documents and code
Findings land in Security Hub alongside everything else
cons: Very new; behaviour and pricing are still settling
Autonomous testing needs careful scoping and change control
Value depends on how much of your estate is on AWS

gcp.note: No separately sold agent. Gemini-driven triage, malware analysis and investigation agents are built into Google Security Operations and Security Command Center, and Google Unified Security bundles them with Threat Intelligence and Chrome.
pros: Included in Security Operations packaging rather than metered separately
Mandiant intelligence grounds the agents' reasoning
Alert triage runs inside the SIEM where the data is
cons: Only available to Security Operations customers
No stand-alone threat modelling or pen-testing agent
Capabilities arrive as features, so they are harder to evaluate
gcp.none: Gemini agents ship inside Google Security Operations and Security Command Center rather than as a stand-alone product.

azure.name: Microsoft Security Copilot
azure.note: Generative assistant and a growing set of agents embedded in Defender, Sentinel, Entra, Intune and Purview, for incident summarisation, phishing triage, conditional access optimisation and script analysis. Capacity is bought as provisioned security compute units, with optional overage units.
pros: Embedded in every Microsoft security console you already use
Agents for phishing triage and identity hygiene ship ready-made
Provisioned capacity makes spend predictable
cons: Security compute units are priced per hour whether used or not
Most useful only with the Defender and Sentinel stack
Output still needs analyst review; trust is earned slowly

rows.pick: Security Copilot is the obvious choice for a Microsoft SOC. AWS Security Agent is the only one aimed at builders, testing code and applications. Google's agents come with Security Operations or not at all.
rows.gotcha: These are assistants attached to each vendor's own security stack, so they deepen lock-in rather than sit above the clouds. Treat their findings as input for a human, and budget review time, not just licence cost.

rows.plain: A shared, versioned filing cabinet for code, so a team can change the same files without overwriting each other and can rewind any mistake.

aws.name: AWS CodeCommit
aws.note: Managed private Git that authenticates with IAM and encrypts with KMS. It paused new sign-ups in July 2024, then returned to full general availability in November 2025; it is plain Git with pull requests, nothing more.
pros: IAM identities and KMS keys, no separate login or SSH key estate
Five active users free, then a small per-user monthly fee
Stays inside the account boundary, which regulated teams like
cons: Bare Git: no issues, wiki, discussions or marketplace
Feature investment thin after the 2024 pause
Small ecosystem, most tooling assumes GitHub or GitLab

gcp.name: Secure Source Manager
gcp.note: Single-tenant Git hosting with issues and pull requests, run as a regional instance inside your perimeter. It replaces Cloud Source Repositories, which closed to new customers in June 2024 and is awaiting a turndown date.
pros: Single-tenant instance, works with VPC Service Controls and customer keys
Issues and pull requests included, Cloud Build triggers natively
Private access with no public endpoint if you want it
cons: Billed per instance, dear for a handful of repositories
Young product with a thin integration ecosystem
Cloud Source Repositories users must migrate before shutdown

azure.name: Azure Repos
azure.note: Unlimited private Git (and legacy TFVC) inside Azure DevOps, with pull requests, branch policies and links to Boards work items. Microsoft also owns GitHub, so GitHub Enterprise is the other first-party answer.
pros: Branch policies, pull requests and work-item linking in one suite
First five users free, then a per-user Basic licence
GitHub is the same company, so the migration path is first-party
cons: New features land in GitHub first, Azure Repos moves slowly
Azure DevOps organisations are a separate permission surface from Azure
TFVC lingers for old projects and confuses newcomers

rows.pick: Azure Repos if you already run Azure DevOps Boards and Pipelines. Otherwise the three are interchangeable and mostly irrelevant: teams put code on GitHub or GitLab and use the cloud's build service as the deploy target.
rows.gotcha: All three still steer most teams to GitHub or GitLab; only Azure owns GitHub. CodeCommit's 2024 closure was reversed in 2025, so notes calling it dead are stale, and Cloud Source Repositories is the one actually going away.

rows.plain: An assembly line that builds, tests and releases code automatically every time someone changes it, so shipping is routine rather than an event.

aws.name: AWS CodePipeline
aws.note: Orchestrates stages that call AWS CodeBuild for builds and tests and AWS CodeDeploy for rollouts to EC2, ECS, Lambda or on-premises. Three services wired together, each with its own YAML dialect.
pros: CodeDeploy's blue/green and canary strategies for EC2, ECS and Lambda are the most complete first-party ones
IAM-native, so deployments hold no long-lived secrets
CodeBuild can run GitHub Actions workflows as managed runners
cons: Three services to wire and three configuration formats to learn
Per action-minute (V2) plus build minutes adds up on chatty pipelines
Console pipeline editing is dated, most teams front it with GitHub Actions

gcp.name: Cloud Build
gcp.note: Serverless build runner triggered from GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket via Developer Connect, paired with Cloud Deploy for progressive delivery to GKE, Cloud Run and Compute Engine. Cloud Deploy is built around Skaffold.
pros: Generous free build minutes each month, then per-minute billing
Private pools reach resources inside your VPC
Cloud Deploy gives canary rollouts with approvals for GKE and Cloud Run
cons: Cloud Deploy is Skaffold-shaped, a learning curve if you do not use it
Default workers are modest, faster machines cost more
VM deployments rely on custom targets, less polished than containers

azure.name: Azure Pipelines
azure.note: YAML pipelines with environments, approvals and gates inside Azure DevOps, plus the older click-built classic release pipelines. GitHub Actions, also Microsoft's, is where new investment goes.
pros: Mature YAML with environments, approvals and gates, and a classic UI for teams that want clicks
Billed per parallel job, a flat amount however busy you are
Microsoft-hosted Windows, macOS and Linux agents
cons: Parallel-job model means queues at peak unless you buy more jobs
New capability lands in GitHub Actions first
Azure DevOps identity and permissions sit apart from Azure subscriptions

rows.pick: Azure Pipelines if you need Windows and macOS build agents or a click-driven release process. Cloud Deploy if you want first-party progressive delivery on GKE and Cloud Run. AWS if CodeDeploy's EC2 and Lambda strategies matter. Otherwise GitHub Actions everywhere.
rows.gotcha: Most teams now use GitHub Actions across all three regardless, and treat the native service as the deploy target. The design trap is authentication: use workload identity federation into the cloud rather than storing cloud keys in the CI system.

rows.plain: Describing your servers, networks and databases in text files so the same environment can be rebuilt, reviewed and version-controlled like a recipe.

aws.name: AWS CloudFormation
aws.note: Declarative JSON or YAML templates deployed as stacks, with StackSets for many accounts and Regions and drift detection. AWS Cloud Development Kit (CDK) writes the same stacks in TypeScript, Python and other languages.
pros: Free, and wired into Service Catalog, Control Tower and StackSets across an Organization
Automatic rollback on failure
CDK gives real languages, types and reusable constructs
cons: Slow deployments and opaque rollback errors
Resource coverage lags new launches, the Cloud Control API narrows the gap
Nested stacks and StackSets scale awkwardly, many teams choose Terraform

gcp.name: Infrastructure Manager
gcp.note: Google runs Terraform for you: it stores state, executes plans and applies through Cloud Build. Config Connector drives Google Cloud from Kubernetes objects. Cloud Deployment Manager lost support in April 2026 and turns down in June 2027.
pros: Standard Terraform, no proprietary template language
State and runs managed by Google, no state bucket to secure
Config Connector lets platform teams manage cloud resources with kubectl
cons: Terraform provider coverage sets the ceiling, Google does not own the language
Thinner than Terraform Cloud: no policy-as-code or drift dashboard
Deployment Manager estates must migrate before June 2027

azure.name: Azure Resource Manager
azure.note: The deployment layer behind every Azure API, driven by ARM JSON templates or Bicep, a readable language that compiles to ARM. Deployment stacks manage a group of resources with deny settings; Azure Blueprints retires in January 2027.
pros: Bicep is free, readable and supports new resource types on day one
What-if previews and deployment stacks with deny settings
Deployments are visible and auditable in the portal
cons: Bicep is Azure-only, so multi-cloud teams still run Terraform
Deployments can be slow with cryptic errors
Blueprints retiring, migrate to deployment stacks and template specs

rows.pick: Single-cloud and deep integration: CloudFormation or CDK on AWS, Bicep on Azure. Google has effectively chosen Terraform for you. Any team spanning two clouds standardises on Terraform and uses the native service, if at all, as the runner.
rows.gotcha: Google dropped its own Deployment Manager and standardised on Terraform, so there is no proprietary template language to learn. Bicep compiles to ARM JSON and CDK emits CloudFormation: on those two clouds the native language is a translation layer, not a different engine.

rows.plain: A ready-made programmer's desk that lives in the cloud, so anyone can start coding from a browser with the right tools already installed.

aws.none: Cloud9 closed to new customers in July 2024 with no successor; CloudShell covers quick browser shells, and teams run Codespaces, Coder or Gitpod on EC2.

gcp.name: Cloud Workstations
gcp.note: Managed developer VMs inside your VPC, built from a container image with Code OSS or JetBrains IDEs, started on demand and stopped when idle. Cloud Shell remains the free browser terminal for quick work.
pros: Runs inside your VPC with private access and VPC Service Controls
Custom images, JetBrains and Code OSS supported
Per-hour billing with automatic stop when idle
cons: You pay VM, disk and a management fee per running hour
Cluster, configuration and workstation hierarchy is more to administer than Codespaces
Regional, with minutes of cold start on first boot

azure.name: Microsoft Dev Box
azure.note: Windows developer workstations delivered like Windows 365 PCs and managed by Intune, closed to new sign-ups since 1 November 2025 and retiring on 18 September 2028 in favour of Windows 365. GitHub Codespaces is the lighter Linux option and Azure DevTest Labs covers test environments.
pros: A complete Windows machine with Visual Studio, managed like any corporate PC
Dev centre and project images per team
Hibernation and auto-stop control cost
cons: Needs Windows Enterprise, Intune and Entra licences on top of hourly compute
Windows only, Linux teams go to Codespaces
Fewer regions than ordinary VMs

rows.pick: Dev Box is closed to new sign-ups, so Windows and Visual Studio shops now go to Windows 365. Cloud Workstations for Linux developers needing private access inside a VPC. On AWS, GitHub Codespaces or self-hosted Coder.
rows.gotcha: AWS has left this market: Cloud9 is closed, and Kiro is a desktop IDE whose companion Kiro Web runs agent sessions in cloud sandboxes, not a hosted workstation. A coding assistant is not a development environment; they are different products with different billing.

rows.plain: A central switchboard for settings and on/off switches in a running app, so you can change behaviour or turn a feature on for some users without redeploying.

aws.name: AWS AppConfig
aws.note: A capability of AWS Systems Manager that deploys configuration and feature flags gradually, with validators, a bake time and automatic rollback when a CloudWatch alarm fires. An agent and Lambda extension cache values locally.
pros: Staged rollouts with bake time and automatic rollback tied to alarms
Validators stop malformed configuration reaching production
Lambda extension and agent cache locally, cutting calls
cons: Billed per configuration request, chatty clients get expensive without the agent
Flag management UI is thin against LaunchDarkly
Lives under Systems Manager, awkward discoverability and IAM

gcp.none: No Google Cloud flag service for servers; Firebase Remote Config now has a server-side SDK for Cloud Run and Cloud Functions, and backend teams otherwise use environment variables, Secret Manager or a partner flag service.

azure.name: Azure App Configuration
azure.note: A managed key-value store with labels, snapshots, Key Vault references and a feature manager offering percentage, targeting and time-window filters. Premium tier adds replicas and geo-replication.
pros: Feature filters for percentage, targeting and time windows, with a manager UI
Key Vault references keep secrets out of settings
Snapshots and geo-replication for safe, repeatable rollouts
cons: Standard tier billed per store per day plus request bands, many stores add up
Richest client libraries are .NET and Java
No staged rollout with automatic rollback, you build it in pipelines

rows.pick: AWS AppConfig if your concern is safe delivery of configuration, because rollback on alarm is its whole design. Azure App Configuration if you want a feature-flag manager for .NET or Java apps. On Google Cloud, budget for a partner product.
rows.gotcha: Not the same shape: AppConfig is a deployment engine, App Configuration a store with a flag UI. Neither is an experimentation platform, and Google offers only Firebase Remote Config's server SDK, so a cross-cloud design keeps flags in a vendor product or your own database.

rows.plain: Renting a cupboard full of real phones and browsers in someone else's building so your app can be tested on them without buying a single handset.

aws.name: AWS Device Farm
aws.note: Runs automated tests and manual sessions on real Android and iOS devices and on desktop browsers, priced per device-minute or as flat unlimited device slots. Private device fleets are available for enterprises.
pros: Real phones and desktop browsers in one service
Per-minute pricing or a flat monthly unlimited slot
Remote access sessions for manual debugging
cons: Devices live only in one US Region, latency and data residency issues
Device catalogue smaller and slower to add new models than commercial farms
Framework support is dated, mostly Appium

gcp.name: Firebase Test Lab
gcp.note: Firebase's device lab runs instrumentation, XCTest and automatic Robo crawls on real and virtual Android and iOS devices, billed per device-hour with a daily free allowance. Android Device Streaming, driven from Android Studio, adds remote access to Firebase-hosted devices.
pros: Free daily quota of virtual and physical device tests
Robo test explores an app with no test code
Virtual devices are cheap for broad matrix runs
cons: Mobile only, no desktop browser testing
Physical device queue times at peak
Firebase billing account and console, separate from the Cloud console habits

azure.none: Visual Studio App Center retired in March 2025; teams use BrowserStack or Sauce Labs for devices, and Azure App Testing for Playwright browser runs.

rows.pick: Firebase Test Lab for mobile teams already on Firebase, especially with Robo tests. Device Farm if you need desktop browsers too or a private fleet. Azure has left the field; buy a device cloud.
rows.gotcha: Only Google's option is mobile-only and only AWS covers desktop browsers, so the 'equivalent' changes what you can test. Azure App Testing is a load and browser-automation service, not a device farm, despite living in the same aisle.

rows.plain: A command line that opens in a browser tab, already logged in to your cloud account with the tools installed, for quick jobs without setting up a laptop.

aws.name: AWS CloudShell
aws.note: A free browser terminal pre-authenticated as your console identity, with the AWS CLI, SDKs and Docker installed and a small persistent home directory per Region. VPC environments can reach private resources.
pros: Free and pre-authenticated, with CLI, SDKs and Docker ready
Persistent home directory per Region
VPC environments reach private resources
cons: Home directory is per Region and wiped after months of inactivity
Sessions time out after about twenty minutes idle
Not available in every Region

gcp.name: Cloud Shell
gcp.note: A free small VM with a persistent home directory, gcloud, kubectl, Terraform and language runtimes, plus the Cloud Shell Editor and a web preview for local servers. Tutorials open straight into it.
pros: Free, with a persistent home and an editor with web preview
gcloud, kubectl, Terraform and runtimes preinstalled
Open-in-Cloud-Shell links power tutorials and quickstarts
cons: Weekly usage quota and a small ephemeral VM
Home disk deleted after months of inactivity
No VPC access, private endpoints are unreachable

azure.name: Azure Cloud Shell
azure.note: Bash or PowerShell in the portal with Az modules, Bicep, Terraform and kubectl, persisting files in a clouddrive file share or running ephemerally. It can be deployed into a virtual network for private access.
pros: Bash and PowerShell with Az modules, Bicep, Terraform and kubectl
clouddrive file share keeps files and can be shared
Can run inside a virtual network for private access
cons: Persistence needs a storage account you pay for, or run ephemeral and lose files
Short idle timeout
Virtual network mode needs a relay and extra setup

rows.pick: Interchangeable: use whichever cloud you are logged into. Google's is the most complete as a mini workstation; Azure's is the only one with PowerShell by default; AWS's is the plainest.
rows.gotcha: None of these is a workstation: small VMs, short idle timeouts and home directories wiped after inactivity. Use them for one-off commands and tutorials, and keep anything you would miss in Git. Private network access is extra on AWS and Azure, absent on Google.

rows.plain: The dashboard and warning lights of a car, for your systems: numbers over time, charts to watch them, and alarms when something drifts out of range.

aws.name: Amazon CloudWatch
aws.note: The metrics, alarms and dashboards hub that every AWS service feeds by default, now also home to logs, traces and Application Signals. Alarms drive Auto Scaling, Systems Manager and EventBridge directly.
pros: Every AWS service emits metrics by default, alarms trigger scaling and automation natively
Composite and anomaly-detection alarms
Cross-account observability for a central view
cons: Custom metrics, alarms, dashboards and API calls are each billed, high cardinality gets dear
Metrics are per Region, a global view means aggregation
Default granularity is one to five minutes, finer costs more

gcp.name: Cloud Monitoring
gcp.note: Metrics, dashboards, uptime checks, SLO monitoring and alerting for Google Cloud, with Prometheus ingestion built in rather than sold separately. A metrics scope lets one project watch many.
pros: Google-service metrics are free and a metrics scope spans projects
SLO monitoring and error budgets are first-party
PromQL and Prometheus ingestion native, no separate service
cons: Custom and Prometheus metrics billed by volume ingested
Alerting policies now carry their own monthly charge
Dashboards plainer than Grafana, many teams add it anyway

azure.name: Azure Monitor
azure.note: One product spanning platform metrics, Log Analytics, Application Insights, alerts and workbooks. Metrics are free for 93 days; almost everything interesting lands in Log Analytics and is billed per gigabyte.
