pros: Metrics, logs, traces and alerts under one roof with workbooks for rich dashboards
Platform metrics free for 93 days
Action groups route alerts to Teams, ITSM tools and webhooks
cons: Logs and Application Insights are billed per GB ingested, and that is where the bill grows
Metric alerts billed per time series monitored
Multi-resource metric alerts limited to certain resource types

rows.pick: Interchangeable for the core job: metrics in, alarms out, dashboards on top. Cloud Monitoring if SLOs and Prometheus matter most; Azure Monitor if you want one query language across everything; CloudWatch if alarms must drive AWS automation.
rows.gotcha: Azure Monitor collects it all and you query with KQL, which is closer to Log Analytics than to CloudWatch Insights. The cost shape also differs: AWS bills per metric and alarm, Google per sample and now per alert policy, Azure per gigabyte of logs.

rows.plain: Every program's diary collected into one searchable archive, so when something breaks you can read what happened rather than guess.

aws.name: Amazon CloudWatch Logs
aws.note: Log groups per application with retention you set, Logs Insights for queries and subscription filters that stream to Firehose, Lambda or OpenSearch. An Infrequent Access class halves ingestion cost for rarely queried logs.
pros: Standard and Infrequent Access classes price logs by how often you read them
Subscription filters stream to Firehose, Lambda or OpenSearch
Retention per group from one day to forever
cons: Ingestion at about USD 0.50 per GB is the dear part, plus per-GB scanned on queries
Query language is CloudWatch-specific and weaker than KQL or SQL
Log groups are per Region and account, central logging is your plumbing

gcp.name: Cloud Logging
gcp.note: Logs flow through the Log Router into buckets, with exclusion filters that drop noise before billing and sinks to BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub or another project. Log Analytics gives SQL over buckets at no extra charge.
pros: Free monthly allowance per project and exclusions filter before billing
Log Analytics gives SQL over buckets with BigQuery underneath, no extra charge
Sinks to BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub or a central project are one line
cons: About USD 0.50 per GiB ingested after the allowance
Default 30-day retention, longer costs extra
Per-project buckets mean an organisation-wide sink is a deliberate design step

azure.name: Azure Monitor Logs
azure.note: Log Analytics workspaces queried with KQL, the same language as Sentinel and Data Explorer, with Analytics, Basic and Auxiliary tiers priced by how often you query. Commitment tiers cut the per-GB price for large estates.
pros: KQL is the most capable log query language of the three and is shared with Sentinel
Analytics, Basic and Auxiliary tiers price logs by access pattern
Commitment tiers cut per-GB cost sharply at scale
cons: Analytics tier costs USD 2 to 3 per GB ingested, several times AWS and Google
Workspace design, one central or many, is hard to change later
Basic and Auxiliary tiers restrict query features and retention

rows.pick: Azure Monitor Logs if analysts will live in the query language, because KQL repays the price. Cloud Logging if you want logs in BigQuery with the least friction. CloudWatch Logs if the consumers are AWS services rather than humans.
rows.gotcha: One query language across logs, metrics and traces is Azure's real advantage: KQL is the same in Monitor, Sentinel and Data Explorer. Azure's Analytics tier costs several times the other two per gigabyte, though, so tiering and sampling are design decisions, not tuning.

rows.plain: Following a single customer request as it hops between a dozen services, timing each hop, so you can see exactly where the slowness or error lives.

aws.name: AWS X-Ray
aws.note: Trace collection and service maps with sampling built into the SDK, now fronted by CloudWatch Application Signals, which adds APM-style service views and SLOs on top of OpenTelemetry. AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry is the portable collector.
pros: First 100,000 traces a month free, then priced per million
Application Signals adds service maps, SLOs and APM views on OpenTelemetry data
Lambda, API Gateway and ECS emit traces with a toggle
cons: X-Ray's own segment format is AWS-specific, OpenTelemetry is the portable path
Application Signals is newer and adds its own charge
Trace retention fixed at 30 days

gcp.name: Cloud Trace
gcp.note: Span ingestion and latency analysis with an OTLP endpoint as the native path, paired with Cloud Profiler for free continuous CPU and heap profiling and Error Reporting for grouped exceptions. No single APM product ties them together.
pros: Millions of spans a month free, then priced per span
Cloud Profiler is free and runs continuously in production
OpenTelemetry native, with an OTLP endpoint
cons: No APM service map with SLO tracking comparable to Application Insights
Trace retention 30 days
Console is thin for deep analysis, teams add Grafana Tempo or a vendor

azure.name: Azure Monitor Application Insights
azure.note: The most complete out-of-the-box APM of the three: application map, live metrics, availability tests, profiler and snapshot debugging, with auto-instrumentation for App Service, Functions and .NET. Telemetry lands in Log Analytics.
pros: Application map, live metrics, availability tests, profiler and snapshot debugger included
Auto-instrumentation for App Service, Functions and .NET with no code changes
OpenTelemetry distro supported
cons: Telemetry is billed per GB in Log Analytics, chatty apps need sampling from day one
Auto-instrumentation depth varies by language, .NET and Java richest
Classic resources retired, old setups needed migration to workspaces

rows.pick: Application Insights is the obvious choice for a .NET or Java team on Azure that wants APM without assembling parts. Elsewhere, instrument with OpenTelemetry and treat X-Ray or Cloud Trace as one backend among several.
rows.gotcha: Distributed tracing. Application Insights is the most complete out of the box, and all three now take OpenTelemetry. Instrument with OpenTelemetry, never a cloud SDK, or the tracing code becomes the lock-in nobody noticed.

rows.plain: The popular free monitoring tools, Prometheus and Grafana, run for you by the cloud so you keep the tools your team knows without babysitting the servers.

aws.name: Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus
aws.note: Prometheus-compatible metric storage billed per sample, with an agentless collector that scrapes EKS for you. Amazon Managed Grafana is the separate, per-user dashboard service with AWS data sources and IAM Identity Center sign-in.
pros: Agentless collector scrapes EKS, no Prometheus servers to run
Billed per sample ingested and queried, no instances to size
Managed Grafana comes wired to AWS data sources
cons: Managed Grafana bills per active user each month, editors more than viewers
Workspaces are regional, cross-Region needs federation
Grafana Enterprise plugins cost extra per user

gcp.name: Managed Service for Prometheus
gcp.note: Prometheus metrics stored in the same Monarch backend as Cloud Monitoring, queryable with PromQL in Monitoring dashboards and alerts. Collection on GKE is a switch; there is no first-party managed Grafana.
pros: Prometheus and Cloud Monitoring metrics share one store and one dashboard
Managed collection on GKE is a checkbox
Scales with Google's own metrics backend
cons: Billed per sample ingested, high cardinality costs the same as elsewhere
No first-party Grafana, run your own or buy Grafana Cloud
PromQL only, Prometheus alerting rules run through Cloud Monitoring

azure.name: Azure Monitor managed service for Prometheus
azure.note: Prometheus metrics stored in an Azure Monitor workspace at a low per-sample price, enabled on AKS by a switch. Azure Managed Grafana is the separate dashboard service, signed in with Entra and pre-wired to Azure Monitor.
pros: Low per-sample price with AKS collection enabled by a switch
Managed Grafana signs in with Entra and comes wired to Azure Monitor
Grafana alerting and Azure Monitor alerts both work
cons: Managed Grafana bills an hourly instance fee plus per active user
Prometheus data lives outside Log Analytics, KQL does not reach it
Managed Prometheus reached regions later than Azure Monitor itself

rows.pick: Interchangeable: every cloud stores Prometheus per sample and Google is the only one without a managed Grafana. Choose Google if you want Prometheus inside the native monitoring product; choose AWS or Azure if you want Grafana as a service.
rows.gotcha: Every cloud eventually gave in and offered hosted Prometheus and Grafana rather than fighting them. Billing differs: Grafana is per user on AWS and per instance plus user on Azure, Prometheus per sample everywhere, so dashboard-heavy and metric-heavy teams pay in different places.

rows.plain: A stock-take that never stops: what you own, how each item is set up, how that has changed over time, and which items break the house rules.

aws.name: AWS Config
aws.note: Records a configuration item every time a resource changes, keeps the timeline, and evaluates managed or custom rules grouped into conformance packs. Remediation runs through Systems Manager Automation; an aggregator spans accounts and Regions.
pros: Full configuration history and timeline per resource
Rules and conformance packs map to compliance frameworks, with auto-remediation
Organisation aggregator gives one view across accounts and Regions
cons: Billed per configuration item recorded and per rule evaluation, churny resources surprise you
Recording is per Region, enable it everywhere
Rules evaluate after the fact, they do not block a deployment

gcp.name: Cloud Asset Inventory
gcp.note: A free inventory of every resource and IAM policy across the organisation, searchable, exportable to BigQuery and streamed as feeds through Pub/Sub. Compliance evaluation lives elsewhere, in Security Command Center and Organization Policy.
pros: Free, with whole-organisation export to BigQuery for SQL
Real-time feeds via Pub/Sub on any change
Policy Analyzer answers who can access what
cons: History retained 35 days only, longer needs your own export
No rule engine, compliance is Security Command Center or Organization Policy
Asset type coverage lags the newest services

azure.name: Azure Policy
azure.note: Rules that audit, deny, modify or deploy at request time across subscriptions, with built-in initiatives for ISO, NIST and CIS. Azure Resource Graph supplies the inventory and fast KQL search, with a fortnight of change history.
pros: Free, and can deny, modify or auto-deploy at request time, not just report afterwards
Built-in initiatives for ISO, NIST, CIS and regulatory frameworks
Resource Graph searches every subscription with KQL at no cost
cons: Only about two weeks of change history, no long configuration timeline
Compliance state can lag up to a day
Broad deny policies bite CI/CD pipelines unexpectedly

rows.pick: Azure Policy if you want to prevent rather than detect, the only one that blocks at deploy time. AWS Config if auditors need a resource-level history. Cloud Asset Inventory if you want the data in a warehouse for free.
rows.gotcha: Azure Policy stands out by being able to deny and auto-remediate at deploy time, not only report drift after the fact. Only AWS Config keeps a long per-resource timeline, and bills for it; Google gives the inventory free but leaves the history to you.

rows.plain: The caretaker for hundreds of servers: patching them, running the same command on all of them, opening a shell on one, and scripting the routine chores.

aws.name: AWS Systems Manager
aws.note: One agent and console for patching, Run Command, Session Manager, State Manager, Inventory and Automation runbooks, with a unified view across accounts and Regions. Incident Manager and Change Manager closed to new customers on 7 November 2025 and receive no new features.
pros: Patching, commands, sessions and runbooks in one agent preinstalled on Amazon images
Mostly free for EC2, pay for on-premises advanced nodes and heavy automation
Session Manager gives shell access with no open ports
cons: A grab-bag of many capabilities with uneven maturity; Incident and Change Manager closed to new customers
On-premises nodes bill hourly at the advanced tier
Cross-account operations need Organizations delegation and careful IAM

gcp.name: VM Manager
gcp.note: OS patch management, inventory and OS policies for Compute Engine fleets through the OS Config agent baked into Google images. Shell access is OS Login plus Identity-Aware Proxy; there is no runbook engine, orchestration goes to Workflows or Cloud Run jobs.
pros: Patch, inventory and OS policies through an agent already in Google images
OS Login and Identity-Aware Proxy give SSH without public IPs
Results flow into Cloud Logging and Monitoring
cons: No runbook or run-command engine, orchestration is Workflows, Scheduler or Cloud Run jobs
Per-VM hourly charge for patching and policies unless on a premium OS image
Compute Engine only, on-premises fleets are out of scope

azure.name: Azure Automation
azure.note: PowerShell and Python runbooks on schedules and webhooks, with hybrid workers for your own machines. Azure Update Manager handles patching for Azure and Arc servers, and the old State Configuration and change-tracking pieces are moving or retiring.
pros: Runbooks with schedules, webhooks and a monthly free allowance of job minutes
Update Manager is free for Azure VMs and covers Arc servers for a flat monthly fee
Hybrid runbook workers run on your own machines
cons: DSC and change-tracking pieces retiring or moving, the estate is in flux
Runbook authoring and debugging is clunky
Arc servers pay per server per month for updates and automation

rows.pick: Systems Manager is the obvious choice for a large EC2 estate, nothing else bundles as much. Azure if the fleet spans on-premises via Arc. On Google Cloud, treat VM Manager as patching only and build orchestration with Workflows.
rows.gotcha: Google's Identity-Aware Proxy is Session Manager's no-open-ports SSH story under another name, and Azure Bastion is the same idea. The gap is runbooks: only AWS and Azure ship a fleet automation engine; on Google you fill it with Workflows, Cloud Scheduler or Cloud Run jobs.

rows.plain: The itemised bill and the household budget for your cloud: what each thing cost, who spent it, and an alert when spending runs ahead of plan.

aws.name: AWS Cost Explorer
aws.note: The console for visualising and forecasting spend, alongside AWS Budgets for thresholds and actions, AWS Data Exports for line-item data in S3, Cost Anomaly Detection and Cost Optimization Hub. Billing Conductor handles chargeback pricing.
pros: Console is free with months of history and forecasts
Budgets can trigger actions such as stopping instances, not just emails
Data Exports give the granular line items a warehouse needs
cons: API billed per request and hourly granularity costs extra
Cost allocation tags must be activated and take a day to appear
Data lags about a day, so budgets are alerts, not caps

gcp.name: Cloud Billing
gcp.note: Billing accounts with reports, budgets and alerts, and an export to BigQuery that most teams treat as the real interface. FinOps hub and Recommender surface savings; budgets can publish to Pub/Sub for automation.
pros: Free, and the BigQuery export is the most natural warehouse-grade billing feed
Budgets publish to Pub/Sub so responses can be automated
FinOps hub and Recommender gather savings in one place
cons: Standard budgets only notify; spend cap budgets that pause services are still preview
Data is organised per billing account, not per organisation, with a delay
Labels must be applied consistently and many resources carry none

azure.name: Microsoft Cost Management
azure.note: Cost analysis, budgets, alerts, scheduled exports (including the FOCUS format) and reservation management for Azure, free in every subscription. The AWS connector was retired in 2025, so it is Azure-only again.
pros: Free, with analysis, budgets, exports and reservation management in one place
Resource groups and subscriptions give allocation boundaries without tagging
Budgets trigger action groups and automation
cons: Costs appear with an 8 to 24 hour lag and budgets alert rather than cap
Tag inheritance for allocation is off by default
AWS connector retired in 2025, Azure only now

rows.pick: Interchangeable at the console level; all three are free and all lag by a day. Google is the obvious choice for teams who analyse in a warehouse, because the BigQuery export is the primary interface rather than an afterthought.
rows.gotcha: Budgets are mostly alerts, not caps: only AWS Budgets actions stop instances or apply deny policies unaided, Google's spend cap budgets are still preview and Azure budgets only alert. Everyone exports billing data to a warehouse eventually, and Google makes that the most natural.

rows.plain: A mechanic who inspects your setup and hands you a list: this is oversized, that is insecure, this could be cheaper, with no obligation to act.

aws.name: AWS Trusted Advisor
aws.note: Hundreds of checks across cost, security, resilience, performance and limits, the full set gated behind Business Support+, Enterprise Support or Unified Operations plans; Business and Developer Support retire on 1 January 2027. Well-Architected Tool runs structured reviews; Compute Optimizer and Cost Optimization Hub give right-sizing.
pros: Hundreds of checks spanning cost, security, resilience, performance and limits
Organisation-wide view with Business Support+ or Enterprise Support
Compute Optimizer and Cost Optimization Hub attach savings figures
cons: Full check set requires a paid Support plan
Daily refresh, no enforcement
Recommendations do not know your intent, cost ones are a starting list

gcp.name: Recommender
gcp.note: The engine behind Active Assist: right-sizing, idle resources, committed-use discounts and, unusually, least-privilege IAM role suggestions drawn from real usage. Free, with an API and BigQuery export; Gemini Cloud Assist now explains and applies them.
pros: Free, with export to BigQuery for portfolio-wide review
IAM recommender suggests least-privilege roles from actual usage
Gemini Cloud Assist explains recommendations and can apply them
cons: Narrower catalogue of checks than Trusted Advisor or Azure Advisor, no architecture review tool
Per project, organisation-wide needs export and aggregation
Idle-resource suggestions rely on short utilisation windows

azure.name: Azure Advisor
azure.note: Free recommendations for cost, reliability, operational excellence and performance in every subscription, with security items fed from Defender for Cloud. An Advisor score tracks progress and a Well-Architected review tool structures the conversation.
pros: Free in every subscription, no support plan needed
Advisor score tracks progress and recommendations can raise alerts
Reliability items map to the Well-Architected Framework with a review tool
cons: Security recommendations come from Defender for Cloud, priced separately
Only as good as the default utilisation thresholds
Suggestions can push reservations that lock in spend

rows.pick: Azure Advisor for breadth without a support contract. Recommender if you want least-privilege IAM suggestions, which nobody else offers. Trusted Advisor is the deepest, but only once you pay for Business Support+ or better.
rows.gotcha: Automated recommendations. Treat the cost ones as a starting list, never as instructions: all three tune thresholds for the average workload and will happily suggest shrinking the machine that handles your month-end peak.

rows.plain: A vending machine of pre-approved building blocks: the platform team stocks it with vetted templates, and other teams press a button to get one without asking permission.

aws.name: AWS Service Catalog
aws.note: Portfolios of products defined as CloudFormation or Terraform, launched by end users under constraints and launch roles they do not personally hold, with TagOptions forcing consistent tags. Portfolios share across an Organization.
pros: Products can be CloudFormation or Terraform, launched under roles users do not hold
Shares portfolios across an Organization
TagOptions force consistent tags at launch
cons: Launching through it is slower and less transparent than a direct stack
Product versioning and sharing are fiddly at scale
Terraform products need a separate engine running in your account

gcp.name: Service Catalog
gcp.note: Curated solutions, Terraform configurations, Marketplace items or plain links, surfaced to projects through the organisation and folder hierarchy. Free, and Terraform solutions deploy through Cloud Build running Terraform, with the module stored in a Cloud Storage bucket.
pros: Free, scoped to organisation, folder or project through the hierarchy
Terraform solutions deploy via Cloud Build from a Cloud Storage bucket
Solutions can point at Marketplace products or any link
cons: No launch constraints or delegated permissions as rich as AWS
Deployment Manager solutions retire with that service
Light adoption, thin documentation and community

azure.name: Azure Deployment Environments
azure.note: Environment definitions kept in Git, offered through a dev centre and deployed into subscriptions with identities developers never hold. It retires on 22 February 2027; Microsoft points to Bicep or ARM with Azure Verified Modules and pipelines, and Managed Applications still covers publishers.
pros: Catalogues live in Git and definitions can be Bicep, ARM, Terraform or Pulumi
Environment types map to subscriptions and identities, developers hold no deploy rights
Managed Applications keep the platform team in control of what they ship
cons: Needs a dev centre and project hierarchy before the first environment, heavy for small teams
Retiring on 22 February 2027, so not a place for new investment
Managed Applications lock resources in a group you cannot edit directly

rows.pick: AWS Service Catalog is the mature choice for a governed multi-account estate. Azure Deployment Environments retires in February 2027; Azure teams should look to Bicep with Azure Verified Modules and pipelines. Google's is a lightweight index, useful mainly with Terraform.
rows.gotcha: The same word covers three depths. AWS enforces at launch with constraints and roles; Azure delegates via environment types; Google mostly points at things. A governance design that leans on AWS-style launch constraints has no direct twin on Google Cloud.

rows.plain: The provider telling you that something on their side is broken or about to be maintained and that it affects your stuff, rather than a generic weather report.

aws.name: AWS Health
aws.note: Personalised events for the resources in your accounts, shown in the AWS Health Dashboard and emitted to EventBridge for automation, with an organisational view and planned lifecycle events for deprecations. The API needs Business or Enterprise Support.
pros: Personalised events with EventBridge integration for automation
Organisational view across accounts
Planned lifecycle events give deprecation dates in advance
cons: API gated behind Business or Enterprise Support
Public status page understates incidents, trust the personalised view
Events are Regional and account-scoped unless the organisational view is enabled

gcp.name: Personalized Service Health
gcp.note: Incidents relevant to your projects and organisation, including emerging incidents before they reach the public status page, with a Cloud Logging feed you can alert on and an API. Maintenance planning sits in Unified Maintenance.
pros: Free, per project and organisation, with a Cloud Logging feed to alert on
API and Pub/Sub-friendly for integration
Surfaces emerging incidents before the public status page
cons: Must be enabled per project or through organisation policy
Covers Google-side incidents, maintenance lives in Unified Maintenance
Newer product with a shorter history

azure.name: Azure Service Health
azure.note: Service issues, planned maintenance, health and security advisories for your subscriptions, with Resource Health per resource and alerts through action groups. Post-incident reviews are published in the same place.
pros: Free, with issues, maintenance and advisories in one place and Resource Health per resource
Alerts route through action groups
Post-incident reviews published in the portal
cons: Incident communication can lag the actual impact
Alerts must be configured per subscription
Resource Health covers only supported resource types

rows.pick: Interchangeable: each is the personalised view you should trust over the public status page, and each can raise an alert. The difference is plumbing: EventBridge on AWS, Cloud Logging on Google, action groups on Azure.
rows.gotcha: Only AWS charges for the programmatic version by gating the API behind a support plan. All three public status pages lag and understate, so a runbook that checks the public page instead of the personalised feed will be the last to know.

rows.plain: Deliberately breaking things in a controlled way, like a fire drill, to prove the system survives a lost server or network before real life tests it.

aws.name: AWS Fault Injection Service
aws.note: Managed experiments that stop instances, throttle APIs, sever networks or simulate a whole Availability Zone losing power, with stop conditions tied to CloudWatch alarms. Billed per action-minute.
pros: Pre-built scenarios simulate an Availability Zone power interruption or lost Region connectivity
Stop conditions tied to CloudWatch alarms halt experiments automatically
Actions span EC2, ECS, EKS, RDS, networking and Systems Manager
cons: Billed per action-minute, long soak experiments add up
AWS-resource faults only, application faults need Systems Manager documents you write
Multi-account experiments need Organizations setup

gcp.none: No first-party fault-injection service; teams run Chaos Mesh or LitmusChaos on GKE, use Gremlin, or script Compute Engine and network disruptions.

azure.name: Azure Chaos Studio
azure.note: Experiments built from service-direct faults on Azure resources, agent-based faults inside VMs such as CPU pressure and latency, and Chaos Mesh faults on AKS. Experiments are ARM resources, so they deploy with Bicep; billed per action-minute.
pros: Service-direct and agent-based faults, plus AKS faults via Chaos Mesh
Experiments are ARM resources, versioned and deployed with Bicep
Per action-minute pricing similar to AWS
cons: Smaller fault library, zone-outage scenarios less turnkey than AWS
Onboarding targets and identities per resource is tedious
Fewer regions than core services

rows.pick: AWS if you want to rehearse an Availability Zone failure with a single scenario. Azure if experiments should live in infrastructure code. On Google Cloud you bring an open-source tool, which also happens to be the portable answer everywhere.
rows.gotcha: The managed services only break their own cloud's resources. A design that relies on infrastructure-level fault injection has no twin on Google Cloud, and if you want portable experiments the answer is Chaos Mesh or LitmusChaos on Kubernetes in all three.

rows.plain: A tireless junior engineer built from a language model who reads your alerts, digs through logs and either explains what broke or, with permission, fixes it.

aws.name: AWS DevOps Agent
aws.note: A frontier agent launched in December 2025 that investigates incidents across CloudWatch, CloudTrail and deployment history, proposes root causes and suggests prevention. Release management and autonomous testing arrived in preview in June 2026; Amazon Q Developer remains the console chat assistant.
pros: Correlates metrics, logs, traces and recent deployments into a root-cause narrative
Works from existing alarms and chat channels rather than a new console
Release management and autonomous testing arriving in preview
cons: New in late 2025, runbooks and guardrails still maturing
Needs tightly scoped IAM, a broad agent role is a new blast radius
Only as good as the telemetry you already send to CloudWatch

gcp.name: Gemini Cloud Assist
gcp.note: The console assistant that understands your actual projects: it explains errors, costs and architecture, drafts gcloud commands and Terraform, and its investigations turn a Logging or Monitoring finding into a root-cause analysis. An assistant more than an actor.
pros: Sits in the console with knowledge of your real projects and resources
Investigations turn a log or alert into a structured root-cause analysis
Drafts gcloud commands and Terraform you can review
cons: Explains rather than fixes, a human runs the commands
Quality depends on the telemetry and IAM visibility you grant it
Advanced features tie into Gemini subscriptions

azure.name: Azure SRE Agent
azure.note: An autonomous agent, generally available since March 2026, that diagnoses incidents on App Service, AKS, Functions and databases and mitigates them behind approval gates, raising GitHub issues and pull requests. Azure Copilot adds six further agents, from migration and deployment to resiliency and troubleshooting.
pros: Diagnoses and, with approval, mitigates incidents rather than only explaining them
Wired to Azure Monitor alerts, GitHub issues and pull requests
Part of a wider Azure Copilot agent family
cons: Azure Agent Units: a fixed always-on hourly charge plus token-based activity, harder to forecast than seats
Needs read and act permissions across subscriptions, governance first
Autonomous mitigation is opt-in and still earning trust

rows.pick: Azure SRE Agent if you want something that acts today; AWS DevOps Agent if your estate is CloudWatch-centred and you want investigation first; Gemini Cloud Assist if you want an explainer in the console with no autonomy to govern.
rows.gotcha: The word agent covers three levels of autonomy: Cloud Assist explains, DevOps Agent investigates, SRE Agent acts. Match the permission model to the level, expect billing by activity rather than by seat, and remember each one reads only its own cloud's telemetry.

rows.plain: The invisible ceilings on how many of anything you may create, and asking for the ceiling to be raised before launch day finds it for you.

aws.name: Service Quotas
aws.note: One console and API for limits across services, with CloudWatch alarms on utilisation and request templates that apply increases to new accounts in an Organization. Many increases still open a Support case behind the scenes.
pros: One place and API for limits across services, with utilisation alarms
Request templates pre-raise quotas for new accounts in an Organization
Free
cons: Many limits are still adjusted through Support cases with human review
Quotas are per Region and per account, multiply your requests
Some hard limits cannot be raised at all

gcp.name: Cloud Quotas
gcp.note: An API and console for viewing and adjusting quotas, with quota preferences you can set in Terraform and a quota adjuster (in preview) that submits increase requests automatically within policy. Requests above thresholds go to human review.
pros: Quota preferences are API and Terraform objects, applied to projects or folders
Quota adjuster (preview) requests increases automatically within limits
Free
cons: Requests above policy thresholds go to human review with unpredictable turnaround
Per project, so a project-per-team layout multiplies the work
GPU and TPU quotas are the scarce ones and are often refused in busy regions

azure.name: Azure Quotas
azure.note: The My quotas page and Quota REST API cover compute, networking and most resource providers, with quota groups to share compute quota across subscriptions. vCPU quota per VM family per region per subscription is the classic blocker.
pros: One page and API for compute, networking and most providers
Quota groups share compute quota across subscriptions
Free
cons: vCPU quota per VM family per region per subscription blocks launches
GPU families need a support request and justification
Not every resource provider is in the API yet

rows.pick: Interchangeable in shape: free, per-region, per-account-or-project ledgers with an API. The difference is how much is raised automatically versus by a human, where Google's quota adjuster, still in preview, is furthest along and Azure's GPU requests are the slowest.
rows.gotcha: Quotas cause more launch-day incidents than capacity does. Raise them in advance, per region and per account or project, and test that the increase applied. Azure's per-VM-family vCPU quota and Google's per-project GPU quota are the usual surprises.

rows.plain: Labels and folders for everything you own in the cloud, so you can find a thing, know whose it is, and add up what each team costs.

aws.name: AWS Resource Explorer
aws.note: Free search across Regions and accounts by name, type or tag from the console search bar. Tag Editor bulk-edits tags, Resource Groups group by tag query, and tag policies in Organizations standardise keys and values.
pros: Free search across Regions and accounts from the console bar
Tag Editor bulk-edits and Resource Groups group by tag query
Tag policies standardise keys and values across an Organization
cons: Tags are free text, only tag policies plus service control policies enforce them at creation
Cross-Region search needs an aggregator Region and some resource types are missed
Cost allocation tags need separate activation and lag a day

gcp.name: Resource Manager
gcp.note: Organisation, folders and projects form the tree that IAM and billing follow, so a project is the natural grouping. Labels are free-text key-values for billing; tags are IAM-governed key-values that Organization Policy and firewall rules can condition on.
pros: Projects and folders give a tree that IAM and billing inherit down
Tags are IAM-governed and usable in Organization Policy and firewall rules
Labels flow into the billing export for allocation
cons: Two systems, labels and tags, with different powers confuse newcomers
Labels are free text with no enforcement
Moving a resource between projects is usually impossible, moving a project is easy

azure.name: Azure Resource Manager
azure.note: Every resource lives in exactly one resource group, a lifecycle container whose deletion removes its contents, under a subscription and management group. Tags apply at any level, inherit only by policy, and Azure Resource Graph searches everything with KQL.
pros: Resource groups give every resource a lifecycle container
Tags on subscriptions and groups can be inherited by policy
Resource Graph searches everything with KQL, free
cons: Tags do not inherit by default, you need an Azure Policy modify effect
A resource lives in one group and moving it has service-specific limits
Resource group region is metadata only, which surprises people

rows.pick: Interchangeable in purpose. The one structural choice is Azure's resource group, a lifecycle container the others lack; on AWS and Google the equivalent boundary is an account or a project, which is heavier.
rows.gotcha: The same failure everywhere: without enforcement at creation time, cost allocation is guesswork within a quarter. Enforcement is tag policies plus service control policies on AWS, Organization Policy on Google tags (not labels), and Azure Policy deny or modify effects on Azure.

rows.plain: A queue is a to-do tray between programs: one drops work in, another picks it up later, so neither has to wait for the other.

aws.name: Amazon SQS
aws.note: Fully managed queues in two flavours: Standard for near-unlimited throughput with at-least-once delivery, FIFO for strict ordering and exactly-once processing. Billed per million requests, with long polling and dead-letter queues built in.
pros: Per-request pricing with a free tier, no brokers or capacity to size
Native trigger for Lambda, EventBridge Pipes and Step Functions
FIFO queues now reach high throughput without giving up ordering
cons: Standard queues can duplicate and reorder messages, so consumers must be idempotent
Message body capped at 1 MiB since August 2025; larger payloads detour through S3
Retention tops out at 14 days and there is no replay of consumed messages

gcp.name: Pub/Sub
gcp.note: One global service: a pull subscription behaves as a queue, a push subscription as a topic fan-out, and Cloud Tasks covers rate-limited dispatch to a single HTTP handler. Pub/Sub Lite is closed to new customers and turns down in January 2027.
pros: Global by default, publishers and subscribers need not share a region
Topic retention up to 31 days with seek lets consumers replay history
Exactly-once delivery and ordering keys without a separate queue type
cons: Priced by data volume with a 1 KB minimum, so tiny messages bill as bigger ones
Ordering holds per ordering key within a region, not across the whole topic
No true point-to-point semantics, every subscription receives every message

azure.name: Azure Service Bus
azure.note: Enterprise broker with queues, topics, sessions for ordering, transactions, duplicate detection and dead-lettering, spoken over AMQP. Azure Queue Storage is the cheap and simple alternative: millions of messages, no ordering, no transactions, priced as storage.
pros: Sessions, transactions and scheduled delivery give real ordered, transactional messaging
Standard AMQP clients, and JMS on Premium, ease lifts from on-premises brokers
Queue Storage sits alongside for pennies when you only need decoupling
cons: Premium tier is billed per messaging unit per hour, running even when idle
Standard tier caps messages at 256 KB and throttles under bursty load
Two products to choose between, and Queue Storage lacks ordering and dead-lettering

rows.pick: Interchangeable for plain decoupling. Pick Service Bus when you need sessions, transactions or JMS compatibility; Pub/Sub when publishers and consumers span regions; SQS when the consumer is Lambda and you want the smallest possible bill.
rows.gotcha: Azure separates the two: Service Bus for ordered, transactional queues, Queue Storage for cheap and simple. Google Cloud uses one Pub/Sub for both push and pull, so a queue there fans out to every subscription, and SQS Standard may deliver twice or out of order.

rows.plain: One program announces something once and every interested program hears it, like a noticeboard rather than a pile of individual letters.

aws.name: Amazon SNS
aws.note: Topic fan-out to many subscribers: SQS queues, Lambda, HTTP endpoints and Firehose, plus SMS, email and mobile push. Delivery is fire-and-forget, so durability comes from pairing a topic with SQS queues, the standard fan-out pattern.
pros: Millions of messages a second with per-request pricing and no infrastructure
Filter policies on attributes and payload cut consumer noise
Doubles as the SMS, email and mobile push channel
cons: Standard topics keep nothing; only FIFO topics archive and replay, so durability means SQS per consumer
FIFO topics deliver only to SQS queues, not straight to Lambda or HTTP
SMS and international push costs vary sharply by country

gcp.name: Pub/Sub
gcp.note: The same Pub/Sub topic that acts as a queue does fan-out: add a subscription per consumer, push to an HTTP endpoint or Cloud Run, or export straight to BigQuery and Cloud Storage. Eventarc rides on top for Google-sourced events.
pros: One service for queue and topic, one fewer distinction to manage
Export subscriptions land data in BigQuery or Cloud Storage with no code
Topic retention and seek let a late subscriber replay history
cons: Volume pricing with a 1 KB minimum per request penalises tiny unbatched notifications
Push endpoints must be public HTTPS or Cloud Run, with authentication you configure
No SMS, email or mobile push, those need Firebase or a partner

azure.name: Azure Service Bus
azure.note: Service Bus topics fan out to durable subscriptions with SQL-style filters and per-subscription dead-letter queues, so each consumer owns a queue. Azure Event Grid is the lighter, reactive alternative and is covered in the event bus row.
pros: Each subscription is a durable queue, slow consumers do not lose messages
Rich filters and actions rewrite or route messages inside the broker
Same connection, client and security model as your Service Bus queues
cons: Up to 2,000 subscriptions per topic and modest throughput on the Standard tier
Premium namespaces bill per messaging unit whether or not traffic flows
Not a notification service, SMS and push live in Communication Services and Notification Hubs

rows.pick: Pick SNS when you also need SMS or mobile push from the same topic; Service Bus topics when every subscriber must receive every message even after an outage; Pub/Sub when you would rather not run two messaging products.
rows.gotcha: Standard SNS topics keep nothing: a missed delivery is gone without an SQS queue behind each subscriber; only FIFO topics archive and replay. Service Bus and Pub/Sub subscriptions buffer unread messages for days, so an SNS design moved to Azure buys storage nobody planned for.

rows.plain: A switchboard that listens for things happening, such as a file arriving or an order changing, and routes each event to whichever programs asked for it.

aws.name: Amazon EventBridge
aws.note: Serverless bus receiving events from AWS services, your code and SaaS partners, with content-based rules, a schema registry, archive and replay. The same product carries Scheduler for cron jobs and Pipes for point-to-point connections with filtering and enrichment.
pros: Pattern matching on the event body, not just headers or attributes
Archive and replay events to rebuild state or test a new consumer
Dozens of SaaS partner sources such as Salesforce, Zendesk and Stripe deliver natively
cons: Per-event pricing plus cross-account and API destination charges add up at volume
At-least-once delivery with no ordering, consumers must tolerate duplicates
Latency of roughly around 130 milliseconds at the 99th percentile, wrong for request-response paths

gcp.name: Eventarc
gcp.note: Routes events from Google services (via Cloud Audit Logs), Pub/Sub topics and a few third-party sources to Cloud Run, GKE, Workflows and functions in CloudEvents format. Eventarc Advanced adds a bus with enrichment and transformation for larger estates.
pros: Every Google service emits audit-log events, so almost anything is a trigger without code
Standard CloudEvents envelope and direct delivery into Cloud Run
Standard Eventarc adds no charge of its own beyond the Pub/Sub and logging underneath
cons: Filters match on event attributes, payload-based routing needs Advanced or your own code
Audit-log triggers depend on Data Access logging being switched on, which costs
Far fewer SaaS sources than EventBridge or Event Grid

azure.name: Azure Event Grid
azure.note: Two shapes in one service: system and custom topics with push delivery to Functions, webhooks, Service Bus and Event Hubs, plus namespaces adding pull delivery and an MQTT broker for devices. Subscriptions filter on subject, type and data fields.
pros: Advanced filters on payload fields and 24-hour retry with dead-lettering to storage
MQTT broker in the same product connects devices without IoT Hub
Cheap per-million-operations pricing with a monthly free allowance
cons: Two models, Basic topics and namespaces, with different features and limits
Webhook endpoints must pass a validation handshake, which trips up third-party receivers
Partner events are limited to Microsoft and a short partner list

rows.pick: EventBridge is the obvious choice when SaaS sources and replay matter; Event Grid when devices publish over MQTT or you already route Azure system events; Eventarc when the whole estate is Cloud Run and audit-log triggers are enough.
rows.gotcha: Eventarc is thinner than its twins: it routes Google events into Cloud Run and filters on CloudEvents attributes, not payload, so content routing you did in EventBridge rules moves into Pub/Sub and code. None of the three orders events; design consumers to be idempotent.

rows.plain: A recipe runner for multi-step jobs: call this, wait for that, retry on failure, branch on the answer, without writing the plumbing yourself.

aws.name: AWS Step Functions
aws.note: State machines defined in JSON with two modes: Standard for long-running, exactly-once workflows up to a year, Express for high-volume, short-lived ones. Direct integrations reach over 200 AWS services without Lambda glue; Simple Workflow Service is the legacy predecessor.
pros: Optimised integrations call DynamoDB, SQS, Bedrock and 200 more services directly
Visual designer, per-step history and built-in retry and error handling
Distributed Map fans out to thousands of parallel items over S3 data
cons: Standard bills per state transition, chatty loops become expensive quickly
Execution history capped at 25,000 events, long loops need child workflows
Amazon States Language is proprietary, nothing else runs your definitions

gcp.name: Workflows
gcp.note: YAML or JSON steps that call HTTP APIs and Google connectors, with retries, parallel branches and callbacks, and executions up to a year. It is lighter than Step Functions, with fewer native integrations; Cloud Composer handles data pipelines instead.
pros: Priced per step with a generous free tier, cheap for low-volume flows
Any HTTP API is a first-class step, with authenticated Google calls built in
Callbacks pause for human approval or external events at no charge while waiting
cons: Fewer connectors than Step Functions, so more steps are hand-written HTTP calls
No visual designer worth the name, everything is authored in YAML
Memory per execution is small, large payloads must round-trip through Cloud Storage

azure.name: Azure Logic Apps
azure.note: Low-code designer with more than 1,400 connectors, in Consumption (per action) and Standard (single-tenant, on the Functions runtime) plans. Code-first teams use Durable Functions inside Azure Functions for orchestrations, fan-out and human-interaction patterns.
pros: Largest connector library, especially into Microsoft 365, Dynamics and SAP
Durable Functions gives orchestration in C#, JavaScript or Python with no DSL
Standard plan can run on Arc-enabled Kubernetes or your own Functions plan
cons: Consumption bills every action and connector call, including polling triggers that fire empty
Enterprise connectors such as SAP and IBM MQ cost extra per call
Two products and two plans to choose between before writing the first step

rows.pick: Choose Step Functions when the steps are mostly AWS services and you want direct integrations. Choose Logic Apps when the steps are Microsoft 365 or SaaS connectors. Workflows fits small teams already on Cloud Run calling HTTP services.
rows.gotcha: Pricing units differ: Step Functions Standard charges per state transition, Workflows per step, Logic Apps Consumption per action including empty polls, so one loop costs pennies in one and pounds in another. Step Functions' integrations are broader, so ports away from it grow HTTP glue.

rows.plain: Ready-made adapters that move data between business apps such as Salesforce, SAP and ServiceNow and your cloud, configured by clicking rather than coding.

aws.name: Amazon AppFlow
aws.note: No-code data flows that copy records between SaaS applications and S3, Redshift or other SaaS, on schedule, on event or on demand, with mapping and filtering. It moves data in bulk; it is not a general workflow or process tool.
pros: Per-flow-run pricing plus data processed, nothing to host
Writes straight into S3 and Redshift with field mapping and masking
Private connectivity to Salesforce and other SaaS via PrivateLink
cons: Around 80 native connectors, small next to Logic Apps; others need the custom connector SDK
Batch and event copies only, no branching logic or human steps
Few destinations beyond AWS storage and a handful of SaaS targets

gcp.name: Application Integration
gcp.note: Low-code integration platform with triggers, mapping and branching, using Integration Connectors as its catalogue of prebuilt SaaS and enterprise adapters, including Salesforce, SAP and ServiceNow. It sits in the Apigee family and shares its enterprise pricing.
pros: Proper iPaaS: triggers, data mapping, conditional branching, error handling and retries
Connectors expose SaaS objects as APIs reusable from Apigee and Workflows
Event-based triggers from Pub/Sub, Salesforce and Cloud Scheduler
cons: Connector nodes bill per node-hour, an idle connector still costs
Younger and less proven than Logic Apps, fewer community examples
Regional availability lags other Google services

azure.name: Azure Logic Apps
azure.note: The same Logic Apps as the workflow row, seen as a connector catalogue: more than 1,400 managed connectors covering Microsoft 365, Dynamics, SAP, Salesforce, ServiceNow and mainframes. Power Automate reuses the same connectors for business users.
pros: By far the largest connector catalogue, especially for Microsoft's own products
Connectors shared with Power Automate and Copilot Studio, one skill set
Standard plan gives fixed pricing and virtual network access for high volume
cons: Per-action Consumption pricing surprises when polling connectors fire every minute
Enterprise connectors (SAP, IBM MQ, IBM 3270) carry a premium per call
Connector versioning and deprecations can break flows on Microsoft's schedule

rows.pick: Logic Apps is the obvious pick when Microsoft 365, Dynamics or SAP is at one end. AppFlow is a data copier, fine for Salesforce to S3 and little else. Application Integration suits Apigee shops wanting process logic around their APIs.
rows.gotcha: The word connector hides three shapes: AppFlow copies records in bulk, Application Integration runs a process, Logic Apps does both and bills each step. Moving from AppFlow's flat per-run price to Logic Apps Consumption turns a nightly sync into thousands of billed actions.

rows.plain: The reception desk for your APIs: one door where callers sign in, get rate-limited, read documentation and are counted, while backends stay hidden.

aws.name: Amazon API Gateway
aws.note: A runtime front door for REST, HTTP and WebSocket APIs with keys, usage plans, throttling and Lambda integration, priced per request. Developer portals and products are recent built-in additions, while monetisation still needs partner tooling such as Kong, Tyk or Apigee.
pros: Pay per request, scales to zero, tight Lambda and IAM integration
WebSocket APIs and private APIs inside a VPC out of the box
Mature, in every region, and understood by every AWS team
cons: Portal and products are recent additions; monetisation still needs partner or self-built tooling
REST APIs cost roughly 3.5 times HTTP APIs, and integration timeouts default to 29 seconds
Per-request billing gets expensive at very high, steady volumes

gcp.name: Apigee
gcp.note: Enterprise API management with proxies, policies, developer portal, products, monetisation and analytics, sold pay-as-you-go or by subscription, with Apigee hybrid running the gateway in your own Kubernetes. The separate API Gateway is a lightweight OpenAPI front for serverless backends.
pros: Complete lifecycle: portal, products, monetisation, analytics and MCP exposure for agents
Apigee hybrid places the runtime on-premises or in other clouds
Long enterprise track record, strong policy engine for legacy and SOAP traffic
cons: Subscription tiers are priced for enterprises; pay-as-you-go bills per call, environment and analytics
Heavyweight to learn, proxies, policies and environments are a discipline in themselves
Two products with similar names, and API Gateway is not a small Apigee

azure.name: Azure API Management
azure.note: Gateway, developer portal, products, subscriptions, policies and analytics in one service, in tiers from Consumption (per call) to Premium (multi-region, virtual network). A self-hosted gateway runs on your Kubernetes, and AI gateway policies meter tokens and route across model deployments.
pros: Whole lifecycle in one product with a hosted developer portal included
AI gateway policies: token limits, semantic caching and load balancing across models
Consumption tier scales to zero, Premium offers multi-region and private networking
cons: Premium units cost thousands a month each and take a long time to provision or scale
Policy XML is powerful but verbose and hard to test outside the service
Consumption tier drops the developer portal and virtual network integration

rows.pick: For a real API programme with a portal, products and partner onboarding, choose Azure API Management on Azure or Apigee where hybrid gateways and monetisation matter. Amazon API Gateway is a front door for Lambda, not a programme.
rows.gotcha: API Gateway means two things: AWS's per-request runtime and Google's OpenAPI front for serverless, and neither is a management suite. Apigee is a much heavier enterprise product with monetisation and analytics. AWS now has a built-in portal; budget for partner tooling if you need monetisation.

rows.plain: An alarm clock for the cloud: run this job every night at two, or once next Tuesday, without keeping a server awake to watch the clock.

aws.name: Amazon EventBridge Scheduler
aws.note: Part of Amazon EventBridge: cron, rate or one-off schedules that invoke over 6,000 API operations across more than 270 AWS services directly, with time zones, flexible windows and retries. Millions of schedules per account make it usable for per-customer reminders, not just nightly jobs.
pros: Targets any AWS API directly, no Lambda needed to start a job
One-time schedules at scale suit per-user reminders and deferred actions
Time-zone aware with daylight saving handled for you
cons: Billed per invocation after a free tier, millions of schedules cost real money
Older EventBridge rule-based schedules still exist, two ways to do one thing
Minimum granularity is one minute, no sub-minute timers

gcp.name: Cloud Scheduler
gcp.note: Managed cron that fires an HTTP endpoint, a Pub/Sub topic or an App Engine target on a Unix cron expression, with retries and time zones. Cloud Tasks handles one-off deferred work; Scheduler is for recurring jobs.
pros: Familiar Unix cron syntax with time-zone support
Three free jobs per account, then about ten cents per job per month
Authenticated calls into Cloud Run and functions with a service account
cons: Per-job monthly pricing, so thousands of one-off schedules belong in Cloud Tasks instead
Regional resource with a quota per project, not a global scheduler
Only HTTP, Pub/Sub and App Engine targets, no direct API invocation

azure.name: Azure Functions
azure.note: There is no standalone scheduler since Azure Scheduler retired: a timer trigger inside Azure Functions runs code on a cron expression, Logic Apps offers a Recurrence trigger for low-code flows, and Container Apps jobs run containers on a schedule.
pros: No extra service or bill, the schedule lives with the code it runs
Logic Apps Recurrence and Container Apps jobs cover low-code and container cases
Durable Functions timers handle long waits and per-entity reminders
cons: Schedules live in code and app settings, there is no central view of every job
Each schedule is a function, thousands of one-off timers need Durable Functions or a queue
Flex Consumption and Premium plans bill for always-ready instances even between runs

rows.pick: EventBridge Scheduler is the obvious choice for huge numbers of one-off schedules, such as a reminder per customer. Cloud Scheduler and Functions timers are fine for a handful of recurring jobs. Azure has no scheduler product, which surprises AWS teams.
rows.gotcha: Pricing shape differs: EventBridge Scheduler bills per invocation, Cloud Scheduler per job per month, Azure per function execution. Ten thousand customer reminders are cheap on EventBridge, ruinous as ten thousand Cloud Scheduler jobs, and on Azure become a Durable Functions or queue design.

rows.plain: A hosted copy of the traditional message brokers older applications already speak to, so you can move them without rewriting how they talk.

aws.name: Amazon MQ
aws.note: Managed Apache ActiveMQ Classic and RabbitMQ brokers on instance-hour pricing, in active-standby or cluster deployments, speaking AMQP, MQTT, STOMP, OpenWire and JMS. Meant for lifting broker-dependent applications; new designs are pointed at SQS and SNS.
pros: Existing JMS, AMQP and MQTT clients connect unchanged
Multi-zone active-standby with managed patching and version upgrades
RabbitMQ option for teams already using it, with quorum queues
cons: Instance-hour and storage billing, the broker runs whether busy or idle
Throughput and connection limits follow instance size, scaling means a bigger box
ActiveMQ Classic only, no Artemis, and upgrades force maintenance windows

gcp.none: No managed ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ; teams use Pub/Sub, Managed Service for Apache Kafka, or a partner broker from the Marketplace running on GKE.

azure.name: Azure Service Bus
azure.note: Not a hosted open-source broker but a native one speaking AMQP 1.0, with JMS 2.0 on the Premium tier, so many enterprise clients connect with a connection string change. RabbitMQ and ActiveMQ on Azure are partner or self-run on AKS.
pros: AMQP and JMS clients migrate with configuration rather than code changes
Fully managed with no broker instances to size or patch
Sessions, transactions and dead-lettering match what enterprise brokers offered
cons: JMS needs the Premium tier, billed per messaging unit per hour
Not wire-compatible with RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ specifics such as exchanges or virtual topics
No MQTT or STOMP, those go to Event Grid or IoT Hub

rows.pick: Amazon MQ is the obvious choice when an application is welded to ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ and must move as-is. Service Bus suits AMQP and JMS clients willing to change a connection string. On Google Cloud you refactor to Pub/Sub.
rows.gotcha: Only AWS sells the actual open-source brokers. Service Bus is compatible at the protocol level, not the product level, so RabbitMQ exchanges and ActiveMQ virtual topics need redesign. Google Cloud has nothing here, and a broker on GKE becomes your operational burden overnight.

rows.plain: Trading partners still swap orders and invoices as rigid electronic documents; this translates them into formats your systems understand, and back again.

aws.name: AWS B2B Data Interchange
aws.note: Managed translation of X12 EDI documents to and from JSON and XML, with partner profiles, transformation mappings and event-driven processing into S3. AWS Transfer Family provides the AS2 and SFTP endpoints that partners actually connect to.
pros: Pay per document transformed, no EDI software licence or server
Generative mapping assistance shortens the classic weeks-long mapping work
Pairs with Transfer Family AS2 for end-to-end partner onboarding on AWS
cons: X12 first; check coverage for EDIFACT and other standards before committing
Young service from 2023, with limited regions and partner integrations
Business workflow around acknowledgements and exceptions lives in your code

gcp.none: No first-party EDI translator; teams run a partner product such as Boomi or Cleo, or a self-hosted translator on GKE.

azure.name: Azure Logic Apps
azure.note: The Enterprise Integration Pack inside Logic Apps: an integration account holds trading partners, agreements, schemas and maps for X12, EDIFACT, AS2 and RosettaNet, with connectors that encode, decode and acknowledge documents inside a workflow.
pros: Broadest standards coverage: X12, EDIFACT, AS2, RosettaNet and flat files
Documents flow straight into the wider Logic Apps connector library
Mature, inherited from BizTalk Server and used by large retailers
cons: Integration account tiers are billed monthly on top of per-action workflow charges
Schemas and maps are authored in Visual Studio tooling, a specialist skill
Partner and agreement limits per tier force upgrades for large trading networks

rows.pick: Logic Apps is the obvious choice for a real trading network with many standards and partners. B2B Data Interchange fits X12-heavy teams already landing files in S3. Google Cloud has nothing native, so a partner product is the answer there.
rows.gotcha: EDI is where cloud-native thinking breaks: partners connect over AS2 and SFTP and expect acknowledgements within hours, so the translator is only part of the job. AWS splits transport (Transfer Family) from translation; Azure bundles both into Logic Apps; on Google Cloud you assemble it.

rows.plain: Keeping thousands of open browser or app connections and pushing updates to them instantly, like live scores or a shared document, without polling.

aws.name: AWS AppSync
aws.note: AppSync Events provides serverless WebSocket pub/sub channels that broadcast to millions of connected clients with authorisation per channel, alongside the original GraphQL subscriptions. Amazon API Gateway WebSocket APIs are the lower-level alternative where you manage connections yourself.
pros: Pay per connection-minute and message, scales to millions of clients
Channel authorisation via Cognito, IAM, API keys or Lambda
Broadcasts from any backend with one HTTP publish call
cons: Events API arrived in 2024, so fewer client libraries and community patterns
Connection-minute billing adds up for always-connected dashboards
AppSync and API Gateway WebSockets overlap, choosing wrong means a rewrite

gcp.none: No managed WebSocket fan-out; teams use Firestore real-time listeners inside apps or run their own Socket.IO servers on Cloud Run.

azure.name: Azure Web PubSub
azure.note: Managed WebSocket service with pub/sub groups, client and server SDKs, and serverless integration with Azure Functions; Azure SignalR Service is the sibling for ASP.NET Core SignalR apps. Units are billed per day with a connection and message allowance.
pros: Standard WebSocket and MQTT clients supported, no proprietary protocol required
SignalR Service gives .NET teams the familiar hub programming model
Unit-based pricing is predictable for steady connection counts
cons: Units are billed daily whether or not clients connect
Per-unit limits (1,000 connections, a million messages a day) make scaling a staircase
Two overlapping products, Web PubSub and SignalR Service, with different client SDKs

rows.pick: Azure Web PubSub or SignalR Service is the obvious pick for .NET teams and steady connection counts. AppSync Events wins for bursty, pay-per-use fan-out to mobile apps on Cognito. On Google Cloud you lean on Firestore or run your own.
rows.gotcha: Only two clouds sell this. Google Cloud's answer is Firestore listeners, a database feature, so a chat or live-dashboard design ported from Azure lands in a different product category. Billing also inverts: AppSync per connection-minute, Web PubSub per unit-day, which changes idle-heavy economics.

rows.plain: Taking inventory of the old data centre, which servers exist, what talks to what, and what it would cost to run them in the cloud.

aws.name: Migration Evaluator
aws.note: Agentless collector and business-case tool that inventories servers, right-sizes them and prices the AWS estate. AWS Application Discovery Service and AWS Migration Hub closed to new customers in late 2025, and AWS Transform now carries discovery and wave planning for VMware estates.
pros: Free of charge, with an AWS-produced business case at the end
Agentless collector, no software installed on every server
Feeds AWS Transform, which plans waves and drives the migration
cons: Migration Hub's single tracking view is gone for new customers
Business case leans on AWS pricing assumptions and sales involvement
Dependency mapping is weaker than Azure Migrate or Migration Center now the agents are retired

gcp.name: Migration Center
gcp.note: Unified discovery, assessment and planning console: agentless discovery of VMware and other estates, cost estimates comparing on-premises to Compute Engine, and fit assessments for VMs, databases and containers. It replaced the older StratoZone tooling.
pros: Free, with total cost estimates and right-sizing built in
Assesses fit for Migrate to Containers and Database Migration Service, not only VMs
Imports inventories from RVTools and other clouds without an agent
cons: Newest of the three, dependency mapping and application grouping still maturing
Business case is Google-centric with fewer licensing scenarios than Azure Migrate
Targets Compute Engine, GKE and Cloud SQL; VMware Engine and bare-metal paths are thinner

azure.name: Azure Migrate
azure.note: One hub for discovery, dependency mapping, assessment and business case across servers, databases, web apps and desktops, then the migration itself. An appliance discovers VMware, Hyper-V and physical servers without agents, with software inventory and SQL and .NET assessment.
pros: Discovery, assessment, business case and migration in a single free service
Deep licensing view: Hybrid Benefit, SQL Server and Windows savings are priced in
Application and code assessment for .NET and Java modernisation
cons: An appliance per source environment, with its own upkeep and connectivity rules
Assessment limits per project and appliance need care in very large estates
Business case assumes Azure pricing and often needs partner tooling for other clouds

rows.pick: Azure Migrate is the obvious choice for a Windows and SQL Server estate, where licensing savings dominate the business case. Migration Center and Migration Evaluator are close for VMware fleets; the choice follows the target cloud rather than tool quality.
rows.gotcha: AWS reshuffled this space: Application Discovery Service and Migration Hub are closed to new customers, so runbooks that name them are stale, and the AWS answer is now Migration Evaluator plus AWS Transform. Azure Migrate and Migration Center remain single, free consoles.

rows.plain: Copying a running server, disk and all, into the cloud in the background, then switching over during a short planned window.

aws.name: AWS Transform MGN
aws.note: Block-level replication of physical, virtual or other-cloud servers into staging instances, with test and cutover launches, wave grouping and post-launch modernisation actions. Renamed from AWS Application Migration Service in June 2026 with the APIs unchanged, now under the AWS Transform umbrella.
pros: Free for 90 days per server, you pay only for staging resources
Continuous replication allows repeated test launches before the real cutover
Post-launch actions apply agents, patches and licensing changes automatically
cons: Agentless mode covers vCenter only; other sources need an agent on each server
Staging volumes and replication servers cost money for the whole replication period
Lift-and-shift only, modernisation is a separate AWS Transform engagement

gcp.name: Migrate to Virtual Machines
gcp.note: Agentless replication from VMware vSphere, AWS and Azure into Compute Engine, with test clones, cutover and right-sizing recommendations, run from the console with no per-server agent. Migrate to Containers converts suitable VMs straight into containers for GKE and Cloud Run.
pros: Agentless for vSphere and cloud sources, one connector per source environment
No charge for the service itself, only the target resources
Sibling Migrate to Containers offers a path beyond lift-and-shift
cons: Physical servers and Hyper-V need a workaround via vSphere or third-party tooling
Replication is snapshot-based, so the cutover data-loss window is minutes not seconds
Smaller ecosystem of partners and runbooks than MGN or Azure Migrate

azure.name: Azure Migrate
azure.note: The Server Migration tool inside Azure Migrate replicates VMware (agentless via the appliance, or agent-based), Hyper-V, physical and other-cloud servers into Azure VMs, with test migrations and cutover. Discovery, assessment and migration share one project and one appliance.
pros: Agentless VMware and Hyper-V replication, no per-server install
Free service, only target storage and compute are billed
Same project as assessment, so waves and right-sizing carry over
cons: Agentless VMware replication has limited concurrency per appliance, large estates need several
Physical and other-cloud servers fall back to the agent-based path with a replication appliance
Large disks and high change rates hit replication limits, forcing agent-based mode

rows.pick: The three do the same block-level lift-and-shift and the choice follows the destination. Azure Migrate is smoothest for Hyper-V; Migrate to Virtual Machines is agentless for vSphere; MGN is the most battle-tested for physical servers with agents.
rows.gotcha: All three copy blocks; none decides whether the VMs should exist. For a VMware estate that cannot be refactored before the data centre lease ends, the VMware-in-cloud services in the compute family are the escape hatch, and these tools become the later second hop.

rows.job: Cloud hardware in your data centre
rows.plain: The provider ships racks or servers into your building, runs them like a small piece of its cloud, and you use them with the same tools.

aws.name: AWS Outposts
aws.note: AWS-owned, installed and maintained racks or small servers in your site, running EC2, EBS, ECS, EKS, RDS and S3 on Outposts with the parent region's APIs. It needs a steady connection to its home region; there is no disconnected mode.
pros: Identical EC2, EBS and EKS APIs, so tooling and skills carry over
AWS installs and maintains racks; you install Outposts servers yourself
Server form factor fits branches and factories without a full rack
cons: One, three or five year commitment on a fixed configuration, capacity cannot flex
Must stay connected to the region, outages degrade or halt control plane operations
Only a subset of services, and pricing is a premium over the region

gcp.name: Google Distributed Cloud
gcp.note: A portfolio, not one box: GDC connected (formerly Distributed Cloud Edge) is Google-managed racks or servers tethered to Google Cloud; GDC air-gapped (formerly Distributed Cloud Hosted) is a fully disconnected sovereign cloud; software-only editions put GKE on your bare metal or VMware.
pros: Air-gapped edition runs with no connection at all, including Gemini models
Software-only editions reuse your existing servers and vSphere
Kubernetes-first, so anything that runs on GKE runs on GDC
cons: Fewer managed services than Outposts or Azure Local, mostly GKE, VMs and data services
Air-gapped deployments are sized and priced for governments and regulated enterprises, not branches
Renamed twice, so documentation and partners still say Edge and Hosted

azure.name: Azure Local
azure.note: Renamed from Azure Stack HCI in November 2024: validated partner hardware you buy, running Azure's hypervisor and storage, managed through Azure Arc, with disconnected operations and low-cost edge devices added. Azure Stack Hub and Azure Stack Edge are the older appliance siblings.
pros: Choice of many hardware vendors and sizes, from two-node edge to large clusters
Managed through Azure Arc like any other Azure resource, with Azure Policy and Monitor
Disconnected operations mode keeps running without the internet
cons: You buy and own the hardware, Microsoft supports the software only
Per-core monthly subscription plus Windows Server and SQL licences on top
Not the full Azure API surface, mainly VMs, AKS and Arc-enabled data services

rows.pick: Outposts when you need the same EC2 and EKS APIs on site and a steady link is guaranteed. Azure Local when you want to pick hardware and already manage through Arc. GDC air-gapped when the site must run disconnected.
rows.gotcha: Ownership differs. Outposts and GDC connected are provider-owned racks you rent; Azure Local is hardware you buy with Microsoft's software on top, and Azure adds Arc to manage what you already own instead of shipping a rack. Only GDC air-gapped and Azure Local run disconnected.

rows.plain: One control panel for machines and Kubernetes clusters wherever they sit, on-premises, at the edge or in a rival cloud.

aws.name: AWS Systems Manager
aws.note: Hybrid activations and the unified node console enrol on-premises, edge and other-cloud machines for inventory, patching, run commands and session access. Amazon EKS hybrid nodes join your own servers to an EKS control plane, and EKS Anywhere runs clusters fully on your hardware.
pros: Patch Manager, Run Command and Session Manager work identically on AWS and elsewhere
Hybrid nodes register free; Session Manager and Run Command bill per session and per invocation
EKS hybrid nodes keep the managed control plane while compute stays on-premises
cons: Sessions and commands on hybrid nodes are metered per use, so chatty automation costs
Servers only, no Arc-style projection of databases or platform services onto other clouds
Agent-based and region-scoped, so a multi-region estate becomes several consoles

gcp.name: Google Kubernetes Engine
gcp.note: Fleet management, Config Sync and Policy Controller are now included in the single GKE tier after GKE Enterprise (earlier Anthos) was dissolved in September 2025, covering attached clusters elsewhere and on-premises GDC software. Plain servers get nothing comparable, VM Manager covers Compute Engine only.
pros: Fleet features included in GKE pricing, no separate Enterprise licence
GitOps configuration and policy across clusters anywhere, including attached EKS and AKS
Same tooling for on-premises GDC software clusters and cloud GKE
cons: Kubernetes only, on-premises servers and VMs get nothing comparable to Arc
GKE on AWS and GKE on Azure end in March 2027, only attached clusters continue
Branding churn (Anthos, GKE Enterprise, GKE) confuses documentation and hiring

azure.name: Azure Arc
azure.note: Projects servers, Kubernetes clusters, SQL Server and Arc-enabled data services from anywhere into Azure Resource Manager, so Azure Policy, Monitor, Defender, Update Manager and role-based access apply to machines in your data centre or in AWS and Google Cloud. Azure Local is built on it.
pros: One control plane over servers, Kubernetes and databases wherever they run
Reaches into the other two clouds, not just your own data centre
Arc-enabled SQL Managed Instance and PostgreSQL run Azure data services on-premises
cons: Arc itself is free but every attached service (Defender, Monitor, SQL) bills per resource
Agent and connectivity requirements, plus Windows Server and SQL licensing implications
The most ambitious surface means the most moving parts to keep patched and connected

rows.pick: Azure Arc is the obvious choice for managing a mixed estate as one, including servers and databases in other clouds. GKE fleets suit Kubernetes-only portfolios. Systems Manager is enough for patching and shell access on a few hundred hybrid servers.
rows.gotcha: Arc is the most ambitious: one control plane over servers, Kubernetes and databases wherever they run, including on the other two clouds, and it manages clusters you already have rather than giving you new ones. Its twins are narrower, so Arc-shaped designs port badly.

rows.plain: Getting decades-old COBOL programs off a leased mainframe: understanding them, rewriting or re-hosting them, and proving the new system produces identical answers.

aws.name: AWS Transform
aws.note: Agentic AI service, generally available since 2025, that analyses, documents and refactors mainframe code, VMware estates, .NET applications and custom code, with human review at each stage. AWS Mainframe Modernization, the managed runtime for re-platformed applications, is closed to new customers.
pros: Agents do code analysis, documentation and refactoring, cutting the assessment phase dramatically
Also covers VMware and .NET, one tool for the whole modernisation portfolio
Human-in-the-loop review and test generation are built in
cons: Young service, transformed code still needs deep testing and specialist partners
Runtime for migrated workloads is now partner or EC2-based since Mainframe Modernization closed
Pricing and outcomes depend on engagement scope, expect a services-heavy project

gcp.name: Dual Run
gcp.note: Runs the mainframe and its cloud replacement side by side on live traffic and compares outputs, proving equivalence before cutover. Mainframe Assessment Tool analyses code and data with Gemini, and Mainframe Connector moves mainframe data into BigQuery and Cloud Storage.
pros: Parallel-run verification is unique and de-risks the cutover decision
Assessment tool uses Gemini to document COBOL and JCL estates
Mainframe Connector unlocks analytics on mainframe data without migrating applications
cons: Dual Run needs the mainframe kept running and licensed for the whole parallel period
Refactoring relies on Google's rewrite tooling and partners, less packaged than AWS Transform
Smaller partner ecosystem for mainframe than the other two clouds

azure.none: No first-party mainframe product; Microsoft relies on partners such as Rocket Software, Kyndryl and Astadia, targeting Azure VMs, AKS and Azure SQL.

rows.pick: AWS Transform when you want a packaged, AI-led path and accept a services-heavy project. Dual Run when the board needs proof of identical results before switching off the mainframe. Azure when a partner such as Kyndryl already runs your estate.
rows.gotcha: The catalogue moved under everyone's feet: AWS Mainframe Modernization is closed to new customers, replaced by AWS Transform's agents plus partner runtimes, and Google's tooling is three products, not one. Nothing here is a service you switch on; each is a multi-year programme with partners.

rows.plain: Tools that take an old application, a virtual machine or a Java codebase, and turn it into containers or refreshed code, with AI doing the grunt work.

aws.name: AWS Transform
aws.note: The same agentic service as the mainframe row, applied to VMware estates (discovery, network conversion, wave planning), .NET Framework to cross-platform .NET porting, and custom code transformations you define. Output is reviewed code and infrastructure plans, not a black-box migration.
pros: Broad scope: VMware, .NET and custom code under one agentic workflow
.NET porting removes Windows licence costs by moving to Linux
Web-based, collaborative workspace where teams review each proposed change
cons: Generated changes still need full regression testing, the agent does not own correctness
Limited to AWS targets, the analysis does not port elsewhere
Custom transformations need well-specified rules, vague intent produces vague code

gcp.name: Migrate to Containers
gcp.note: Converts Linux and Windows VM workloads into container images and Kubernetes manifests for GKE, GKE Autopilot or Cloud Run, extracting the application layer and discarding the operating system. It modernises packaging, not source code; code refactoring is Gemini Code Assist territory.
pros: Free CLI tool, no agents to install; console UI removed May 2024, last release v1.15.0
Gets legacy apps onto GKE or Cloud Run without a rewrite
Fit assessment tells you which VMs are worth containerising
cons: Packaging only, the code inside is unchanged and still legacy
Works best for simple Linux and Windows web apps, not clustered or licensed software
Resulting images need ongoing base-image and dependency maintenance you did not have before

azure.name: Azure Migrate
azure.note: Application and code assessment inside Azure Migrate scans .NET and Java apps for Azure readiness; GitHub Copilot's app modernisation agents then upgrade frameworks and rewrite for Azure targets such as App Service, Container Apps and Azure SQL.
pros: Assessment sits in the same hub as server and database migration
