Copilot agents upgrade Java and .NET versions and fix build errors iteratively
Targets Azure platform services directly, App Service and Container Apps rather than only VMs
cons: Two products, Azure Migrate and GitHub Copilot, with separate licensing
Copilot modernisation needs paid Copilot seats and a developer in the loop
Copilot upgrades cover Java, .NET and C++; Azure migration scenarios only .NET and Java

rows.pick: AWS Transform when the estate is VMware or .NET Framework and AWS is the target. Migrate to Containers when you want VMs into GKE quickly without touching code. Azure Migrate plus Copilot when teams already live in GitHub and .NET.
rows.gotcha: Modernisation means different depths: Migrate to Containers repackages the VM, Copilot rewrites code, AWS Transform does both plus infrastructure planning. Compare like with like, and remember every one outputs code you must test and own; the agent leaves the day it finishes.

rows.job: Provider zones near users or telcos
rows.plain: Small slices of the cloud placed in a city or inside a mobile network so that a game, factory or trading app responds within a few milliseconds.

aws.name: AWS Local Zones
aws.note: AWS-run mini-zones in metro areas without a full region, offering EC2, EBS, some load balancers and databases as an extension of a parent region. AWS Wavelength does the same inside telecom operators' 5G networks for traffic that must stay on the carrier.
pros: Dozens of metros worldwide, deployed as a subnet of your existing VPC
Wavelength reaches single-digit millisecond latency for devices on the carrier's 5G
No hardware to buy or host, AWS runs the facility
cons: Limited instance types and services, priced above the parent region
Wavelength traffic and instance choices are tied to one operator's network
Data transfer between zone and region is billed, so chatty designs pay twice

gcp.name: Google Distributed Cloud connected
gcp.note: Google-managed racks or servers placed at your site or a telecom operator's facility, connected to Google Cloud and running GKE workloads and selected services. Rather than a Google-run metro zone, the hardware sits in a building you or the carrier control.
pros: Google installs and manages the hardware, you keep the site
Built for telecom network functions and factories, with local data residency
Same GKE tooling and fleet management as cloud clusters
cons: You provide space, power and connectivity, unlike a provider-run zone
Kubernetes-centred, with a smaller catalogue of VM and managed services
Minimum footprint and term make it a project, not a subnet

azure.name: Azure Extended Zones
azure.note: Small Microsoft-run footprints in metro areas such as Los Angeles and Perth, offering a subset of Azure services closer to users. General availability began in November 2024.
pros: Microsoft runs the site, so there is no hardware to own
Metro latency instead of a distant region
cons: Very few locations and a small subset of services
Capacity and pricing are decided per zone, so check before designing around one

rows.pick: AWS is the obvious choice for a low-latency footprint without owning a site: Local Zones for a metro, Wavelength for a carrier. Google Distributed Cloud connected suits operators and factories hosting a rack. Azure teams use the nearest region.
rows.gotcha: Compute pushed close to users or into a telco network serves the small set of workloads where tens of milliseconds matter. Shapes differ: AWS runs the zone, Google ships a rack, Azure runs metro Extended Zones as well as regions and Azure Local appliances, so the question is who owns the building.

rows.plain: A full Windows or Linux desktop that lives in the cloud and streams to any laptop or thin client, like renting an office PC you never carry.

aws.name: Amazon WorkSpaces
aws.note: Persistent or pooled desktops billed monthly or hourly, with Windows and Linux bundles; WorkSpaces Core supplies infrastructure for Citrix or Omnissa brokers. PCoIP-based Personal desktops end support on 31 October 2027 and Pools on 31 December 2027, closing to new customers from July 2026.
pros: Hourly billing suits part-time users; monthly suits full-time staff
Bring-your-own Windows licence or use bundled Windows Server desktops
Native to IAM, Directory Service and VPC, no broker to run
cons: Windows client OS needs Microsoft licensing terms that catch teams out
PCoIP-based desktops end support October 2027 and Pools December 2027, forcing a protocol migration
Fewer regions than EC2; latency dictates where users can sit

gcp.none: Google sells no desktop service; teams run Citrix or Omnissa on Compute Engine, or push users to ChromeOS and browser-delivered apps.

azure.name: Azure Virtual Desktop
azure.note: Multi-session Windows 11 desktops and published apps on Azure VMs you size, with Entra ID and Intune management built in. Windows 365 sells the same idea as a fixed-price Cloud PC per user; AVD classic retires in September 2026.
pros: Windows 11 multi-session is exclusive to Azure and cuts per-user cost
Microsoft 365 licences often already include the AVD entitlement
FSLogix profiles and Entra ID make Windows estates feel native
cons: You run the host pools, patching, images and scaling yourself
Consumption billing for VMs and storage is hard to predict
AVD classic retires September 2026; old deployments must move to ARM

rows.pick: Windows-heavy organisations with Microsoft 365 licences pick Azure Virtual Desktop or Windows 365, because multi-session Windows 11 and included entitlements make it cheapest. AWS WorkSpaces wins where the estate is already on AWS or needs Linux desktops.
rows.gotcha: Microsoft licensing decides the design, not the cloud. Windows 11 multi-session runs only on Azure; on AWS you rent Windows Server desktops or bring qualifying licences on dedicated hosts. Google has nothing, so a partner broker on Compute Engine becomes your VDI platform.

rows.plain: Running one desktop programme in the cloud and showing just its window in a browser, so users get the app without a whole remote desktop.

aws.name: Amazon WorkSpaces Applications
aws.note: Streams individual Windows or Linux applications from fleets you image and size, billed per streaming hour plus a monthly Windows user fee. Renamed from AppStream 2.0 in November 2025 and now sits inside the WorkSpaces family.
pros: Elastic fleets scale to zero, so occasional users cost little
App blocks and session scripts package software without golden images
Works with SAML, no client install, any browser
cons: Monthly Windows user fee applies once a user connects, even briefly
Image building and fleet capacity tuning is real operations work
Windows apps need Microsoft licences on top of AWS charges

gcp.none: Cameyo, bought by Google in 2024, streams Windows apps to ChromeOS but is sold outside Google Cloud; teams otherwise use Citrix or Omnissa.

azure.name: Azure Virtual Desktop
azure.note: RemoteApp publishing in Azure Virtual Desktop presents single applications from a multi-session host pool instead of a full desktop. It is a mode of AVD rather than a separate product, so it shares AVD pricing, images and Entra ID setup.
pros: No extra product; the same host pool serves desktops and apps
Multi-session Windows 11 keeps per-app-user cost low
App Attach mounts MSIX, Appx or App-V packages at sign-in without rebuilding images
cons: No scale-to-zero by default; you script autoscale plans yourself
Windows only; Linux apps need a partner or a full VM
Network and profile design for AVD must be done first

rows.pick: Pick WorkSpaces Applications when you need a self-contained, elastic app-streaming service that scales to zero. Pick Azure Virtual Desktop RemoteApp when you already run AVD and just want to publish apps to Windows users.
rows.gotcha: AWS bills a monthly user fee the moment a user streams once, so a wide but shallow user base costs more than the hourly rate suggests. Azure RemoteApp is a feature not a service, so it inherits every AVD dependency, including host pools and FSLogix.

rows.plain: Ready-made login, database, file storage and functions for a phone or web app, so a small team ships without building servers.

aws.name: AWS Amplify
aws.note: A CLI, libraries and console that wire Cognito, AppSync, DynamoDB, S3 and Lambda into a typed backend defined in TypeScript, plus hosting. Amplify Gen 2 leans on CDK, so what you get is real AWS resources you can open in the console.
pros: Everything is ordinary AWS resources you can inspect and extend
Cognito auth and AppSync GraphQL come pre-wired with authorisation rules
Gen 2 sandboxes give each developer an isolated backend
cons: Steeper than Firebase; you meet IAM and CloudFormation quickly
Pay per underlying service, so cost is spread across many bills
Realtime sync exists via AppSync but is less turnkey than Firestore

gcp.name: Firebase
gcp.note: Google's mobile platform: Authentication, Firestore, Cloud Functions, Storage, Cloud Messaging, Crashlytics and Hosting behind one SDK and console. Firebase projects are Google Cloud projects underneath, so Firestore and functions appear in both consoles.
pros: Fastest path from idea to app; generous free Spark tier
Firestore live sync and offline cache are the best in class
Crashlytics, Analytics and Remote Config cover the app lifecycle
cons: Per-read and per-write Firestore pricing surprises chatty apps
Security rules are a separate language teams learn late
Deep coupling to Firebase SDKs makes migration painful

azure.none: App Center retired in March 2025 and Azure Mobile Apps is retired too, replaced by the open-source Community Toolkit Datasync library; teams assemble App Service, Cosmos DB, Entra External ID and Notification Hubs.

rows.pick: Firebase is the obvious choice for a consumer mobile app that needs live sync, push and crash reporting from day one. Amplify wins when the rest of the company runs on AWS and wants the backend as inspectable infrastructure.
rows.gotcha: Firebase hides Google Cloud; Amplify exposes AWS. A Firestore document model and security rules do not translate to DynamoDB and IAM, so switching means rewriting data access, not just the SDK. Customer identity stays separate from workforce identity on all three.

rows.plain: Publishing a website's HTML, scripts and images from a global edge network, with a git push doing the deploy, like a printing press near every reader.

aws.name: AWS Amplify
aws.note: Amplify Hosting builds from a git branch and serves static sites and server-side rendered Next.js through CloudFront, with preview branches and custom domains. The manual pattern of S3 behind CloudFront remains the cheapest for plain static files.
pros: Git-connected builds with per-branch preview URLs
SSR for Next.js, Nuxt and others without managing servers
S3 plus CloudFront costs pennies for low-traffic sites
cons: Build minutes and per-GB serving charges add up on busy sites
Framework support lags the latest Next.js releases
S3 plus CloudFront needs you to wire OAC, caching and invalidations

gcp.name: Firebase Hosting
gcp.note: Serves static assets from Google's edge with one-command deploys, preview channels and rewrites to Cloud Run or functions. Firebase App Hosting adds git-connected builds for Next.js and Angular on Cloud Run; Cloud Storage behind Cloud CDN is the bare option.
pros: Free tier and simple CLI deploys suit small sites
Preview channels per pull request with expiry
App Hosting runs full-stack frameworks on Cloud Run with no servers to manage
cons: A Firebase product, so it sits outside most Google Cloud IaC
Cloud Storage plus Cloud CDN needs a global load balancer with a fixed hourly cost
Bandwidth beyond the free tier is billed per GB

azure.name: Azure Static Web Apps
azure.note: Builds from GitHub or Azure DevOps and serves static front ends globally with an integrated Azure Functions API, staging environments per pull request and free SSL. The Free plan has no SLA; Standard adds custom auth, SLA and larger apps.
pros: Free plan with custom domains and SSL, ideal for small sites
Managed Functions API and built-in auth providers in one resource
Pull-request staging environments out of the box
cons: Storage and bandwidth caps are tight on both plans
Managed Functions are limited; bring-your-own Functions needs Standard
Fewer framework adapters for SSR than Amplify or Firebase

rows.pick: The three are largely interchangeable for a static or Jamstack front end; pick the one attached to your backend cloud. Static Web Apps wins on the free tier, Amplify on SSR breadth, Firebase on developer speed.
rows.gotcha: Edge behaviour differs. CloudFront runs Lambda@Edge and CloudFront Functions at the edge; Cloud CDN attaches to a global load balancer with a fixed hourly charge and no edge compute; Static Web Apps runs its API in one region. Cache invalidation semantics also differ.

rows.plain: Sending a short alert to phones and browsers even when the app is closed, like a doorbell that rings on millions of devices at once.

aws.name: AWS End User Messaging
aws.formerName: Amazon Pinpoint (SMS, push and voice channels)
aws.note: End User Messaging Push sends to APNs, FCM, Baidu and ADM through one API, spun out of Pinpoint in 2024. Amazon SNS mobile push does the same job more simply; Pinpoint's campaign engine ends on 30 October 2026.
pros: Same service handles SMS, voice and WhatsApp, so one integration
SNS mobile push is very cheap for simple broadcast
Sits behind EventBridge and Lambda for event-driven sends
cons: No device SDK; you collect tokens and manage registrations yourself
Pinpoint campaigns, segments and journeys vanish October 2026
Two overlapping AWS options confuse newcomers

gcp.name: Firebase Cloud Messaging
gcp.note: FCM is the delivery channel for Android and the de facto route for web push, with SDKs for iOS, Flutter and Unity too. It is free at any volume and pairs with Firebase Analytics for targeting and open-rate reporting.
pros: Free with no volume limit
Android delivery goes through Google's own channel, so highest reliability
Topics and device groups without you storing tokens
cons: No SMS or email; it is push only
Web and iOS still need the Firebase SDK in your app
Targeting beyond topics needs Firebase Analytics or your own segmentation

azure.name: Azure Notification Hubs
azure.note: A hub that fans one message out to APNs, FCM, WNS and Baidu with tags and templates for personalisation, billed per push in tiers. It has changed little for years and needs the FCM v1 migration completed.
pros: Tag expressions route one send to many audiences
Templates render per-platform payloads server-side
Fixed tiers with free pushes make cost predictable
cons: Feature development has been slow; it feels dated
Registration management and installations API are your responsibility
No analytics; you wire Application Insights yourself

rows.pick: Firebase Cloud Messaging is the obvious choice for any app already using Firebase, and it is free. On AWS or Azure, use the native fan-out service only when you need SMS alongside or a single hub for many platforms.
rows.gotcha: Every cloud still routes Android pushes through FCM and iOS through APNs; the cloud service is only a fan-out layer. AWS teams must leave Pinpoint before October 2026, and FCM's legacy HTTP API is gone, so token and payload code written before 2024 needs revisiting.

rows.plain: Sending sign-up confirmations, receipts and newsletters from your app at scale, and keeping them out of spam folders.

aws.name: Amazon SES
aws.note: High-volume SMTP and API sending with dedicated IPs, Virtual Deliverability Manager, inbound receipt and Mail Manager rules. À la carte pricing stays per thousand with no platform fee; new accounts start on Essentials at 16 cents per thousand, and Pro and Enterprise add monthly fees.
pros: Ten US cents per thousand à la carte with no minimums; Essentials plan is 16 cents
Inbound mail, event publishing and suppression lists built in
Dedicated IPs and warm-up managed for you
cons: Sandbox on new accounts blocks real sending until approved
Templates and campaign tooling are thin compared with marketing platforms
Reputation is your problem; a bad list gets you throttled

gcp.none: Google has no application email service; Gmail is for people. Teams use SendGrid, Mailgun or Postmark, or Workspace SMTP relay for small volumes.

azure.name: Azure Communication Services
azure.note: The Email channel of Azure Communication Services sends transactional mail from Azure-managed or custom domains via API or SMTP, with Entra authentication. It is younger than SES and geared to transactional rather than bulk marketing volume.
pros: One resource also gives you SMS, chat, voice and video
Azure-managed domains let you send in minutes
Entra-based auth and private endpoints fit regulated tenants
cons: Newer, with fewer deliverability tools than SES
Default sending limits are low and raised by support ticket
Costs per message and per MB of data, higher than SES

rows.pick: Amazon SES is the obvious choice for high-volume transactional or bulk email on price and maturity. Choose Azure Communication Services Email when you want one Azure resource for email, SMS and calling. On Google Cloud, bring a third party.
rows.gotcha: Deliverability is not portable. Sender reputation, dedicated IP warm-up, DKIM and SPF records are all bound to the provider, so moving clouds means a fresh warm-up and weeks of degraded inbox placement. Plan the migration like a domain move.

rows.plain: Adding text messages, phone calls or video meetings to your own app through an API, instead of building a phone company.

aws.name: AWS End User Messaging
aws.formerName: Amazon Pinpoint (SMS, push and voice channels)
aws.note: End User Messaging covers SMS, voice, push and WhatsApp with number provisioning and country registration. Amazon Chime SDK adds embedded voice, video, PSTN calling and meetings; the Chime meetings app itself closed in February 2026.
pros: Chime SDK meetings scale to large sessions with media pipelines
Ten-digit long code and toll-free registration handled in-console
Pay per message or per minute, no platform fee
cons: Two services, two consoles, two SDKs to learn
SMS country coverage and sender ID rules vary widely
Chime SDK is lower level than Communication Services; expect WebRTC work

gcp.none: Google offers no SMS, voice or video API; teams use Twilio or Vonage, or Google Meet add-ons for meetings inside Workspace.

azure.name: Azure Communication Services
azure.note: One service for SMS, voice, video, chat and email with the same media stack as Teams, plus Teams interoperability and Call Automation for IVR. Numbers, calling plans and Direct Routing come from the same resource.
pros: Teams interop lets your app join and host Teams meetings
Call Automation builds IVR and contact flows with AI
Chat, SMS, calling and email under one billing line
cons: Phone number availability is limited to a set of countries
Video features follow Teams; less control than raw WebRTC
Per-minute and per-message pricing is higher than the cheapest carriers

rows.pick: Azure Communication Services is the obvious choice when the app must interoperate with Microsoft Teams or reuse its calling stack. AWS wins for programmatic SMS at scale with Chime SDK for custom video. Google Cloud users go to Twilio.
rows.gotcha: Telephony regulation, not the API, drives design. Sender registration, ten-digit long codes and alphanumeric sender IDs differ per country and per provider, so a messaging stack built on one cloud's number inventory rarely lifts to another without re-registering everything.

rows.plain: The software behind a customer helpline: routing calls and chats to agents, scripts, recordings and increasingly AI that answers first.

aws.name: Amazon Connect Customer
aws.note: Omnichannel contact centre with pay-per-use telephony, Contact Lens analytics, Customer Profiles, cases and generative agent assistance. Renamed Amazon Connect Customer in April 2026 alongside new Connect Decisions, Talent and Health products that reuse the platform.
pros: No seats: pay per minute and per message, so seasonal spikes cost less
Telephony, IVR, chat, analytics and forecasting in one console
Lex, Bedrock and Lambda plug in for self-service and custom logic
cons: Flows and routing need in-house builders or a partner
Per-use pricing gets expensive for always-busy agents
Renaming and product sprawl in 2026 complicate documentation

gcp.name: Contact Center AI Platform (Google Cloud CCaaS)
gcp.note: A full cloud contact centre with routing and telephony, sold alongside Agent Assist, Customer Experience Insights and Conversational Agents for virtual agents. Google's stronger play has been the AI layer, which also plugs into Genesys, Avaya and others.
pros: Agent Assist and virtual agents lead on conversational AI quality
AI layer works with third-party contact centre platforms too
Customer Experience Insights mines every conversation for topics and quality
cons: Platform is younger and less common than Connect or Genesys
Telephony footprint and country coverage is narrower
Frequent renames (CCAI, Customer Engagement Suite, CCaaS) confuse buyers

azure.name: Dynamics 365 Contact Center
azure.note: Microsoft's Copilot-first contact centre sold under Dynamics 365, using Azure Communication Services for voice and Copilot Studio for self-service bots. It is licensed per agent and integrates with Teams and any CRM, not just Dynamics.
pros: Per-agent licensing is predictable for steady teams
Copilot summaries and knowledge come from the Microsoft 365 estate
Works with Salesforce and ServiceNow, not only Dynamics CRM
cons: A Dynamics product, so procurement and admin sit outside Azure
Newer than Connect; fewer reference deployments
Voice depends on Communication Services number coverage

rows.pick: Amazon Connect Customer is the obvious choice for a variable or seasonal centre because you pay per use. Dynamics 365 Contact Center suits Microsoft 365 shops with steady seats. Google CCaaS and Agent Assist win when AI quality matters most.
rows.gotcha: Pricing models are opposite: AWS bills per minute, Microsoft per agent seat, so the same centre can cost double on the wrong model. Google's AI layer is platform-agnostic, while Connect and Dynamics tie AI to their own routing. Telephony numbers rarely port cleanly.

rows.plain: Map tiles, address search, routes and geofences your app calls over an API, like renting the atlas and the sat-nav together.

aws.name: Amazon Location Service
aws.note: Maps, places, routing, geofencing and device tracking using Esri, HERE, Grab and Open Data providers under AWS terms and billing. The 2024 standalone APIs simplified pricing, and tracking data stays inside your AWS account.
pros: Provider data under AWS terms, so no separate contract
Trackers and geofences integrate with EventBridge for alerts
Cheaper than Google Maps for high-volume geocoding
cons: Map detail, Street View and Places richness trail Google
Fewer client SDK features and community examples
Terms restrict caching and storing some provider results

gcp.name: Google Maps Platform
gcp.note: The consumer Google Maps data as APIs: Maps, Routes, Places, Street View, Environment and Address Validation, billed per request with free monthly usage per SKU. It is billed through Google Cloud projects but under Maps Platform terms.
pros: Best-in-class map data, Places and Street View coverage
Free monthly usage on each SKU covers small apps
SDKs for web, Android, iOS and Flutter with a huge community
cons: Per-request prices rise sharply beyond the free usage
Terms forbid storing most results or using them with non-Google maps
The 2025 move from a flat credit to per-SKU tiers forced re-budgeting

azure.name: Azure Maps
azure.note: Maps, search, routing, weather, time zones and geofencing with data from TomTom and others, billed per transaction with Entra and RBAC controls. Bing Maps for Enterprise is winding down and points customers here.
pros: Weather and time zone APIs are unusual and useful
Entra ID authentication instead of API keys
Cheaper than Google Maps at high volume
cons: Coverage and Places detail are weaker than Google
Creator indoor maps was retired, narrowing the roadmap
Smaller developer community and fewer libraries

rows.pick: Google Maps Platform is the obvious choice when users will look at the map or search places, because data quality shows. Location Service and Azure Maps win for back-end geocoding, routing and geofencing at volume where terms and cost matter.
rows.gotcha: Licensing, not APIs, is the trap. Google forbids caching results or displaying its data on other maps, while AWS and Azure terms differ by data provider. A design that stores geocodes or mixes providers can be legal on one cloud and a breach on another.

rows.plain: Building simple internal apps and forms from spreadsheets and connectors with little or no programming, so business teams ship their own tools.

aws.name: Amazon Honeycode
aws.note: Honeycode was a no-code spreadsheet-style app builder launched in 2020 and shut down on 29 February 2024. AWS now points builders to Amplify for front ends and to partner tools, so there is no first-party low-code product.
pros: Spreadsheet metaphor suited business users
Ran inside AWS with no separate tenant
cons: Retired February 2024 with no direct replacement
Amplify is a developer tool, not a business-user builder
Teams turned to Retool, Appsmith or Power Apps

gcp.name: AppSheet
gcp.note: No-code builder that turns Sheets, BigQuery, Cloud SQL or SQL Server data into mobile and web apps with automations, bundled into many Workspace plans. It leans on Workspace identity, so it fits Google-first organisations best.
pros: Included in Workspace Enterprise plans; often already paid for
Generates offline-capable mobile apps automatically
Connects to BigQuery and Cloud SQL as well as Sheets
cons: Weak for complex UI or workflows; hits limits quickly
Governance and lifecycle tooling is thin
Per-user licensing outside Workspace bundles is not cheap

azure.name: Power Apps
azure.note: Microsoft's low-code platform with canvas and model-driven apps over Dataverse, hundreds of connectors and Copilot generation, licensed per user or per app through Microsoft 365. It is sold as Power Platform rather than Azure but runs on Azure and integrates with it.
pros: Largest connector catalogue and deepest Microsoft 365 integration
Dataverse gives governed data with security roles
Managed environments and CoE kit for governance at scale
cons: Licensing tiers and premium connectors are notoriously confusing
Dataverse capacity and API limits bill separately
A Power Platform tenant, not an Azure resource, so separate admin

rows.pick: Power Apps is the obvious choice for organisations on Microsoft 365, because identity, data and licensing are already there. AppSheet fits Workspace shops with spreadsheet-driven needs. AWS has no offering, so teams use third-party builders.
rows.gotcha: These are productivity-suite products, not cloud services: they bill per user through Microsoft 365 or Workspace and are governed by that tenant's admins, not your cloud account. Apps built on Dataverse or Sheets do not migrate; only the data does.

rows.plain: Letting staff or contractors open internal or SaaS websites through a browser the company controls, so data never lands on an unmanaged device.

aws.name: Amazon WorkSpaces Secure Browser
aws.note: A managed remote Chromium browser streamed from AWS with SAML sign-in, URL and clipboard controls and session logging, billed monthly per active user. Renamed from WorkSpaces Web in 2024 and useful for contractors who never get a desktop.
pros: No client software; users open a link and authenticate
Data-loss controls on clipboard, print and downloads
Cheaper than a full WorkSpaces desktop per user
cons: Monthly active-user fee applies after a single session
Pixel streaming adds latency for heavy web apps
Available in fewer regions than WorkSpaces

gcp.name: Chrome Enterprise Premium
gcp.note: Zero-trust access and data protection delivered through the managed Chrome browser and Identity-Aware Proxy rather than pixel streaming, with per-user licensing. Sensitive apps get context-aware access, DLP and threat protection without a remote browser.
pros: Uses the browser the user already has; no streaming latency
Context-aware access with device posture from Chrome
Covers SaaS and internal apps behind Identity-Aware Proxy
cons: Not isolation: content still renders on the device
Per-user licence plus Chrome management overhead
Unmanaged devices get a reduced experience

azure.none: Microsoft covers this with Entra Internet Access and Edge for Business, sold outside Azure; teams needing true isolation publish Edge through Azure Virtual Desktop.

rows.pick: WorkSpaces Secure Browser is the obvious choice for contractors on unmanaged devices who need isolation. Chrome Enterprise Premium suits Google-first organisations with managed Chrome fleets. Azure users lean on Entra and Edge or publish a browser from AVD.
rows.gotcha: AWS isolates by streaming pixels; Google secures the local browser; Microsoft does both through Entra and AVD. A security policy that says browser isolation means one thing on AWS and something weaker on GCP, so write the requirement in outcomes, not product names.

rows.plain: The always-on doorway that millions of small devices report to: a broker, like a post office that receives every device's messages, checks who sent them and hands them on to your systems.

aws.name: AWS IoT Core
aws.note: MQTT, HTTPS and LoRaWAN broker with per-device X.509 identity, device shadows, rules engine and fleet indexing; Device Management and Device Defender add onboarding and auditing. IoT Analytics, IoT Events and 1-Click have retired and FleetWise is closed to new customers.
pros: Pay per message and connection minute, no hub tiers
Rules engine routes straight to Kinesis, S3, Lambda and Timestream
Largest ecosystem of certified hardware and ExpressLink modules
cons: Shrinking add-on portfolio means more DIY around the core broker
Message pricing punishes chatty devices with small payloads
Basic Ingest and topic design require care to control cost

gcp.name: Cloud IoT Core
gcp.note: Cloud IoT Core was Google's managed MQTT and HTTP device gateway, shut down in August 2023. Google now points customers to partner brokers such as ClearBlade, EMQX and HiveMQ from the Marketplace, feeding Pub/Sub.
pros: Fed telemetry directly into Pub/Sub and BigQuery
Partner brokers today still land data in Pub/Sub, so analytics is unchanged
cons: Gone since August 2023; nothing first-party replaces it
Partner brokers mean a second vendor contract and support path
Device identity and fleet management are now your own design

azure.name: Azure IoT Hub
azure.note: Bi-directional device hub with device twins, direct methods, Device Provisioning Service and per-unit tiers sized by daily messages. IoT Central wraps it as an application platform and IoT Operations is the newer Arc-based industrial route; Time Series Insights retired in 2025.
pros: Device twins and direct methods make command-and-control simple
Provisioning Service handles zero-touch onboarding at scale
Defender for IoT and Data Explorer are natural neighbours
cons: Tiered units billed per hub, so quiet fleets pay for capacity
Two overlapping stories, IoT Hub and IoT Operations, blur the roadmap
Message size quotas make large payloads expensive

rows.pick: AWS IoT Core is the default for a new device fleet: widest hardware support, per-use pricing and the most complete surrounding services. Azure IoT Hub suits Windows-oriented OT estates and Arc-managed sites. Google Cloud needs a partner broker.
rows.gotcha: Only two clouds still run a first-party device broker. Google exited in 2023, so a design that assumes managed MQTT does not port to GCP without a partner. Pricing also inverts: AWS charges per message, Azure per hub unit, so one fleet can favour either.

rows.plain: Software that runs on a gateway or factory server so devices keep working, filtering and reacting locally when the internet link is slow or down.

aws.name: AWS IoT Greengrass
aws.note: Open-source edge runtime that deploys components, Lambda functions, ML models and stream managers to gateways, with local MQTT and cloud sync. Greengrass v2 is current; v1 reaches end of support in October 2026.
pros: Component model with public catalogue and private components
Runs on anything from Raspberry Pi to industrial PCs
Deploys and monitors fleets from IoT Core with no extra fee
cons: v1 estates must migrate before October 2026
Edge hardware, OS patching and networking remain yours
Local ML and stream management need careful sizing

gcp.name: Google Distributed Cloud connected
gcp.note: Google-managed racks and servers placed at your site or a telco edge, running GKE and selected services with connectivity back to Google Cloud. It is hardware plus Kubernetes rather than a device-level agent, so device logic runs as containers.
pros: Google operates the hardware and the Kubernetes layer
Same GKE tooling on-site and in region
Air-gapped variant exists for sovereign or disconnected sites
cons: Rack-scale commitment, not a free agent for a gateway
Costly and slow to procure compared with software runtimes
No first-party device broker to pair with, so partner MQTT again

azure.name: Azure IoT Edge
azure.note: Container-based runtime that pushes modules, Stream Analytics jobs and ML to Linux or Windows devices managed through IoT Hub. Azure IoT Operations is the newer Arc-enabled stack with an MQTT broker and dataflows for industrial sites running Kubernetes.
pros: Modules are plain containers; any language works
IoT Operations brings Arc management and a local MQTT broker
Offline operation with store-and-forward built in
cons: Two runtimes, IoT Edge and IoT Operations, with different management models
IoT Operations needs Kubernetes on the edge; heavier than IoT Edge
Windows support for IoT Edge is via EFLOW, a Linux VM

rows.pick: Greengrass is the obvious pick for constrained gateways and mixed hardware. Azure IoT Operations wins for factory sites already running Arc-enabled Kubernetes. Google Distributed Cloud connected is a different animal: choose it when you want Google to own edge racks.
rows.gotcha: The word edge means three sizes here: Greengrass is an agent on a gateway, IoT Edge or IoT Operations is containers on a device or small cluster, and Google Distributed Cloud connected is a managed rack, like Outposts or Azure Local. Compare like with like.

rows.plain: A live software model of a building, plant or machine that mirrors real sensor data, so you can see and simulate the physical thing.

aws.name: AWS IoT TwinMaker
aws.note: Builds entity graphs of equipment and spaces, connects them to SiteWise, Timestream, S3 or your own data via connectors, and renders 3D scenes in Grafana dashboards. Pay per entity and query, plus scene storage.
pros: Connectors let the twin read data where it lives, no copying
3D scene composer and Grafana plugin included
Pairs tightly with IoT SiteWise for industrial hierarchies
cons: Limited regions and modest adoption
Scenes and dashboards need front-end effort
Graph query language is proprietary

gcp.none: Google has no twin service; teams model twins in BigQuery or Spanner Graph, or use Siemens, Bentley and other partner platforms.

azure.name: Azure Digital Twins
azure.note: Graph of twins defined in the open DTDL modelling language, updated from IoT Hub or any source, queried with a SQL-like language and streamed out via Event Grid or Event Hubs. Time-series history lands in Azure Data Explorer.
pros: DTDL is an open modelling language with industry ontologies
Event routing makes the twin a hub for downstream apps
Data history to Data Explorer gives strong time-series queries
cons: No 3D or visualisation layer; bring your own
Per-operation and per-message billing is hard to forecast
Modelling discipline is essential or the graph decays

rows.pick: Azure Digital Twins is the obvious choice for buildings and campuses because of DTDL ontologies and Microsoft's partner ecosystem. TwinMaker wins for industrial plants already using SiteWise and wanting 3D dashboards quickly. Google needs a partner.
rows.gotcha: Neither twin store is the system of record; both are graphs pointing at time-series data elsewhere. TwinMaker reads in place through connectors while Azure Digital Twins expects events pushed in, so the data pipeline shape, not the modelling, dominates a migration.

rows.plain: Turning uploaded or live video into the many sizes and formats screens need, then packaging it so millions can watch smoothly.

aws.name: AWS Elemental MediaConvert
aws.note: File-based transcoding billed per output minute, part of a full broadcast chain: MediaLive for live encoding, MediaPackage for origin and DRM, MediaTailor for ads, MediaConnect for transport and Interactive Video Service for low-latency live. Elastic Transcoder and MediaStore closed in November 2025.
pros: Broadcast-grade features: captions, HDR, Dolby, DRM, ad markers
Complete chain from contribution to playback under one vendor
Per-minute pricing with reserved queues for steady workloads
cons: Many services to assemble; expect a media engineer
Costs stack across encode, origin, CDN and ad insertion
Elastic Transcoder users had to re-platform in 2025

gcp.name: Transcoder API
gcp.note: Serverless file transcoding into HLS and DASH with per-minute billing, alongside Live Stream API for live channels and Video Stitcher API for ad insertion. Media CDN delivers at scale; there is no first-party DRM key service, so partners fill that gap.
pros: Simple API, no fleets or channels to size
Media CDN uses the YouTube delivery footprint
Cheap for straightforward adaptive bitrate outputs
cons: Narrower feature set than Elemental; fewer codecs and broadcast controls
No first-party DRM or packaging origin
Smaller media partner ecosystem

azure.name: Azure Media Services
azure.note: Azure Media Services provided encoding, streaming origin, DRM and Video Indexer until it retired on 30 June 2024. Microsoft points customers to Azure AI Video Indexer for insights and to partner encoders and streaming platforms on the Marketplace.
pros: Bundled encode, origin and DRM in one resource
Video Indexer survived as a separate AI service
cons: Retired June 2024; nothing first-party replaces encoding or streaming
Migration means a partner platform plus Azure Storage and Front Door
Existing pipelines had to be rebuilt within a short window

rows.pick: AWS Elemental is the obvious choice for anything broadcast-like or needing DRM, live and ad insertion together. Transcoder API suits simple upload-and-play workloads. Azure has left the market, so pair partners with Blob Storage and Front Door.
rows.gotcha: Media pipelines are not portable. Azure retired its whole media stack in 2024 and AWS retired Elastic Transcoder in 2025, so favour standard outputs (HLS, DASH, CMAF) and keep orchestration code separate from the vendor's job definitions.

rows.plain: Running and scaling the servers that host multiplayer matches around the world, then putting players into the right one quickly.

aws.name: Amazon GameLift Servers
aws.note: Dedicated server fleets on EC2 or containers with FlexMatch matchmaking, queues and spot-based cost savings, plus Anywhere mode for your own hardware. Renamed from Amazon GameLift in March 2025 when GameLift Streams launched.
pros: FlexMatch matchmaking and global queues included
Spot fleets and Anywhere mode cut hosting cost
Server SDK for Unreal, Unity and C++
cons: Server SDK integration is invasive and version-sensitive
Pay for EC2 plus GameLift duration; idle fleets cost
Anywhere and container fleets are newer and less documented

gcp.none: Game Servers was retired in 2023; Google co-maintains the open-source Agones and Open Match, which teams run on GKE.

azure.name: Azure PlayFab
azure.note: PlayFab Multiplayer Servers host Windows or Linux containers with dynamic standby and regional scaling, alongside PlayFab's player accounts, economy, matchmaking and LiveOps services. Billing is by server hours and tiers of the PlayFab platform.
pros: Backend-as-a-service for players, economy and analytics, not just servers
Dynamic standby scales ahead of demand
Free tier and Microsoft-owned studios prove it at scale
cons: A gaming brand with its own portal and billing, loosely tied to Azure
Less control over infrastructure than GameLift or Agones
Feature velocity has slowed since 2023

rows.pick: GameLift Servers is the obvious choice when you want control over fleets and mature matchmaking. PlayFab wins when you want the whole backend, accounts and economy included. On Google Cloud you run Agones yourself, which suits Kubernetes-fluent studios.
rows.gotcha: Portability lives in the open source layer. Agones runs anywhere Kubernetes runs, including EKS and AKS, while GameLift and PlayFab server SDKs lock game code to one platform. Studios that expect to switch publishers often choose Agones for that reason alone.

rows.plain: Renting the always-on computers that keep a copy of a blockchain, so your app can read and write to it without hosting nodes yourself.

aws.name: Amazon Managed Blockchain
aws.note: Managed Hyperledger Fabric networks for private consortia plus access to Ethereum and Bitcoin through dedicated nodes or serverless Access endpoints, billed hourly per node and per request. QLDB, the centralised ledger database, closed in July 2025.
pros: Only one of the three offering managed permissioned Fabric networks
Serverless Access endpoints avoid running nodes at all
Bitcoin and Ethereum support with token and query APIs
cons: Hourly node pricing is steep for small experiments
Chain coverage is narrow compared with specialist RPC providers
QLDB retirement shows AWS appetite for ledgers is limited

gcp.name: Blockchain Node Engine
gcp.note: Fully managed Ethereum nodes with private endpoints, alongside Blockchain RPC (preview, Ethereum only) for public JSON-RPC endpoints and Blockchain Analytics datasets in BigQuery. Google leans on data and Web3 developer tooling rather than private consortium chains.
pros: Blockchain RPC (preview, Ethereum only) offers a free tier for public chain reads
BigQuery public datasets make on-chain analytics trivial
Nodes get Google's network and security defaults
cons: No permissioned Fabric or consortium networking
Supported chains are a short list
Node hourly costs rival running your own on Compute Engine

azure.none: Azure Blockchain Service retired in 2021. Teams run nodes on VMs or use Azure confidential ledger, a tamper-proof ledger in hardware enclaves, for audit trails.

rows.pick: Managed Blockchain is the obvious choice for a private Hyperledger Fabric consortium. Blockchain Node Engine or Blockchain RPC suits public chain access with analytics in BigQuery. Azure users needing tamper-evidence usually want confidential ledger, not a blockchain.
rows.gotcha: Most enterprise blockchain projects since 2021 have quietly become ledger or database problems. Azure exited, AWS retired QLDB and Google focuses on public chains, so validate that you need decentralisation before designing around any managed node service.

rows.plain: Renting time on experimental quantum processors and simulators through the cloud, like booking a slot on a rare scientific instrument.

aws.name: Amazon Braket
aws.note: Pay-per-shot access to hardware from IonQ, IQM, Rigetti and others plus managed simulators and Hybrid Jobs for variational algorithms, with a Python SDK and PennyLane support. Notebooks and results live in your AWS account.
pros: Multiple hardware modalities under one SDK and bill
Hybrid Jobs run classical and quantum steps together
Free simulator hours on the free tier
cons: Per-shot and per-task pricing makes big experiments costly
Device availability windows and queues slow iteration
Vendor line-up changes as providers come and go

gcp.none: Google's quantum work with Cirq and Willow is research, not a rentable service; teams use Braket, Azure Quantum or vendor clouds directly.

azure.name: Azure Quantum
azure.note: Access to Quantinuum, IonQ, Rigetti and other hardware, the Q# language and QDK, resource estimation and the Elements chemistry tooling, with credits for new users. Microsoft's own Majorana research feeds the roadmap but is not a rentable device.
pros: Q# and resource estimator suit long-horizon algorithm research
Quantinuum access is a differentiator
Chemistry and materials tooling for scientific users
cons: Provider pricing is opaque and varies per machine
Q# ecosystem is smaller than Qiskit or Cirq
Marketing about topological qubits outruns available hardware

rows.pick: Braket for Python-first teams wanting the widest hardware list and hybrid jobs; Azure Quantum for Q# users, Quantinuum access and resource estimation. Google Cloud offers nothing rentable, so researchers there use vendor portals.
rows.gotcha: You are buying access, not a cloud service. Hardware vendors set prices, queues and calibration, and the same IonQ machine appears on both AWS and Azure, so cloud choice affects tooling and billing far more than the physics. Expect providers to change yearly.

rows.plain: Renting antennas that talk to your satellites as they pass overhead, so downlinked data lands straight in the cloud without building dishes.

aws.name: AWS Ground Station
aws.note: Per-minute scheduling of AWS-owned antennas in several regions with data delivered to S3 or EC2 in the same region, supporting narrowband and wideband contacts. It is the only hyperscaler ground station still operating.
pros: Pay per contact minute, no antenna capital
Data lands in S3 next to processing and ML services
Agent for wideband downlink to your own pipelines
cons: Limited antenna sites constrain pass opportunities
Onboarding requires licensing and AWS review per satellite
Sole remaining vendor means no competitive pressure on price

gcp.none: Google never sold a ground station; operators use KSAT, Viasat or other networks and land data in Cloud Storage.

azure.name: Azure Orbital Ground Station
azure.note: Azure Orbital Ground Station scheduled Microsoft and partner antennas with data delivered into Azure until it retired on 18 December 2024 and the antennas were sold. Microsoft now points space customers to partner networks feeding Azure Storage.
pros: Partner antenna network gave wide coverage while it ran
Integrated with Azure networking for data delivery
cons: Retired December 2024; no first-party replacement
Customers had to move to partner networks quickly
Earth observation work on Azure now starts from storage, not antennas

rows.pick: AWS Ground Station is the only choice among the three, so pick it when your satellite and licensing fit its sites, otherwise contract a commercial ground station network and deliver into whichever cloud runs your processing.
rows.gotcha: The market shrank to one. Any architecture that assumed ground station as a service is portable was wrong by 2025; keep the downlink contract separate from the processing cloud and treat the antenna provider as a partner, not a cloud feature.

rows.plain: Storing and exchanging patient records and medical images in the standard formats hospitals use, with the privacy controls regulators demand.

aws.name: AWS HealthLake
aws.note: HIPAA-eligible FHIR R4 store with SQL and natural-language processing over clinical text, alongside HealthImaging for DICOM at scale, HealthScribe for ambient clinical notes and HealthOmics for genomics. Amazon Connect Health added agentic patient workflows in 2026.
pros: Separate purpose-built services for FHIR, imaging, omics and notes
HealthImaging cuts DICOM storage cost with lossless compression
Analytics via Athena, Quick and SageMaker without export
cons: Four services means four bills and integration work
HealthLake per-store hourly charge even when idle
No first-party HL7v2 conversion; you build interfaces

gcp.name: Cloud Healthcare API
gcp.note: One API for FHIR, HL7v2 and DICOM stores with de-identification, BigQuery streaming and Pub/Sub notifications, plus Healthcare Data Engine to harmonise records into a longitudinal FHIR view. Priced per request and per GB stored.
pros: FHIR, HL7v2 and DICOM in one service and one IAM model
Streams to BigQuery for analytics with de-identification built in
Healthcare Data Engine does the hard record harmonisation
cons: Cloud Life Sciences genomics pipelines were retired in 2025
Fewer clinical AI add-ons than AWS
Regional availability for healthcare stores is limited

azure.name: Azure Health Data Services
azure.note: Managed FHIR, DICOM and De-identification services in one workspace with Entra authentication, export to Data Lake and Fabric analytics; the MedTech device-ingestion service is deprecated, support ending 3 May 2028. Azure API for FHIR retires on 30 September 2026 and must migrate here.
pros: De-identification service ships alongside FHIR and DICOM; MedTech device ingestion is deprecated
Workspace groups FHIR and DICOM under one identity and network boundary
Fabric and Power BI reach clinical data without custom pipelines
cons: API for FHIR retirement forces migrations by September 2026
Health Insights AI models retired in December 2025
Imaging analytics is thinner than AWS HealthImaging

rows.pick: The three are close for a FHIR store. Google wins when HL7v2 feeds and BigQuery analytics dominate, AWS when imaging, genomics or ambient documentation is the point, Azure when the hospital already lives in Microsoft 365 and Fabric.
rows.gotcha: FHIR is standard; the stores are not. Search parameters, bulk export, versioning and de-identification differ, and AWS splits imaging into a separate service. Azure API for FHIR shuts on 30 September 2026, so any inherited Azure design must be checked first.

rows.plain: Analysing satellite imagery and map data at planetary scale to answer questions like where crops are failing or how a coastline moved.

aws.name: Amazon SageMaker AI
aws.note: SageMaker AI geospatial capabilities give notebooks, prebuilt earth-observation jobs and map visualisation over Sentinel-2 and Landsat data held in the open data registry on S3. It is a feature inside the ML platform rather than a standalone service. In maintenance and closed to new customers since 30 July 2026.
pros: Open data on S3 avoids egress and sits next to compute
Prebuilt jobs for cloud masking, band math and land cover
Any SageMaker AI model can consume the outputs
cons: Geospatial features live in one region and in Studio, not as an API
Imagery catalogue is narrower than Earth Engine's
Heavy machinery for a team that only needs raster queries

gcp.name: Earth Engine
gcp.note: Planetary-scale analysis over a multi-petabyte catalogue of satellite and climate data with Python and JavaScript APIs, sold commercially through Google Cloud with BigQuery integration. BigQuery geography functions cover vector geospatial analytics.
pros: Largest ready-analysed imagery catalogue anywhere
Server-side computation; no downloading terabytes
BigQuery geospatial and Earth Engine share a project and billing
cons: Commercial pricing is per compute unit hour and can surprise
Proprietary API; notebooks do not port to other clouds
Exporting large results is slow and quota-bound

azure.name: Microsoft Planetary Computer Pro
azure.note: Enterprise geospatial data management that catalogues your own imagery with STAC, serves tiles and connects to Fabric and Foundry for analytics and AI; generally available since June 2026. The public Planetary Computer catalogue remains for open datasets.
pros: STAC-native catalogue works with open-source tooling
Bring your own imagery and serve it to Fabric, Power BI and AI
Open datasets remain free to access
cons: Young service with a thinner analysis layer than Earth Engine
Compute is bring-your-own via Fabric or Foundry
Regional availability is limited at launch

rows.pick: Earth Engine is the obvious choice for scientific or agricultural analysis of public imagery. Planetary Computer Pro wins when the organisation owns its imagery and reports in Fabric. SageMaker AI geospatial suits AWS-based ML teams building models on earth-observation inputs.
rows.gotcha: Earth Engine is a compute engine with its own language; the other two are catalogues you bring compute to. Moving an Earth Engine workflow means re-implementing algorithms, not re-pointing a bucket. Check licence terms too: some catalogue imagery is research-only.

rows.plain: Testing robot software in a cloud-hosted virtual world before loading it on real hardware, like a flight simulator for robots.

aws.name: AWS RoboMaker
aws.note: RoboMaker ran ROS simulation jobs and fleet deployment in the cloud from 2018 until support ended on 10 September 2025; IoT RoboRunner closed in March 2024 and SimSpace Weaver on 20 May 2026. AWS now suggests containerised simulators on Batch or EKS.
pros: Managed Gazebo and ROS environments without workstation GPUs
WorldForge generated randomised indoor test worlds
cons: Retired September 2025 with no first-party successor
Fleet deployment moved to Greengrass and plain containers
Users rebuilt pipelines on Batch, EKS or Isaac Sim

gcp.none: Google never offered a robotics simulation service; Intrinsic is a separate Alphabet company. Teams run Gazebo or Isaac Sim on GKE or GPU VMs.

azure.none: Microsoft never shipped a managed robotics simulator; ROS on Windows was discontinued. Teams run Isaac Sim or Gazebo on GPU VMs or AKS.

rows.pick: None of the three sells robotics simulation any more, so the choice is which cloud gives you cheap GPU capacity and container orchestration for Isaac Sim or Gazebo. That usually means whichever cloud already hosts your data and ML.
rows.gotcha: AWS RoboMaker's retirement in 2025 is the lesson: niche managed services in this space have a short life. Build simulation on containers and standard robotics stacks so the cloud is interchangeable, and treat GPU VM availability as the real differentiator.

rows.plain: Running a game or 3D experience on cloud GPUs and streaming the video to any phone or browser, so players need no console or download.

aws.name: Amazon GameLift Streams
aws.note: Streams Windows and Linux game builds from GPU fleets to browsers via WebRTC with per-stream-hour pricing and a web SDK, launched in March 2025. It targets trials, demos and instant play rather than replacing a consumer cloud gaming service.
pros: No client install; a web SDK embeds the stream
Per-stream-hour billing with always-on or on-demand capacity
Existing builds upload with little modification
cons: GPU stream hours are expensive for long sessions
Region list and GPU classes are limited
New in 2025; ecosystem and tooling are thin

gcp.name: Immersive Stream for XR
gcp.note: Streamed Unreal Engine 3D and augmented-reality experiences from Google GPUs to mobile browsers and AR viewers, aimed at product configurators, retail and marketing rather than full games. It has since been withdrawn, leaving Google Cloud with no first-party game or 3D streaming service.
pros: Unreal projects deploy with minimal changes
Works on mobile browsers with AR placement
Concurrency-based capacity is easy to budget
cons: Unreal only; no Unity or native builds
Positioned for XR marketing, not multiplayer games
Limited regions and quota by request

azure.none: Xbox Cloud Gaming is a consumer service, not rentable, and Azure Remote Rendering retired in September 2025; teams run Pixel Streaming on GPU VMs.

rows.pick: GameLift Streams is the obvious choice for streaming a finished game build to browsers for trials or instant play. Google has withdrawn Immersive Stream for XR and Azure has nothing first-party, so elsewhere use GPU VMs with Pixel Streaming.
rows.gotcha: Cloud rendering has a poor survival record: Azure Remote Rendering, Spatial Anchors and Object Anchors are gone since 2024 and Google's Immersive Stream for XR has followed. Only GameLift Streams remains live, so keep the streaming layer replaceable and budget GPU hours, which dominate cost.

rows.plain: Collecting readings from factory machines in the languages they speak (OPC UA is the common one), arranging them into a tree of sites, lines and machines, and feeding dashboards.

aws.name: AWS IoT SiteWise
aws.note: Gateways on Greengrass collect OPC UA and Modbus data, an asset model organises it into hierarchies with computed metrics, and SiteWise Monitor gives no-code dashboards. Priced per message, computation and dashboard user; Lookout for Equipment and Monitron, its analytics partners, are winding down.
pros: Asset models and transforms replace custom time-series code
SiteWise Edge processes data on-site during outages
Feeds TwinMaker, Timestream and Quick directly
cons: Pricing has many meters and surprises at scale
Anomaly detection partners Monitron and Lookout are retiring
Dashboards are basic; most sites add Grafana

gcp.name: Manufacturing Data Engine
gcp.note: Ingests and contextualises factory and machine data through partner connectors such as Litmus into BigQuery, with prebuilt data models and Looker dashboards. It is a data platform on top of Pub/Sub, Dataflow and BigQuery rather than a device or edge service.
pros: BigQuery scale for plant-wide analytics and ML
Prebuilt manufacturing data models and Looker blocks
Partner connectors handle the shop-floor protocols
cons: Edge connectivity depends on partners, not Google
Suits analytics more than real-time control or alarms
Smaller install base than SiteWise or Azure IoT Operations

azure.name: Azure IoT Operations
azure.note: Arc-enabled Kubernetes stack for factory sites with an MQTT broker, OPC UA connector, dataflows and a unified namespace, sending data to Event Hubs, Fabric Real-Time Intelligence and Data Explorer. Azure Digital Twins models the plant on top.
pros: Open protocols (MQTT, OPC UA) and unified namespace pattern
Fabric Real-Time Intelligence and KQL are strong for time series
Arc manages many sites from one control plane
cons: Requires Kubernetes at the edge, a skill many plants lack
Young service with a fast-changing surface
Time Series Insights retirement means rebuilding older dashboards

rows.pick: SiteWise is the obvious choice for a greenfield plant wanting managed asset models and edge with least Kubernetes. Azure IoT Operations suits sites already on Arc and Fabric. Manufacturing Data Engine wins when the goal is plant-wide analytics in BigQuery.
rows.gotcha: Three different layers wear the same label: SiteWise is asset modelling, IoT Operations is edge messaging, Manufacturing Data Engine is analytics. Time-series storage also differs, with Timestream, BigQuery and Data Explorer, and KQL queries do not port to SQL without rework.
